3.2 Political History of Egypt
Before attempting to analyze the salient features of the Egyptian civilization, let us first
have a look at the history of the Country. The political history of Egypt has been rendered by
the Egyptian priestly writer Manetho of 3rd century B.C. Original text of his ‘Annals’ have not
survived. Abstracts are preserved in later writers accounts. Apart from the ‘Annals’ the spade of

the archaeologists has brought to light many inscriptions and papyrus which contain lists of
Kings and their activities. Their culture is revealed from the many monuments doming at the
two banks of the river Nile.
It has long been customary to divide Egypt’s ancient history into dynasties (periods of
monarchic rule by one family). In all there were thirty-one dynasties, beginning with the legendary
Menes and ending with the dynasty that fell to the Persian invaders in 525 B.C.E. The greatest
were those of the pyramid-building epoch and those of the Empire, about 1500 – 1300 B.C.E.
The dynasties are traditionally grouped under three kingdoms: Old, Middle, and New.

36
3.2.1 Old Kingdom (3100 – 2200 B.C.E.)
The Old Kingdom which extended from Menes to the First Intermediate Period was
ancient Egypt’s most fertile and successful era. During these 900 years, both form and content
were perfected in most of those achievements that made Egypt remarkable: art and architecture,
divine monarchy, religion, social and economic stability, and prosperity. The pharaohs of this
epoch seem to have been unchallenged leaders who enjoyed the willing loyalty of their people.
Later cultural and intellectual developments were almost always only a slight variation or a
deterioration of the pattern established during the Old Kingdom.
3.2.2 Middle Kingdom (2100 – 1650 B.C.E.)
The Middle Kingdom followed the First Intermediate Period with 500 years of political
stability and the continued refinement of the arts and crafts. The country under pharaoh’s rule

was extended up the Nile to the south. Trade with neighbors, including Mesopotamia and
Nubia became more extensive. The condition of the labouring poor in the hundreds of Nileside villages seems to have gradually worsened, however. Religion became more democratic
in its view of who could enter the afterlife, and a small middle class of the officials and merchants
began to make itself apparent.
3.2.3 New Kingdom (1550 – 700 B.C.E.)
The New Kingdom is also called the Empire, although the name really belongs only to
its first three centuries (1550 – 1250). The New Kingdom began after the defeat of the Hyksos
invaders in the 1500s (the Second Intermediate Period). It lasted through the years of imperial
wars against the Hittites and others for control of Mesopotamia, which ended with Egyptian
withdrawal. Then came long centuries of sporadic weakness and resurgence that ended with

Egypt’s permanent conquest by foreigners.
The Empire was an ambitious experiment in which the Egyptians, headed by aggressive
pharaohs, attempted to convert their eastern neighbours to their lifestyle and government theory.
The experiment did not work well, however. Apparently no one else was able to understand
the Egyptian view of life or wanted it to be imposed on them. The Empire did not last because
of both military reversals starting around the time of Pharaoh Akhnaton (1300s B.C.E.) and
internal discontent. By 1100, the pharaoh again ruled only the Nile valley.

37
During their last 300 years of independent existence, the Egyptians were frequently
subjected to foreign invasion, both over the Sinai Desert and from the south by way of the
great river. Before the Persians arrived in 525, others such as the Kushites (Ethiopians) and
the Nubians (Sudanese) had repeatedly invaded – a sure sign that the power of the god-king
over his people was weakening. But even after the Persian conquest, which marked the real
end of ancient Egypt’s existence as an independent state (all the way until the 20th century), the
life of ordinary people in the fields and orchards saw no marked change. Only the person to
whom taxes and rents were paid was different. The cultural forms and beliefs of the inhabitants
were by now so deeply rooted that no foreign overlord could alter them.
3.2.4 Egyptian Government

The government of the Empire was an absolute monarchy. The monarch was called
‘Pharaoh’ – the word derived from the term ‘pero’ meaning the ‘Great house’ from where he
ruled and where all the offices of the government were situated. He had a professional army at
his disposal. He made laws, acted as supreme judge, commanded the army and made offerings
to gods. He had a host of officials to assist him in government. A Council of Elders served as
an advisory body. The nation was divided into more than 50 administrative units, each of
which was under a Governor. The local government was conducted by officials known as
‘monarchs’.
3.3 Social and Economic Developments
The development of agriculture and industry in Egypt led to the establishment of new
social orders, quite different from those that existed in the earlier period. The inhabitants

38
became differentiated into easily distinguishable classes: a leisure class, forming the upper
stratum; and a slave class, making up the lower. The distinction between these two groups
was not sufficient to constitute a caste system, such as existed in India. It was possible for an
individual to pass from the lower class to the other, even as high as the priesthood or to a
leading government position. The rise of the leisure class, undemocratic as it was, did permit
progress in the arts, science, and industry. Slave economy permitted the construction of
pyramids, palaces, irrigation projects, and many other types of structure, which otherwise might
have been impossible.
Generally speaking, the Pharaoh and his court stood at the top of the social ladder. Next
came the landed nobles and the priests, the independent middle class (free landholders, artisans,

and merchants), and at the bottom of the list, the serfs and the slaves. The greatest variation
in status was in the middle class, which changed when economic conditions altered and when
favours and concessions were granted. In time, its members were the most powerful single
group, but they were superseded by professional soldiers about the middle of the 7th century
B.C.
3.3.1 Egypt’s People and their Daily Lives
The Egyptian population was composed overwhelmingly of peasants, who lived in the
villages that crowded along the Nile. Most were free tenant farmers who worked on the estate

39
of a large landholder or government official, who had been granted the land as payment for
services to the crown. Each village followed a similar pattern: the huts were set close together
within, and the fields lay outside. Several adults lived in each hut. Each day the peasants
would go out to work in the fields, care for the irrigation works, or tend the animals. Besides
farmers, many small merchants and craftspeople lived in the villages. But Egypt had no real
cities as in Mesopotamia, where neighbourhoods were filled with specialized wholesale and
retail markets, and dozens of crafts were practiced in hundreds of workshops. Egypt’s successive
capital cities, such as Memphis, Tel el Amarna, and Thebes, were really royal palaces, shrines,
and pleasure grounds for the wealthy, not commercial centres. The common people had

nothing to do with the capitals except for occasional huge labour projects.
As the centuries passed, daily life changed remarkably little. Slavery was originally rare
but increased during the Empire, when professional soldiers became necessary and prisoners
of war became common. As in Mesopotamia, slavery was most often the result of owing debts
to a landlord or committing a serious crime. A kind of serfdom – lifelong restrictions on one’s
physical and social mobility – also came into existence in later Egypt. Free tenant families
were gradually turned into serfs, probably because of debt, and then had to work the land in a
system of sharecropping that ensured that they remained in their village. All in all, however,
the common people of Egypt were better off more of the time than the commoners in almost
any other ancient society.
3.3.2 Position of Women

The position of women was a unique characteristic of Egyptian society. Queen ruled the
country from time to time. The wife was independent in her own right, and her property and
inheritance rights were fully recognized. The wife of a ruler was the keeper of the royal heritage
and transmitted the right of kingship to her children. The position that women held in Egypt
was not equaled in any other early civilization, and not until very recent times has it been
surpassed.
3.3.3 Agriculture
Agriculture was the most important occupation of the Egyptians. The actual work was
done by slaves, but government officials and scientists aided in its development. Government

40
officials carefully supervised the work, decided on the crops to be planted and the fields to be
used, and collected the government’s share (from 10 to 20 per cent) of the grain at harvesting
time. Government engineers and scientists constructed the irrigation projects, worked out
calendars to designate the time for planting crops, and devised methods for measurement of
land. The farm implements used were very crude, yet most of them were not improved upon
for many centuries. The ox and the donkey were the most valuable beasts of burden. Sheep
and goats were driven over the planted fields, in order to tread in the grain and cover it with soil.
The more important crops were wheat, barley, millet, onions, beans, lettuce and peas. Flax
and cotton were grown, the fiber being used to make cloth.
3.3.4 Crafts

Egyptian occupations were not limited to agriculture, although it was the most important
activity. There was a comparatively large industrial population. The construction of pyramids
and palaces necessitated a large group of trained mechanics. Granite quarrying, brick making,
masonry, metalworking, and wood carving were important occupations. Shipbuilding became
an important trade, as well as pottery making and cloth weaving. Linen cloth was made with
such care that it looked like silk to the naked eye. Fine products of Egyptian craftsmen have
been found in tombs; beautifully glazed and painted clay jars, furniture, vessels of gold and
silver, and jewellery, which show that the artisans attained a high level of technique and an
aesthetic appreciation of beauty.
3.3.5 Commerce
In Egypt, commerce never developed as extensively as it did in Mesopotamia, largely

because agriculture was more profitable. It is known, however, that some trade existed. Goods
were carried up and down the Nile; exchange was carried on by barter and, later, by established
weights of gold and silver. Spices, dyes, cosmetics, and perfumed woods were brought from
Arabia and India. Gold, ivory, and Negro slaves were brought from Sudan. As early as 1900
B.C.E., a canal was constructed across the Isthmus of Suez, but it was discarded because of
the difficulties encountered in sailing the Red Sea. Next to agriculture, trade provided the most
important source of royal revenue.

41
Ancient Egyptian Seafaring Ship
3.4 Religion and Eternal Life
Egypt’s religion was almost infinitely polytheistic. At least 3000 separate names of
Gods have been identified in Egyptian writings, many of them the same deities but with different
names over the centuries. Chief among them were the Gods of the sun, Amon and Ra, who
were originally separate but later combined into one being. Other important deities included
Isis, goddess of the Nile and of fertility; Osiris, ruler of the afterlife; their son, Horus, made
visible as the ruling pharaoh; and Ptah, the God of all life on earth.
The Egyptians believed firmly in the afterlife. Originally, it seems to have been viewed as
a possibility only for the upper class, but gradually the afterlife was democratized. By about
1000 B.C.E., most Egyptians apparently believed in a scheme of eternal reward or punishment

for their ka, which had to submit to a moral Last Judgement by Osiris. Ka referred to the lifeessence that could return to life, given the correct preparation, even after the death of the
original physical body.
Mostly, it seems, Egyptians expected reward. They thought of eternity as a sort of endless
procession by the deceased’s ka through the heavens and the Gods’ abodes there. In the
company of friends and family, watched over by the protective and benevolent Gods, the
individual would proceed in a stately circle around the sun forever. There was no need to work
and no suffering. Such was heaven. The notion of hell as a place where the evil paid for the
sins came along in Egypt only during the New Kingdom, when things had begun to go sour.

42
The priests played an important role in Egyptian culture, although they were not as
prominent as in several other civilizations. At times, they seem to have been the power behind
the throne, especially when the King had made himself, unpopular or was unusually weak in
character.
In the reign of the young and inexperienced Akhnaton (1367 – 1350 B.C.E.), the priests
vehemently opposed a unique experiment; the pharaoh’s attempt to change the basic polytheistic
nature of Egyptian religion. Why the young Akhnaton (aided by his beautiful wife Nefertiti)
chose to attempt to introduce a monotheistic (“one-God”) cult of the sun God, newly renamed
Aton, we can only guess. This attempt at monotheism was a great novelty in ancient civilization,
and it was not to be heard of again until the emergence of Judaism, five or six centuries later.

The pharaoh announced that Aton was his heavenly father and that Aton alone was to be
worshiped as the single and universal God of all creation. The priests naturally opposed this
revolutionary change, and as soon as Akhnaton was dead (possibly by poison), they denounced
his ideas and went back to the old ways under the boy-pharaoh Tutankhamen.
3.5 Cultural Achievements
Egyptian art began in the service of religion. All the tombs, temples and sculptures were
made for the purpose of religious rites. Egyptian artists made the work for Eternity. He has
created the temples and statues to last forever. Besides, the wealth of the pharaoh and the
willingness and skill of his people allowed the erection of the most stupendous monuments put
up by any people or government anywhere: the pyramids and temples of the Old Kingdom.

Visitors have marveled at these stone wonders ever since. The Egyptians created their Pyramids,
temples and other buildings in a massive way which can withstand the climatic conditions in
Egypt. Here the architecture was conditioned by the landscape. For the Egyptians artist,
sculpture was merely an architectural decoration.

43
3.5.1 Architecture
The Egyptians invented square-block masonry and the pyramid design in architecture.
These massive constructions were built as burial places for the Pharaohs. The grave was
placed at the bottom of a shaft under the structure. By the use of vaulting and arching, passages
were constructed, so that the soul could move about freely. The Great Pyramid of Khufu
(Cheops), located a few miles outside present-day Cairo, is easily the largest and grandest
commemorative edifice ever built. The pyramids (built between 2600 and 2100 B.C.E.) were
designed as tombs for the living pharaoh and were built while he was still alive. They possessed
immense – and still unknown – religious significance for the Egyptians. Much is still unknown
about the pyramids’ true purposes, but the perfection of their construction and the art of the

burial chambers show Egyptian civilization at its most impressive.
The pyramids were not the only stone monuments erected along the Nile. In the period
around 1300, several warrior-pharaohs celebrated the fame of their empire by erecting enormous
statues of themselves and their favoured gods, and even larger temples in which to put them.
At the Nile sites of Karnak and Tel el Amarna, some of these still stand. Most losses of artistic
and architectural wonders in Egypt have been caused not by time or erosion but by vandalism
and organized tomb and treasure robbers over many centuries. All of the pharaohs’ tombs
discovered to date, except one, have long since been robbed of the burial treasure interred
with the mummy of the dead god-king. The exception is that of the famous King Tutankhamen
– King Tut – whose underground burial chamber was discovered in the early 1920s.
Egypt, Giza Sphinx Egyptian Hieroglyphic

44
Egyptian monarchic statuary is distinguished by the peculiar combination of graceful and
natural lines in association with great dignity and awesomeness. This awe is reinforced by the
art and architecture that surround the great statues, which are designed to impress all onlookers
with the permanence and power of the Egyptian monarchy. The Egyptians’ mastery of stone is
rivaled in Western civilization only by the artistry of the classical Greeks and Romans. And
most of this art was apparently created by artists and architects who did not know the principle
of the wheel and had only primitive tools and what we would consider very clumsy maths and
physics!
3.5.2 Sculpture
Next to architecture, sculpture was the most varied form of artistic expression practiced
by the Egyptians. Permanence and realism were ideals uppermost in the minds of their sculptors

as well as their architects. For making sculptures the Egyptian artist has used coarse and soft
varieties of stones, red granite, black granite, basalt, slate, schist, limestone and Alabaster
which were popular in different periods. Metals like copper and bronze were also used for
making sculptures. Gold was used for making small figures of god. Ivory was also used.
Though the Egyptian artists excelled in their form during the 4th and 5th dynasties, they
were tied to conventions, the dignity of the figure was never lost. In the standing figures the
man is moving forward towards the spectator, in the seated figures he is essentially the master
of the house or estate, in the squatting figures there is a simple but convincingly dignity. Another
great period of Egyptian art was the middle kingdom. During this period the sculptors showed
preference for portraits of men in middle age.

The Sphinx (composite animal with a lion’s body and a falcon’s or ram’s head) was a
portrait of the monarch. In the later years, the ram’s head turned to be the face of the human
with lion’s mare surrounding it. There was some sort of degeneration in the art in the period of
New Kingdom. Portrait sculptures were carved in stone or wood and painted. They are the
earliest portraits in the history of art. They are superb pieces of art.
3.5.3 Other Art Forms
Other art forms in which Egypt excelled included fresco painting (tinting freshly laid plaster
on interior walls), fine ceramics of all sorts and uses, imaginative and finely worked jewellery in
both stones and metals, and miniature sculpture. When upper-class Egyptians died, hundreds

45
of small statues would be buried with their mummified remains. The Egyptians believed that
what had been precious to a person in earthly life would also be desired in the next (a belief
shared by the people of Mesopotamia), so they interred statues and models representing the
person’s earthly family and friends, his or her interests and activities. Music and dance were
also well developed, as we know from their lively portrayal in thousands of paintings and statuary
groups depicting the life of the people of all ranks, from the nobles to the poorest peasants.
Egypt’s artistic heritage is exceeded by that of few, if any, other peoples.
3.5.4 Egyptian Writing and Learning
Egyptian writing developed differently from that of Mesopotamia. Hieroglyphics (literally,
“sacred carvings”) were pictographs that could convey either an idea, such as “man”, or a

phonetic sound, by picturing an object that begins with a strong consonant sound. The word
for owl, for example, began with the consonant “m” sound in spoken Egyptian, so a picture of
an owl could be used to indicate that sound. This beginning of an alphabet was not fully
developed, however. The use of hieroglyphics, which began as far back as 3000 B.C.E., was
confined to a small group of educated persons and gradually faded out after Egypt lost its
independence in the 6th century B.C.E. The complete repertory of 604 hieroglyphic symbols is
now deciphered, enabling the reading of many thousands of ancient inscriptions.
The Egyptians made contributions to culture and learning aside from literature. Learning
was priced very highly. They developed astrology, but scientific astronomy was neglected
except for star tables. In mathematics, they produced decimal system. Embalming gave them

experience in the study of anatomy. They studied diseases and physical injuries, which they
classified and sought means to combat. A papyrus roll, 15 feet long, dating about 1600 B.C.E.,
is one of the oldest treatises on medicine. There was little knowledge of chemistry. The
Egyptians had a government-supervised educational system, in which commerce and politics
were taught. The pupil, after graduation from the temple school, was sent to a more advanced
course conducted by officials of the state treasury. On graduating, he was apprenticed to an
official, who taught him the practical side of the profession. Here was one of the earliest school
systems in history.
To sum up, compared with modern standards, the civilization of the Egyptians may not
be impressive, but one should not forget that they were pioneers, originators of civilization.

They fell short of actually perfecting, but they were practical originators. They set civilization
on its way after eons of struggle. The people of Egypt decidedly raised themselves above

46
barbarians and lived gracefully and joyously. They achieved success in government and law,
in architecture and art, in literature and religion, and in agriculture and industry. They had a
system of writing and a scientific calendar. The Hebrews, the Phoenicians, and the Greeks
were all students of Egyptian culture and borrowed much from it. Writing, science, architecture,
literature and religion were all started on the road of progress by the ancient Egyptians, who
passed on to successive civilizations a priceless heritage.
The reasons for the decline of Egyptian civilization afford interesting speculation. The
failure to perfect a workable political system, adaptable to expansion and imperial administration,
was a contributing factor. Exploitation of the power classes and religious intolerance had a

retarding influence. The priesthood sapped the people of their material wealth and discouraged
independent thinking. Finally, Egypt was confronted with formidable rivals more efficient in the
art of war. Assyrians, Persians, Macedonians and Romans subjected Egypt, in the order
mentioned. Though the country’s political independence was destroyed, her civilization
continued. The city of Alexandria was built by Alexander the Great of Greece at a time when
Egyptian political independence had long been a thing of the past; but the new seaport became
a commercial and intellectual centre of Hellenistic civilization, with a pervasive Greek influence.

47
3.6 Summary
 It is Egypt that provided the basis and stimulus for numerous intellectual achievements
of later centuries.
 The states of Egypt and western Asia were the ancestors of the West.
 The Nile River, with its dependable annual flooding, gave ancient Egypt fertile soil,
economic prosperity, and an optimistic worldview.
 Egypt invented the idea of worshiping the king as a god; eventually, the king became
known as pharaoh.
 The rulers of Egypt were uniquely successful, maintaining two thousand years of prosperity
and isolation from contacts with others, except on their own terms.
 Egyptians believed in a happy afterlife after death, as long as the gods judged that the
dead person had led a life without sin.
 Egypt’s New Kingdom was a great military power that expanded into southwest Asia.

 Our alphabet dates back to an alphabet invented in the 1300 B.C. in the cosmopolitan
city-state of Ugarit, a Meditterranean port in today’s Syria.
 The first alphabet is even earlier (1900 – 1800 B.C.) and has been discovered in Egypt.
 The Egyptians excelled at architecture, such as the pyramids, as well as at sculpture and
medicine, and they invented the solar calendar that we still use (in the revised form)
today.
 The divine kings lost their stature, and the static civilization of the Nile fell under the sway
of once disdained aliens from the east and south.
 The Persian conquest in 525 B.C. completed the decline of the pharaohs’ state into
dependency.

4.1 Introduction
The most fertile part of Mesopotamia is the level plain, about 240 kilometres long, between
the western end of the Persian Gulf and the point at which the great Rivers Tigris and Euphrates
come nearest to each other. This is called the ‘Plain of Shinar’. In ancient times the Persian
Gulf extended much further to the north-west, and the Rivers Tigris and Euphrates did not join
together before flowing into the Persian Gulf, as they now do. Where Basra now stands there
was nothing but the sea. What was the cause of this change? It was due to the great quantity

of fertile mud which the two rivers bring down from the Armenian mountains where they raise.
The whole of the Plain of Shinar has been gradually built up from that mud. That is why it was
so fertile. The land between the Rivers Tigris and Euphrates is called as Mesopotamia. The
Greek word ‘Mespot’ means ‘between two rivers’. It stretches from the mountains of Asia
Minor and Armenian south east to that of the Persian Gulf. The lower part of it was called
Babylonia and its chief city was Babylon.
It consisted of two districts Sumer and Akkad. Sumer was really the delta of the Tigris
and Euphrates, formed by the silt of the two rivers. The civilization which flourished in
Mesopotamia is known as Mesopotamian civilization which has certain unique features. Unlike
Egypt which was comparatively immune from external attacks, Mesopotamia was vulnerable
to foreign invasions so much so her political history is marked by sharper interpretation. This

53
region witnessed the rise and fall of not one, but many civilizations in quick succession. Thus
the Mesopotamian civilization is made up of several strands: Sumerian, Babylonian, Assyrian
and Chaldean – all contributing to its fullness and glory. Four stages in Mesopotamian history
may be noted in the political history of Mesopotamia.
The great influx of various nomadic racial types into the Tigris-Euphrates Valley produced
such a complexity that classification is difficult. The Sumerians were neither pure Mediterranean
nor Alpine in their physical characteristics. Also, they cannot be classified as Semitic – a term
that must be regarded as cultural or linguistic rather than racial. They were stocky in stature
and had oval faces and high, straight noses. The Hittites, the Turanians, and the Kassites,

although not of the same type as the Sumerians, were not Semitic. The most important group
of people that inhabited the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent possessed a Semitic culture.
Racially, they were generally listed as Mediterranean. They came into the valley as nomadic
people from the Arabian Desert. The Babylonians and the Assyrians made the greatest advance
politically and culturally.
4.2 Early History of Mesopotamia
(a) First Stage – Sumer and Akkad
The first stage is that of Sumer and Akkad. The Sumerians ruled over region until about
2300 B.C. when they evolved the earliest of the cultures of region, this region, became Semitic
in language at the time of Sargon of Akkad.

54
(b) Second Stage – Hittites
Other Semitic speaking people, the Amorites, later occupied Babylon and extended their
control over Akkad and Sumer. Their greatest ruler was Hammurabi (1948 B.C. to 1905 B.C.)
their state was called old Babylonia and it marked the second stage. Sedentary agricultural
and urban life made the Amorites or Babylonians, like the Sumerians before them, unfit to
resist the vigorous Hittite newcomers who, about 1900 B.C. descended upon them from the
uplands to the north. The Hittites were followed by Kassites, whose great contribution was to
introduce the practice of extensive horse breeding into Mesopotamia. The Kassites, rude and
comparatively uncivilized, temporarily brought Babylonian civilization to a halt.
(c) Third Stage – Assyria to 606 B.C
The third phase of Tigris-Euphrates civilization was that of Assyria. Its centre was Assur,

a town on the banks of the Tigris occupying a geographically strategic position that could be
easily defended. The Assyrians, who spoke a Semitic language, had moved from the desert of
Arabia into Mesopotamia long before 2000 B.C. they began to extend their rule over the Fertile
Crescent. They seized Damascus (732 B.C), Palestine and even the delta of Lower Egypt.
The important rulers of Assyria were Sargon II (722 B.C. to 705 B.C.), Sennacherib (705 B.C.
to 681 B.C.) and Assurbanipal (668 B.C. to 626 B.C.). But the stern and brutal government of
the Assyrians, the contemptuous disregard of the rights of subjects and the extremely cruel
suppression of revolts produced the bitterest hatred. Chief of their enemies were the Chaldeans
who occupied Akkad and Sumer. Originally they were a Semitic tribe that, like the Akkadians

55
and Assyrians, became powerful politically. In their great hatred of the oppressor, they joined
with the Medes and Persians and stormed, sacked and destroyed capital city of Nineveh,
putting an end to the Assyrian state in 606 B.C.
(d) Fourth Stage – Chaldea 606 B.C. to 539 B.C.
Chaldea or New Babylonia represents the fourth stage of Tigris-Euphrates cultural history.
The ancient city of Babylon became the capital of the New Chaldean Empire, which embraced
Sumer, Akkad, Damascus and Palestine. The Chaldeans flourished for less than a century in
spite of the fact that their state was powerful and their rulers were strong Nebuchadnezzar was
the most important king of Chaldeans. The imperial rule of the Chaldeans was resented to by
their subjects; and finally, in 539 B.C. the empire fell before the attacks of the Medes and
Persians.
4.3 Sumerian Contributions

The Sumerians were a non-Semitic people. They spoke an agglutinative language. They
were the earliest invaders from the mountainous region to the north-east of Mesopotamia.
Sumerian tradition tells the story of a long period of prosperity and a well-developed, orderly
society. They occupied the lower part of Babylonia, the land of Sumer, between 4000 B.C and
3000 B.C. They drained the marshes, dug ditches and constructed embankments and irrigation
canals. They organized themselves into communities developed into Sumerian city-states.
There are records of floods that destroyed cities and accounts of the rebuilding of these cities.
The rise of these city-states marked the beginning of the Sumerian city-states. The clue to
Sumerian civilization was provided by the excavation of ancient Sumerian cities like Ur and
Lagash and the discovery of clay tablets containing Sumerian writing.

4.3.1 Sumerian Political System
The Sumerians drained the marshlands and developed a powerful political system that
lasted almost 1,500 years. The king of a city – patesti, in the Sumerian tongue – was the
“tenant farmer” of the god. His “lease” was renewed each year, during a great festival held in
honour of the God. The city-states were independent carried on war with each other, and in
short, acted like great territorial states. Ur, Umma, Nippur and Lagash were the most important
city-states. Each city-state was governed by a patesti or a priest-king. The Patesti was the
ruler, the commander and the chief priest. He represented the god of the city-state through him

56
the god spoke to the people. The priest-rulers formed long dynasties and according to ancient
accounts ruled an incredible number of years. When one Patesti, conquered neighbouring
cities he called himself lugal’ or ‘great man’. The ruler distributed tracts of land to his chieftains
who in turn rendered military service to the king. The duties of the king included collecting
offerings, supervising farming and workshops, legalizing all business transactions, and defending
the city. The protection of the rights of the individual gave a breadth and balance to Sumerian
culture.
4.3.2 Economic system
Agriculture was the main occupation of the Sumerians, Extensive canals with dams and
dikes were constructed and irrigation provided constant moisture. The Sumerians used a plough
developed from the old Neolithic hoe, but additionally equipped with a sort of tubular seed drill.

The first sickles discovered are of stone, shaped the jaw-bones of animals. The date palm was
a common source of food, and dairying and the rising of bees were important occupations. The
chief animals for pulling carts of chariots were oxen and donkeys, sheep, goats, cows, pig and
dongs were plentiful. The sledge was used for carrying goods and the Sumerians were the
earliest people to use the wheel. The Sumerians also learned the art of weaving. Bone spindles
and needles have been discovered and it is said that both men and women were often tattooed.
The Sumerians also made decorated pottery,
Because the soil of Sumer was alluvial; copper, gold silver and stone had to be imported.
A brisk trade sprang up with strangers to north, east and west and perhaps even beyond the
Persian Gulf. Necessaries were paid for by the superior products of Sumerian industry, such

as woollen and linen cloth, leather and foodstuffs. Business letters, receipts ad bills of sale,
loans and interest were common features of their busy life. This means that in addition to the
large peasant communities, there also developed at an early date an extensive class of
merchants, who made their living by buying and selling foodstuffs and dealing in manufactured
articles.
4.3.3 Law
The Sumerians developed a rule of law partly determined by the idea of a hierarchy
under a city god and his temporal representative. One of the earliest Sumerian rulers, Uru Ka-
Gina of Lagash (C.2370 BC) has left inscriptions describing his efforts to impose respect for
customs which had been perverted and to curb the oppression of the poor by the officials and

57
priests. Nammu, a Sumerian king of the third dynasty of Ur issued the first known ‘code of
laws’.
The only Sumerian laws are on seven fragmentary tablets consisting sixty one sections
or portions of sections. The contents of these laws are very much similar to those of Hammurabi’s
laws. However, their arrangement is haphazard and they seem to be extracts from scholastic
text-books. The Sumerian code of laws was as crude and simple but was not as severe as that
of Hammurabi. The law covered commercial as well as social relations and regulated all loans
and contracts. All buying and selling, all adoptions and bequests. Justice was dispensed in
temples by priests who acted as judges. The concept of equality before law was not known.
Punishments were given according to the nature of crimes and in some cases depending on

the rank of the offender. For the killing of an aristocrat was regarded a more serious offence
than killing a commoner and it was amicably settled through arbitrators.
4.3.4 Religion
Sumerian religion was mainly nature worship. Each Sumerian city-state had its special
gods. So the Sumerians worshipped a number of gods. At first, the gods of a victorious city
conquered their rivals and the greatest confusion resulted but gradually a more or less ordered
pantheon was formed. Thus Anu became the supreme god of the sky, En-lil of air and earth,
and Ea of the waters of the sea, Ishtar, daughter of Anu, was the popular goddess of fertility.
These and other gods together with their families dwell in temples. They were served by priests,
who made libations, consulted omens, and performed rites of purification. The priests read the

deep secrets of the gods from the appearance of the liver and entrails of slain animals. They
also read the will of God from the way oil dropped into water. All sorts of signs were looked for
a white dog entering a palace meant that a siege was at hand, dreams revealed the course of
event and astrologers claimed that they could predict the future.
The Sumerian gods had to be propitiated and so received food in the form sacrifices
regularly performed in temples. There were also human sacrifices. The Sumerian religion was
devoid of any ethical content. Unlike the Egyptians, the Sumerians did not believe in a future
life. They built temples for their gods which are huge structures with lofty towers called ‘Ziggurat’.
Thus the Sumerian temple itself came to be called a ‘Ziggurat”. Each temple had a large

number of scribes, servants and priests attached to it. The temples owned land and levied
taxes. They served as libraries and schools where priests imparted education. Women were
attached to every temple as domestic servants.

58
4.3.5 Science
In science, the Sumerians made noteworthy progress. As in the case of Egyptian Science,
however, such scientific progress came from practical experience in advanced economic, social,
political life. The Sumerians reckoned by sixties. There were sixty seconds in a minute. Sixty
minutes in an hour, and sixty shekels in a pound or miua. The circle was divided into three
hundred and sixty degrees. The year was composed of twelve lunar months of third days each,
but since by this mode of reckoning five days in each year were lost rulers occasionally included
an extra month whenever it seemed necessary to catch up with the yearly course of the sun. In
some years, accordingly, there were three hundred and ninety days. Day and night were each
divided into twelve hours. As in Egypt, the Sumerians named the years after a striking event,
instead of numbering them.

Discovering that the sun appeared each day, vanished during the night, and repeated its
cycle each year, the Sumerians, further noted that the stars operated according to a fixed rule.
Because the sun was the beneficent creator of crops and sustainers of man and beast, they
inferred a causal connection between the majestic circling of sun and stars and the destiny of
man. They identified the planets and named them after their gods.
4.3.6 Art
Temples and houses were constructed from sun-baked bricks. Towns were surrounded
by walls of brick. The streets of the older towns were constructed without plan. But in newer
centres they crossed each other at right angles. In the midst of each city stood a temple, by the
side of which rose the Ziggurat, a tower composed of a series of cubes, each smaller than the

one below, with flight of stairs leading to the shrine on top. The interior or temples was decorated
with enamelled tiles, rare woods, marble etc.
Sumerians were skilful builders, using such architectural forms as the arch vault and
dome, later to be appropriated by the architects of the Greek and Roman world. Their goldsmiths
made magnificent gold and silver vessels, their potters the finest stone vases cups and bowls
of lapis lazuli and obsidian. Sumerian stone cutters became famous for their clever carving of
small figures on hard stone surface such as cylinder seals. Their sculptures were plain and
blunt and lacked grace. As artists their greatest achievements were in the field of metal work
and gem-carving.

59
4.3.7 Cuneiform Writing
The Sumerians at first used picture writing. They drew picture with a reed pen upon soft
clay which became hard when exposed to sunlight. Later the Sumerians used three hundred
and fifty signs, each sign representing a syllable. Owing to the curious wedge shaped character
of this writing, it is called cuneiform. (Cuneus is the Latin word for wedge). The cunei-form
writing was adopted by Semitic invaders of the Tigris-Euphrates valley such as the Babylonians
and Assyrians and even by non-Semitic Hittites. The development of the cuneiform writing
was the outstanding contribution of Sumeria to mankind.
4.3.8 Literature
The literature of the Sumerians was largely religious in origin and content. Two great
epics are outstanding, one relating to the story of creation and the other the story of the flood.

Their legends are also notable. The legend of Ptana and the legend of Adapa are the two
famous legends of the Sumerians. The two Sumerian epics – the fall of the flood and the tower
of Babel are similar to the later Hebrew stories of those events as found in the Old Testament.

60
4.4 Hammurabi and his Code of Law
When the Babylonian first came to the Euphrates – Tigris valley they had no culture of
their own worth the name. They borrowed from the Sumerians who had already developed a
great civilization. As a conquering nation in the midst of a hostile people, one of their paramount
needs was the creation of a unified strong state. This task was accomplished by their great
king, Hammurabi. He united Mesopotamia and established a centralized government. He was
more famous as ruler and organizer than as warrior. The land was administered with an
interest and initiative similar to that with which a patriarch of the desert ruled his family.
Hammurabi governed with an iron hand, his authority being based upon divine origin. As his
power was absolute, the fate of the country and of the people depended on his mercy. He put

an end to the old system of local autonomy and made the power of the king supreme. He also
introduced a system of royal taxation and compulsory military service. And, Hammurabi prepared
a new code of laws and ruled the state with an iron hand. There are two chief sources of
information for the study of Hammurabi’s rule, a collection of 55 of his letters, and a monument
bearing the code of laws. Among the numerous matters touched upon in the letters is “an
order to finish cleaning out the canal in the city of Erich” and “an inquiry concerning the
misappropriations of temple revenues”. Many things that cannot be found in any other source
are revealed clearly in these letters.
The code of laws is the most famous of all the remains of Hammurabi’s rule. One copy,
carved upon a diorite stone shaft about 8 feet high, has been preserved. The code of Hammurabi

was unearthed at Susa in 1902. Like that of Moses this legislation was a gift from heaven, for
one side of the cylinder shows the king receiving the laws from Chamash, the Sun God. The
code of Hammurabi was composite and heterogeneous character. It begins with compliments
to the gods. But it makes no further notice of them and runs into an astonishingly secular
legislation. It mingles the most enlightened laws the most barbarous punishments and sets
the Lex Talionis with trial by ordeal alongside elaborate judicial procedures. It consists of two
hundred and eighty five laws. These laws are arranged almost scientifically under the headings
of personal, property, real estate trade and business, the family, injuries and labour.
Hammurabi tried to make his subjects believe that the laws were divine, thus giving them

sanctity and enhancing the position of the king. It is apparent that Hammurabi did not originate
all the laws, for many of them appear in old Sumerian records. What he did do was to codify
and enforce them. This code, the oldest known in a complete form, is modern in several

61
respects. Judges were appointed to try cases, a greatest advancement over the blood-feud
system practiced by most of the people at that time. Hammurabi’s code was more advanced
and civilized than that of Assyria. It contained much that was old, some of the ideas dating back
to the stone ages, as for example, the principle that any guilty person or upon one of his
relatives.
The principle of “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” continued to be practiced, but
under the supervision of the state. If a house collapsed and killed the purchaser, the architect
or builder must die. If the accident killed the buyer’s son, the son of the architect or builder
must die. If a man kill a girl, his daughter must suffer the penalty of death. A man accused of
sorcery or a woman charged with adultery was invited to leap into the Euphrates and the gods

were on the side of the best swimmers. If the woman emerged alive, she was innocent, if the
sorcerer was drowned, his accuser receives his property; if he was not drowned, he receives
the property of his accuser.
Another primitive feature of the code Hammurabi was to assess fines according to the
political and social status of the person who had been wronged. If an animal had been stolen
from a temple, the fine was thirty-fold the value of the animal. If the animal had been stolen
from a man of low status, the fine was only tenfold. According to the code of Hammurabi, a
man who struck his fathers had hands cut off. A physician, whose patient died or lost an eye as
a result of an operation, had his fingers cut off. Death was decreed for a variety of crimes like
kidnapping, burglary, incest, procurement of a husband’s death by his wife in order to marry

another man, cowardice in the face of enemy and malpractice in the selling of beer.
One of the civilized features of the code was the substitution of money payments for such
penalties as mutilation of an eye or the breaking of a bone to average similar injury inflicted on
another. Destroying an eye of a man of low estate might be atoned for by paying sixty shekels
or in the case of a slave by paying only thirty shekels. With certain limits the state regulated
prices, wages and fees. What the surgeons might charge was established by law and wages
were fixed by the code of Hammurabi for builders, brick makers and tailors. The widow received
her dowry and her wedding gift remained head of the household as long as she lived. There
was no right of primogeniture: the sons inherited equally and in this way the largest estates

were soon redivided, and the concentration of wealth was in some measure checked. The very
first law of the code reads: “If a man brings an accusation against a man and charges him with
a capital crime, but cannot prove the crime then the accuser shall be put to death”.

62
4.5 Babylonian Contributions
The Babylonians were a people with Semitic culture, who gained control of Mesopotamia
following the supremacy of the Akkadians, and who succeeded in assimilating Sumerian and
Semitic accomplishments into a single cultural tradition. The name of the new kingdom was
derived from Babylon, the chief city. Semites, Sumerians and many other divergent elements
were to be included under one term, Babylonian.
4.5.1 Babylonian Society
Much has been learned from the code about Babylonian social and economic conditions.
Inequality of social groups and special privileges to the select were recognized. The Babylonian
society was divided into three classes namely the rich, the middle class consisting of the
merchants and workmen and the slaves. The wealthy could exact retaliation in kind for personal

injuries and paid heavier fees and fines. The second group had to accept payment for injuries;
and the third group, the slaves, were treated as personal property. Weavers, dyers, carpenters,
brick-makers, goldsmiths, jewellers, sculptors, potters, tailors, metalworkers, and brewers were
mentioned and their rights were guaranteed. The craftsmen were held to strict regulations for
the quality of their work. Canals and roads were built by forced labour.
There was no religious ceremony at a wedding. We do not know whether the husband
and wife made their own choice, or whether the marriage was arranged. The bride brought with
her a dowry. In case of a wife’s lasting illness, the man can remarry, but was bound to look
after the invalid. Very often children were adopted into families in order to look after the parents

in their old age. It is noteworthy that it was the custom for sons to inherit equality, the eldest
being entitled to no special rights.

63
The women had freedom in the society. They could also hold private property and had a
right to seek divorce under special circumstances. If the woman ran her husband’s business
during his absence, she was entitled to one-third of profits. Women wore a variety of ornaments
like necklaces, bracelets and strings of bead.
4.5.2 Babylonian Economy
Agriculture, which was highly developed, comprised the chief basis of economic life.
Herodotus wrote, “Of all countries that we know there is none which is so fruitful in grain.... It is
so fruitful as to yield commonly two-hundred fold....The blade of the wheat plant and barley
plant is often four fingers in breadth”. Orchards of fruits and nuts and, above all, the date, were
common in Mesopotamia. The grape and the olive were cultivated and later introduced into

Greece and Rome. Trade was regulated under government supervision. Business contracts
are mentioned in the code. Deeds of settlements, leases, land deeds, promissory notes, and
interest rates were all standardized and defined. The Babylonians grew varieties of cereals
and pulses. Gardens of fruit and nuts especially of date-plans became a common sight in
Babylonia. Vine cultivation was introduction into Greece from Babylonia. Wine pressed from
the date and beer brewed from corn became the common drinks of the Babylonians. Weavers,
dyers, carpenters, brick-makes, goldsmiths, sculptors, potters and metal workers were the
important economic classes. Copper, lead, iron, silver and gold were mined. The Babylonians
used weaver’s loom and the wheel of the potter. Fine fabrics were made of cotton and wool.
Industries were organised into guilds.

The temples were the centres of business, as well as of the religion of Babylonia. Trade
prospered due to an organized system of finance. Babylonia did not have a regular coinage,
but ingots of gold and silver weighed out at every transaction served the purpose. A shekel was
the lowest unit of money; a mina consisted of 60 shekels; and a talent consisted of sixty minas.
There was no banking system. But banking became the business of certain families which
granted loans particularly to farmers. The Babylonian civilization was essentially a commercial
civilization since most of the documents that have come down to us relate to business transaction.
4.5.3 Religion
The Babylonians were religious minded. They worshipped a number of gods. Their chief
god was Marduk of Babylon. Istar was the Mother Goddess representing the creative principle.
She was the goddess of love and war and was addressed as Holy Virgin. Besides the chief

64
gods, who were in early days patrons of their cities, there were lesser deities. Some of these
had many shrines, and were responsible for the minor comforts and necessities of life, such as
good health and sage travelling. In order to represent himself as always in prayer before the
god, a man could leave a small clay figure of himself in the shrine. Rows of such figures have
been found usually in a rock adjoining the one where the statue of the god or goddess stood.
There were also the household gods, who were supposed to be intimately connected with the
spirits of the departed, and were responsible for the fortunes of the family. The Babylonians
prayed to their gods for their long life, prosperity, material comforts and the preservation of the
family.
The Babylonians built temples. Each temple had a large retinue of staff. Beside secretaries,

they included shepherds and fishermen, as well as the household servants of the priests and
their families. The temples were regarded as the connecting link between god and man. Both
national and private prayers were conducted in the temples; the services were accompanied
by musicians who played on lyres, drums, tambourines, reed pipes and cymbals, while the
choir kept up mournful chanting.
In addition to the large staff of priests, there were also priestess and the position of high
priestess was a very important one; the kings often bestowed it on their daughters. Attached to
the temple were also seers, who predicted the future. Usually they based their utterances on
marks of the livers of sacrificial animals; they also poured oil on water and foretold happenings
of national importance from the shapes it took.

Food and drinks were the common objects used in sacrifices. Sometimes lambs were
offered. The sacrifices could be offered only by the priests who knew all the ceremonials.
During the time of sacrifices, appropriate rites were used and prayers were offered. The common
man was expected to take part in the annual processions during which the image of Marduk
was carried into the streets. Intellectually and artistically the Babylonians phase of the
Mesopotamian civilization represented a stage of political decline since nothing of importance
was added to what the Sumerians had already accomplished, may in certain fields there was
actually deterioration. That is why this period is considered to represent ‘one of the most
pronounced cultural retrogressions’ in history.
4.5.4 Science
Nevertheless the Babylonians made some distinct contributions in the field of science.
Mathematics, Algebra and Geometry were developed by them. Arithmetic was taught to the

65
students in the schools which were opened by the Babylonians. In Mathematics, different sign
had been invented by the Babylonians and they were used for commercial purposes. The
Babylonians divided the circle into three hundred and sixty degrees. The year was divided into
360 days and each minute consisted of sixty seconds. Water clock was used by the Babylonians
to find out the time. Their year was divided into twelve months out of these twelve months, six
months had thirty days each and the rest had twenty nine days each. As that made three
hundred and fifty four days, a thirteenth month was added occasionally. Every month was
divided into four weeks. Geometry was so advanced as to measure complex and irregular
areas.
The Babylonians had also made progress in astronomy. They fixed the position of various

stars, observed the rising and setting of Venus, mapped the skies, plotted the orbits of the sun
and the moon and forecast eclipses. The Babylonians considered the planets as their gods.
The sun was Shamush, the moon was Sin; Jupiter was Marduk; Saturn was Ninib; Mars was
Nergal; and Venus was Ishtar. The Babylonians studied the movements of stars and planets
to trace their influence on men. They read their future in their movements. Some of the
Babylonians priests possessed abundant knowledge of astronomy and it helped them to cast
horoscopes. The science of medicine was so much mixed up with religion that it remained
stagnant. Disease was considered as due to possession by evil spirit.
4.5.5 Art
Art flourished during the period of Babylonian civilization. The Babylonians built palaces
and temples. The palaces were solid and spacious but without much of ornamentation. Houses

were built of sundries mud bricks. The Babylonians manufactured glazed tiles and articles in
bronze, iron, silver and gold. They were also good in wood work. They were skilful in embroidery.
The Babylonians evinced interest in music. Their musical instruments included flutes, harps,
lyres, drums, reed-pipes, cymbals and tambourines. Orchestras were popular. People sang
individually and chorally in temples and palaces and at the feasts given by the rich.
4.5.6 Literature and Learning
The Babylonians prized learning very highly. “Ye who shall excel in tablet writing shall
shine like the sun”, was one of their proverbs. Men were trained for clerical work in temple
schools and other types of cultural pursuits were encouraged. They adopted the Sumerian
cuneiform writing, altering it somewhat; but it never reached the alphabet stage. The priests

66
supervised and passed upon the written works before they were preserved in the temples.
Mythology and epics were favourite forms of literature. Their most important literary work is the
Epic of Gilgamesh. It seals with the story of Gilgamesh, a legendary ruler of Erich who had
survived the Deluge. He is described as a sort of Samoon powerful handsome and courageous.
The Babylonians also produced psalms, hymns and prayers. They also developed temple
literature.
The Babylonians were scientific-minded. They surveyed the universe and arranged their
conclusions in tabulated forms. They followed the start made by the Sumerians in numeration
by sixties and established the idea of giving value to numbers in accordance with their position.
Three figures were used for numeration; a sign for 1, which could be repeated up to 9; a sign

for 10, repeated up to 50; and a sign for 100. Mathematicians worked out tables for multiplication
and division and for the halves, quarters, thirds, squares and cubes of the most important
numbers. They developed a lunar calendar, divided the year into 12 lunar months. They
perfected a sundial, and mapped the movements of the sun, the moon and the planets.
Preventive medical practice consisted mostly of incantations, but it is clear that herbs were
used to combat certain diseases. Sun flower seed was recommended for toothache, milk for
stomach trouble and an oil shampoo and beer were prescribed for baldness.
Several libraries were attached to temples and palaces. The clay tables which contained
the writings of the Babylonians were preserved in these libraries. Most of these libraries have
been destroyed except that of Borsippa. Those tablets were copied and kept in Assurbanipal’s

library at Ninevah.
To sum up, the importance of Babylonian civilization as a background for later
developments is just beginning to be fully appreciated. Archaeological discoveries, particularly
those of the Germans, have thrown a flood of light upon the high state of this culture. Many
things that for a long time were considered of later origin are now known to have had their
beginnings in Babylonia. Most of the succeeding civilizations in south-western Asia and even
in Greece owe much to the Babylonians. They studied the past, unhampered by the idea of
future life. They preserved many legends – not only their own, but also those of other people
– which present an interesting background for the Hebrew Bible. Science made a real beginning
under their critical and analytical observations. They developed units for the measurement of

length, cubic capacity, time and weight. In literature, they evolved the epic, penitential palms,
fables and proverbs. The foundations of mathematics, astronomy, archaeology, history,

67
medicine, grammar, lexicography and philosophy were established. Indeed, the Babylonians
charted previously unknown routes on the sea of learning. Their intellectual signposts guided
many a scholar in centuries that followed.
4.6 Summary
 The land between the Rivers Tigris and Euphrates is called as Mesopotamia. The lower
part of it was called Babylonia and its chief city was Babylon.
 It consisted of two districts Sumer and Akkad. The civilization which flourished in
Mesopotamia is known as Mesopotamian civilization which has certain unique features.
 The most important group of people that inhabited the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent
possessed a Semitic culture. The Babylonians and the Assyrians made the greatest
advance politically and culturally.
 The Sumerians drained the marshlands and developed a powerful political system that
lasted almost 1,500 years.

 The duties of the king included collecting offerings, supervising farming and workshops,
legalizing all business transactions, and defending the city.
 The Sumerians developed a rule of law partly determined by the idea of a hierarchy
under a city god and his temporal representative.
 Sumerian religion was mainly nature worship. Each Sumerian city-state had its special

 They built temples for their gods which are huge structures with lofty towers called
‘Ziggurat’.
 The Sumerians at first used picture writing. Later the Sumerians used three hundred and
fifty signs, each sign representing a syllable. The cunei-form writing was adopted by

Semitic invaders of the Tigris-Euphrates valley such as the Babylonians and Assyrians
and even by non-Semitic Hittites.
 The code of laws is the most famous of all the remains of Hammurabi’s rule. The code
of Hammurabi was unearthed at Susa in 1902. Like that of Moses this legislation was a
gift from heaven, for one side of the cylinder shows the king receiving the laws from
Chamash, the Sun God.

68
 Much has been learned from the code about Babylonian social and economic conditions.
 Agriculture, which was highly developed, comprised the chief basis of economic life.
Trade was regulated under government supervision. Business contracts are mentioned
in the code.
 The Babylonians were religious minded. They worshipped a number of gods. Their chief
god was Marduk of Babylon. The Babylonians prayed to their gods for their long life,
