5.1 Introduction
The ancient kingdom of Assyria was located in present-day northern Iraq. It bordered
eastern Syria and south- eastern Asia Minor. It covered the most northerly portion of the
Mesopotamian plain, with the river Tigris flowing through it. The land was flanked to the north
and east by the Zagros mountains, to the west and south by desert. The climate of northern
Mesopotamia is cooler than in southern Mesopotamia, and the levels of rainfall higher. This
means that irrigation is not essential to farming, though, as with agriculture in many parts of the
world, it does allow more intensive farming than would otherwise be the case. Assyria belonged

to the world of ancient Mesopotamia. However, whilst steeped in Mesopotamian culture from
early times, Assyrian society developed some distinct features of its own. Its exposed position
– bordering as it did lands of warlike mountain peoples and desert tribesmen – meant that its
people developed a strong military tradition. This enabled them to survive periods of invasion,
and then to conquer the largest empire world history had yet seen. At its height this empire
stretched from Egypt to the Persian Gulf, taking in the areas covered by the modern countries
of Israel, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, plus parts of Jordan, Turkey, Armenia and Iran on the way.
5.2 Assyrian Polity
In the first millennium B.C.E., ancient Mesopotamian civilization pioneered the first true
multinational empires in world history. The Assyrian empire was the first of these. The kingdom

of Assyria emerged as a major regional power in the second millennium B.C.E; however, it was
in the early first millennium B.C.E. that it expanded into a huge empire. Assyria occupied a
very prominent place in the history of the Near East, but the Assyrians borrowed most of their

72
culture from the Babylonians. The Assyrians were cruel conquerors and for nearly 300 years
their mighty armies moved from one victorious battle to another. Assur, the Assyrian capital,
was located on the Tigris River about 200 miles north of Babylon. For 300 years, from 900 to
600 B.C., the Assyrian Empire expanded, conquered and ruled the Middle East, including
Mesopotamia, Egypt, the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, and parts of today’s Turkey, Iran
and Iraq. Since around 1250 B.C., the Assyrians had started using war chariots and iron weapons,
which were far superior to bronze weapons. These tools and tactics made the Assyrian army
the most powerful military force of its time, both doctrinally and technologically advanced.
Sargon II (722 – 705 B.C.) and his son Sennacherib (705 – 681 B.C.) conquered the

whole of the Fertile Crescent and extended the Assyrian domain from the Taurus to the
borderlands of Egypt. Ashurbanipal (668 to 627 B.C.) became the most literate of the Assyrian
kings, collecting a vast library of cuneiform tablets from all over the known world. Ashurbanipal
was the last great Assyrian king. After his reign of 42 years, the huge empire began to fall
apart. It had become too large, taxes were too high and entire regions rebelled. In 612 B.C.,
Nineveh itself was razed by a host of Persians, Babylonians and Medes. The great Assyrian
empire was destroyed by the Medes and the Persians about 606 B.C. In 612 B.C. Ninevah,
the later capital of the Assyrians and the most magnificent of all ancient cities were completely
destroyed by a host of Persians, Babylonians and Medes. Babylon was rebuilt by the Chaldeans,

the last of the great Semitic empires in Mesopotamia, and for a brief period the proud city again
ruled the fertile valley of the two rivers.

73
5.2.1 Militarism
Assyria was a military state with a deliberate policy of territorial expansion. The Assyrians
had a matchless army. Their empire existed by and for its army, which was the most highly
trained and most efficient of its day. It was the first to be completely equipped with iron weapons.
The main weapons of the Assyrians were the bows and iron-tipped arrows. After a stream of
well-directed arrows had weakened the enemy, the Assyrian heavy cavalry and chariots would
smash with relentless fury the rank of their foes, driving them headlong from the field. After the
Assyrian victory, came great feasts and celebrations of triumph. Huge parades were held in
which the Assyrian soldiers showed off their body and long lines of miserable prisoners who
were soon to suffer cruel deaths and torture. The Assyrians followed the practice of systematic

terrorization. They were extremely cruel and heartless. Following a battle the Assyrian soldiers
would search the field for wounded foes, whose heads would be cut off and brought back to
camp. Assyrians military history is a dreadful chronicle of massacres and barbarous cruelties
to captives. In boasting of his military exploits, one Assyrian emperor inscribed on a monument,
“their booty and possessions, cattle sheep, I carried away: many captives I burned with fire. I
hung up on high their heads on trees on the vicinity on their city. I devastated the city and
burned it; I annihilated it”.
King Ashurbanipal (modern representation) Assyrian Militarism
5.2.2 Political Administration
As with all Mesopotamian states, Assyria was a monarchy; the king was the divinelyappointed, all-powerful ruler of the Assyrian people. His titles claimed universal sovereignty:

74
“Great King, Mighty King, King of the Universe, King of the country of Ashur”. Like all previous
Mesopotamian monarchs, the king of Assyria was the national god’s appointed representative
on Earth. He was the chief law-maker, the chief administrator, and above all, the commanderin-chief of the Assyrian army. The king was surrounded by a large court of ministers, officials
and servants. His chief ministers included a chief of the army and a chancellor, who probably
headed the large administrative staff. There were also palace officials who ran the huge royal
household, buildings and grounds. The role of some of these officials closest to the king, such
as the chief cup-bearer, must have blurred the line between domestic and public: if he was in
the king’s confidence then he will certainly have exercised considerable influence over matters
of state.

The Assyrians were predominantly a nation of warriors. The exigencies of war determined
the whole character of the Assyrian system. The state was a great military machine. The army
was the most vital part of the government. Chariots, cavalry and infantry constituted the main
limbs of the military organization. Siege mechanism was highly developed and the ‘battering
ram’ was the main siege equipment. All Assyrians owed duties to the king. All adult males were
liable to military service, and the core of the Assyrian army was made up of such men. When
not on campaign they formed a reserve from which soldiers could be recruited.
A depiction of King Tiglath Pileser II Stone depiction of an Assyrian
besieging a town Soldier on Horseback
The Assyrian rulers developed a well co-ordinate system of political administration. Within

the Assyrian empire, a closely knit cosmopolitan civilization developed. The forcible
transplantation of people from their homeland after conquest by the Assyrians served to make
the Assyrian civilization more cosmopolitan. By using new agencies of internal organization
and centralization, the Assyrians created a better co-ordinate state than the Egyptian empire.

75
Royal messengers continually traversed the Assyrian empire, carrying the dictates of the Assyrian
emperor to his provincial governors.
The Assyrian monarch had absolute powers over his empire. He appointed all the
provincial governors, who were always Assyrian by birth, and were all powerful in their several
districts, owing allegiance only to the king. The chief factor in the success of this method in
Assyria was that the governors could always rely on support from the central government in
times of need. The provincial governors had to be in charge of their troops and they were
expected to promote the material prosperity of their districts.
An efficient system of communications between royal court and provincial governors
was set up, consisting of special couriers who carried messages swiftly between the king

(wherever he happened to be) and his governors. Fire signals were also used. The roads were
kept in good repair, wooden bridges were constructed across bridges and paved ways were
driven through mountainous country, to facilitate the swift passage of messages. This system
acted as the precursor of later imperial road networks in the Persian, Hellenistic and Roman
empires. The Assyrians also ran a state espionage service, to keep themselves informed of
potential unrest. The Assyrians also developed the first postal system.
5.2.3 Law
The system of law in Assyria seems to have sprung from an entirely different source from
that used in Babylonia. The code of Hammurabi must have been too mild for this fierce fighting
people, who were constantly coming into contact with the ferocious northern tribes, which
perpetually attempted to invade the country. Punishments were severe: among the mildest

were slitting of ears and noses, whipping from twenty to a hundred lashes, and imprisonment
with hard labour. The other punishments were pulling out the tongue and beheading. Adultery
and some forms of theft were capital crimes.
According to Will Durant, “In general, the Assyrian law was less secular and more primitive
than the Babylonian code of Hammurabi which apparently preceded it in time”. There were
comprehensive laws for the management of the Assyrian empire including state benefits for
widows.

76
5.3 Assyrian Society, Economy and Religion
5.3.1 Society
Information about Assyrian society is scant; the following represents a best stab at an
outline based on current evidence. Assyrian society was divided into three groups: free Assyrians
(with “free” meaning not subject to personal servitude, rather than enjoying the freedoms that
citizens of Western democracies expect); serfs (or “dependants”) on royal and other estates;
and slaves. The freemen were divided into three classes, viz. the nobles; the commoners and
the craftsmen. The commoners consisted largely of soldiers.
All three categories had defined rights in Assyrian law; even slaves were not on a par
with cattle in the way that, say, Roman slaves were. The wide-ranging Assyrian conquests did
not give rise to a vast slave trade as Roman expansion would, in which human beings were

traded on the free market. Conquered populations became free subjects of the Assyrian king,
even if deported to another area within the empire.
At the other end of the social scale, the Assyrian royal family headed a landed aristocracy
which had dominated Assyrian society from time immemorial. It was from this that the bulk of
ministers, commanders, provincial governors and high officials were selected. They had estates
both within Assyria and scattered throughout the empire. These would have been farmed by
unfree workers whether serfs or slaves. However, the majority of Assyrians themselves seem
to have been free peasant farmers, owning their own plots of land. It was these whose obligation
to do military service provided the recruits for the core of the Assyrian army.

77
The towns and cities had the usual population of craftsmen and workers, but they also
had an elite group of leading citizens, made up of priests, scribes, merchants and leading
craftsmen, plus families of those who owned estates nearby. The craftsmen were divided into
guilds and they included bakers, traders, scribes, potters, carpenters and masons. The slaves
had their ears pierced and heads shaven to distinguish them from the rest of the society. They
were compelled to do forced labour in public works. The Assyrian women were completely
subject to men. Their position was far worse than in Babylonia.
In the vassal kingdoms and provinces, the pre-existing societies continued more or less
as before, unless their population had been completely uprooted. In this case they soon lost

their identity and were absorbed into Assyrian society. They will undoubtedly have been secondclass citizens, but probably only for a generation or two before being fully absorbed into the
society of the Assyrian empire. For one of Assyria’s enduring legacies was to break down local
barriers and create an international Aramaic-speaking society which covered much of the Middle
East.
5.3.2 Economy
During the period of the Assyrian civilization, iron came into wide use. This must have
begun to make farming more productive, as for the first time in world history farmers were able
to replace or supplement their implements of wood, bone or stone (which their forebears had
used since the Stone Age) and start using tough but inexpensive iron tools. However, although
the coming of iron would undoubtedly have a huge impact on agriculture and the economy in

later times, the generally poor character of the Assyrian level in excavated sites in countries
occupied by the Assyrians (and the frequent references to spoil, massacre and destruction in
the royal annals), points to impoverishment, or at best stagnation. Clearly, the tribute exacted
from the provinces was so high that economic development was stifled.
Similarly, the mass deportation of different peoples, and the Aramaization of the Middle
East which resulted from this, might have been expected to foster higher levels of long-distance
trade. Of course, there is no evidence during the Assyrian period. Perhaps the deportees
were too traumatized or demoralized; perhaps trade was unable to flourish in the atmosphere
of constant resistance and rebellion which pervaded the Assyrian empire; perhaps the tribute

levied by the Assyrian government was simply too onerous to leave much wealth over for
commerce. In any case, the archaeological record shows no flourishing cities outside Assyria
itself.

78
Within the Assyrian homeland, however, the great cities of Ninevah, Harran, Nimrud and
Ashur clearly flourished. Kings such as Sennacherib undertook an enormous amount of
construction work, erecting temples and other public buildings, restoring towns, and completing
great irrigation schemes which boosted agriculture in the country. Clearly, Assyria was benefitting
from the wealth extracted from her subject peoples. Banks grew up and the Assyrian coinage
consisted of metal lumps of standard weight, first of lead and later of silver and gold. The
Assyrians dyed their textiles and carried on glass industry. They mined metal or imported it
from foreign countries since they were so totally absorbed in military pursuits. It is natural they
neglected industry and trade. They did practice agriculture but much of the industry and trade
was left in the hands of the Arameans.
5.3.3. Religion

The Assyrians shared in the religion of the Mesopotamian civilization at large. The Assyrian
religion included the worship of a number of gods. Ishtar and Ashur were regarded as the most
important gods of the Assyrians. However Ashur was the national god of Assyria, taking the
chief place in the pantheon. Ashur was a solar deity who supposed to take delight in sacrifices
of prisoners. The Assyrians never started a campaign without being assured of the support of
Ishtar. In addition to Ashur and Ishtar, sixty other “great gods” were worshipped by the Assyrians.
Like all Mesopotamians, the Assyrians had a deep and all-embracing belief in signs and
omens. The gods, they felt, were always wishing to communicate their wishes to men, and did
so through the movements of sun, moon or stars, the flight of birds, the state of chicken livers

and so on. No major decision was taken without consulting priests on whether it was in the will
of the gods. This included major issues of state, and the king had a staff of expert astrologers
to aid him in his policy-making.
The religion trained the people to be patriotic and at the same time docile. There was a
prevalent belief in magic. The Assyrians performed human sacrifice in order to please their
gods. They believed in the power of the demons and were armed with incantations and talismans
to ward off their evil influences. The omens explained every coming event and methods were
prescribed to face the evil influences. An impressive ritual existed for the expiration of sins.
5.4 Assyrian Culture
The Assyrians were the inheritors of Mesopotamia’s long history of cultural achievement.
In fact, modern scholars have much to be grateful to the Assyrians for, as they collected or

79
commissioned thousands of documents which contain literary (myths and legends) and other
texts from previous periods of Mesopotamian history, and stored them in huge libraries. These
documents, written on clay tablets, have been found in the ruins of Assyrian palaces and
temples, to be studied in museums and universities around the world. Many of the Assyrian
monarchs were men of culture and refinement, as well as being fearsome warriors.
Ashurnasirpal, for example, had a taste for zoology and botany, bringing back from the lands
through which he “travelled” exotic animals and plants for the imperial parks and gardens at
home.
5.4.1 Fabulous Jewels
Under Assyrian patronage Mesopotamian artists and craftsmen reached a peak of
perfection in their work. The royal tombs of Ninevah and Nimrud have yielded jewels of such

quality and quantity to utterly astonish the archaeologists who found them. It has been estimated
that the amount of gold discovered was over 57 kilos; and the skill with which they were fashioned,
marrying gold with ivory, alabaster, glass and semi-precious stones, made the hundreds of
jewellery items and objects of immense beauty.
5.4.2 A Passion for Building
The Assyrian kings also had a passion for building – the mark of all great Mesopotamian
monarchs. They built themselves magnificent palaces, temples and other public buildings, and
laid out beautiful royal parks. Some built whole new capital cities, whilst others extended and
beautified existing capitals. Ninevah was probably the grandest city of its day as befitted its
status as the capital of the world’s mightiest power. Unsurprisingly for an imperial power, the

Assyrians injected a new scale into Mesopotamian art. The style of their sculptures and friezes
remains faithful to past Mesopotamian norms, but many were far larger than previous examples.
This can be clearly seen today by all visitors to the British Museum, in London, where one of
the main ground floor halls is dominated by several enormous statues of mythical beasts taken
from Assyrian archaeological sites.
In order to glorify themselves and enhance their prestige, Assyrian rulers built imposing
and luxurious palaces. Sargon’s palaces at Khorsabad, built into the wall of the city, were on a
high platform, and its walls were thick and heavy, like a fortress. It contained not only the king’s
living quarters and the royal stables but also a temple and Ziggurat. The arch, borrowed from
Babylonia, became an impressive feature in Assyrian palace gates. They also erected rows of

80
pillars. The floors were paved with alabaster slabs and the walls were paneled with costly
woods. To guard the palace gateways, the Assyrians installed huge human headed winged
bulls carved from imported stone. These impressive creatures were carved with five legs so
that they could not seem to be lacking a leg when seen from the front or the side. The Assyrians
knew a great deal about the anatomy of men and animals. They exaggerated and stylized
muscles, suggesting strength and brutality.
Assyrian Palace
The inside brick walls of the royal palaces were marked below with stone reliefs and
painted above in bright colours. Assyrian cruelty and ferocity were reflected in the vigorous
reliefs, especially in battle and hunting scenes. The winged bulls functioned primarily as symbolic
architectural decorations, while the reliefs depicted a story. The sculptors were very proficient

in depicting animal figures – lions, horses, deer, etc. Tiglath Pilesar I rebuilt the temple of
Ashur. Sennacherib constructed a royal mansion at Ninevah. Ashurbanipal built a beautiful
palace at Kalakh.
The Assyrians seem also to have taken the art of landscape gardening to a new level,
laying out vast parks and gardens near their palaces and diverting whole rivers to water them.
It seems likely that the famous Hanging Gardens of Babylon, as reported by the Greek writer
Herodotus, may actually refer to Assyrian parks. No evidence of such gardens has been found
in Babylon, while there is compelling evidence for large-scale, sophisticated landscaping in
Nineveh.

81
5.4.3 Ashurbanipal’s Library
Assyrian kings were very much interested in preserving the past. In fact, annals of the
kings were preserved with unrivaled exactness. The emperor Ashurbanipal collected over
22,000 clay tablets and kept them in his library. Only a few tablets contained the literary
records of Assyria. This library was known as Ashurbanipal’s library. Assyrian official records,
genealogies of kings, Sumerian hymns, Babylonian literary records and medical texts were
found in the library. On each tablet was the emperor’s mark of ownership and just as a modern
library stamps a warning on its books against superstitious removal. Ashurbanipal had inscribed
on his tablets: “whosoever shall carry off this tablet…. may Ashur and Belit overthrow him in
wrath and anger and destroy his home and posterity in the land”.
Ashurbanipal’s Library
5.4.4 Scientific Achievements

The Assyrians were gloomy and fanatical in their beliefs. They had little deductive
reasoning power and always imagined that, of two succeeding events, the first was the cause
of the second. Their love of collecting data was of great use to later nations. Greek progress
in astronomy was facilitated by the carefully arranged mass of observations made by the
Assyrians for purposes of astrology. The Assyrians borrowed medicine and astronomy from
the Babylonians. The stars were studied by the Assyrians for the purpose of divination. They
added some practical knowledge to chemistry in making glass and in the preparation of ores.
Assyrian philologists made lists of plants which slightly contributed to the growth of botany.

82
The scientific knowledge possessed by the Assyrians was carefully recorded for the benefit of
posterity. The Assyrians had a certain medical skill. Since the health of the army was important,
they took particular interest in developing medicine. More than 500 drugs were catalogues
and their use was indicated.
To sum up, the Assyrian empire’s legacy to world history is significant. As one of the final
chapters in the long history of ancient Mesopotamian civilization, the Assyrian empire acted as
a conduit of Mesopotamian know-how to later peoples. It was through them that the Greeks
learnt about Mesopotamian science and other knowledge, which had a major impact on their
own thought. It may be appropriate here to examine how such a mighty military power as
Assyria disintegrated so soon. Assyria’s economic strength depended too much on profitable

conquest. A decisive defeat in war could endanger its economic stability. Assyrian military
power was becoming weaker as in each war the bravest and the strongest died. Due to their
pre-occupation with war the Assyrians neglected the other professions which in turn impaired
the economic vitality of Assyria. The large influx of captives and destitute aliens destroyed
national unity and acted as disintegrating force. Subjugated nations chafing under her cruel
despotism were waiting for an opportunity to regain their freedom.
5.5 Chaldean Contribution
After the fall of the Assyrian empire, the Chaldeans established their empire. Babylonia
became the capital of the Chaldean empire. Hence, the Chaldean empire was also known as
the New Babylonian Empire. Once again there was true prosperity in the land, and trade

flourished as in the days of Hammurabi. The Chaldeans seem to have absorbed the culture of
their predecessors in the country. During their rule, science and art made progress. An attempt
was made to revive the glories of Hammurabi’s times.

83
5.5.1 Chaldean Religion
Old Babylonian religious ideas underwent a thorough transformation. Though the old
Babylonian pantheon was revived, the revival was only superficial. The new gods were divested
of their old human attributes and were now elevated to the position of omnipotent beings, their
ways and intentions being regarded as something beyond the comprehension of human beings.
This gave rise to the doctrine of fatalism – since god’s way cannot be known, man can do
nothing else except to submit to the will of god.
The Chaldeans worshipped many gods. They gave the names of stars to their important
gods. Their most important god was Marduk. Nabopolassar was the Chaldean king who
rebuilt the temple of Marduk. Nebuchadnezzar continued the task of the temple. Nabu and
Ishtar were the other important gods of the Chaldeans. The power of the Chaldean king

depended largely on the support of the priests; the lack of hereditary right to the throne had to
be made up by a favourable opinion from the oracles. Consequently, the Chaldean kings of
Babylon became very pious.
5.5.2 Science
The Chaldeans made contribution in the field of science and they excelled their
predecessors in this field. Their most important science was astrology and through its study
they gained much astronomical knowledge. The equator was divided into three hundred and
sixty degrees and the twelve signs of the zodiac were mapped out. The Chaldeans had a
strong belief in the influence of the stars on the lives of men; observatories were set up all over
the country, and popular books on the subject were much sought after by the common people.
The prediction of eclipses was common. Many superstitions still in vogue are inherited from

the Chaldeans. They invented the seven day week and divided the day into twelve double
hours. The Chaldeans were more advanced than any of their contemporaries in the study of
medicine. They used at least five hundred and fifty different kinds of drugs. The doctors used
instruments of bronze.
5.5.3 Art and Literature
Nebuchadnezzar was a great builder. In spite of perpetual warfare, he found time to
beautify Babylon. Babylon was now rebuilt and it became one of the greatest cities of its day.
Its fame began to spread throughout the world. Herodotus, the Greek historian has left a

84
graphic description of Babylon. In the centre of the city ran the famous procession street,
which passed through Ishtar Gate. This great arch, still standing, is the best example of Chaldean
architecture. In the city there were also several imposing temples, the grandest of which was
dedicated to the Chaldean deity, Marduk. As mentioned earlier, Nebuchadnezzar continued
the task of reconstruction of the temple of Marduk after the death of Nabopolassar.
Hanging Gardens of Babylon Marduk – Chaldean God
A beautiful palace was also built by Nebuchadnezzar at Babylon. On the terraces of the
palace, he laid out luxurious gardens, filled with rare plants and beautiful trees. These gardens
came to be called as the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. They are considered as one of the
Seven Wonders of the World. Nebuchadnezzar built a bridge across the Euphrates. This

bridge is said to be the earliest bridge to have been constructed.
Their literature lacked originality. They merely copied and re-edited the writing of the Old
Babylonians without adding any thing that was new.
To sum up, the immense amount of documentary material and correspondence that has
survived has not yet been fully analyzed. No new system of law or administration seems to
have developed during the period of Chaldeans. The Babylonian dialect gradually became
Aramaicized; it was still written primarily on clay tablets that often bore added material in Aramaic
lettering. Parchment and papyrus documents have not survived. In contrast to advances in
other fields, there is no evidence of much artistic creativity. Aside from some of the inscriptions
of the kings, especially Nabonidus, which were not comparable from a literary standpoint with

those of the Assyrians, the main efforts were devoted to the rewriting of old texts. In the fine
arts, only a few monuments have any suggestion of new tendencies.

85
5.6 Summary
 Assyria belonged to the world of ancient Mesopotamia. However, whilst steeped in
Mesopotamian culture from early times, Assyrian society developed some distinct features
of its own.
 Ashurbanipal (668 to 627 B.C.) became the most literate of the Assyrian kings, collecting
a vast library of cuneiform tablets from all over the known world.
 Assyria was a military state with a deliberate policy of territorial expansion. The Assyrians
had a matchless army. All Assyrians owed duties to the king. All adult males were liable
to military service, and the core of the Assyrian army was made up of such men.
 There were comprehensive laws for the management of the Assyrian empire including
state benefits for widows.
 Assyrian society was divided into three groups: free Assyrians (with “free” meaning not

subject to personal servitude, rather than enjoying the freedoms that citizens of Western
democracies expect); serfs (or “dependants”) on royal and other estates; and slaves.
 The Assyrians shared in the religion of the Mesopotamian civilization at large. Ishtar and
Ashur were regarded as the most important gods of the Assyrians.
 The Assyrians were the inheritors of Mesopotamia’s long history of cultural achievement.
Under Assyrian patronage Mesopotamian artists and craftsmen reached a peak of
perfection in their work.
 The Assyrian kings also had a passion for building – the mark of all great Mesopotamian
monarchs. They built themselves magnificent palaces, temples and other public buildings,
and laid out beautiful royal parks.
 In order to glorify themselves and enhance their prestige, Assyrian rulers built imposing

and luxurious palaces. The arch, borrowed from Babylonia, became an impressive feature
in Assyrian palace gates.
 It seems likely that the famous Hanging Gardens of Babylon, as reported by the Greek
writer Herodotus, may actually refer to Assyrian parks.
 Assyrian kings were very much interested in preserving the past. Only a few tablets
contained the literary records of Assyria. Assyrian official records, genealogies of kings,
Sumerian hymns, Babylonian literary records and medical texts were found in the library.

86
 After the fall of the Assyrian empire, the Chaldeans established their empire. Babylonia
became the capital of the Chaldean empire. Hence, the Chaldean empire was also
known as the New Babylonian Empire.
 The Chaldeans worshipped many gods. Nabopolassar was the Chaldean king who rebuilt
the temple of Marduk. Consequently, the Chaldean kings of Babylon became very pious.

6.1 Introduction
As early as 1000 B.C., a strange people from the northern steppes, east and northeast of
the Caspian Sea, appeared on the borderland of the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent.
These people are called Indo-Europeans. The Medes and the Persians were the two most
powerful tribes of Indo-Europeans who came into southwestern Asia. They were intruders,
being racially different from the Semites, whose supremacy, until this time, had not been
challenged in Asia Minor. They were vigorous and hardy people. Herodotus wrote that the

Persian fathers taught their sons three things: to ride, to use a bow and to tell the truth. “Better
death than to be guilty of a falsehood” was a common proverb among the Persians. For a long
time they were without writing or art, but they preserved in their minds rich traditions, which
later formed the basis for their religion and literature. They had a spoken language which was
closely related to Sanskrit and to the languages of ancient and modern Europe.

6.2 Persian Government
6.2.1 Early History
The Persians lived for centuries in the highlands overlooking the Tigris-Euphrates valley.
The Persians (Phoenicians) rose to prominence after the downfall of the Aegean’s and their
history begins from about 1300 B.C. They were a Semitic people closely related to the Canaanites.
The term ‘Phoenicians’ was coined by the Greek and it is derived from the Tyrian purple dye
made from shell-fish found along the coast of their capital Tyre by settling along the Syrian
coast they developed a love for sea. They were essentially a sea-faring nation and were among
the first to send out explorers and colonies throughout the Mediterranean area.
From time to time they took part in the wars, as allies of Semitic kings who could offer
them sufficient inducement. In the 9th century B.C., they began taking part in campaigns against

the Assyrians. In 702 B.C., Sennacherib was hard pressed by the united forces of the Medes
and the Persians and, in 680 B.C., they invaded the Assyrian Empire. The Persian ruler, Cyrus,
conquered the greater part of the Near East and the Ionian coast towns and established a great
empire.
6.2.2 Political History of Persia
In 559 B.C. a prince by the name of Cyrus became the king of a Southern Persian tribe;
soon he made himself ruler of all Persians, organized a strong army consisting of hardy peasant
soldiers and built up an efficient army on the Assyrian model world superb generalship and
courage he conquered the greater part of the Near East area the lonian coast towns and

91
established a great empire. The empire created by Cyrus and extended farther by his son
Cambyses was one of the greatest political organizations of antiquity. Except for his military
victories, little is known of Cyrus, who earned the title of “the Great”.
a)Cyrus the Great (549-529 B.C)
Cyrus, the Great is one of the most famous conquerors of the world except for his military
victories, little is known about him. Soon after he became the ruler of the Persians, he was able
to become the King of the Medes as well. The first conquest of Cyrus was the kingdom of Lydia
in 546 B.C. In 539 B.C. taking advantage of the populate discontent and political conspiracies
in the Chaldean empire, he captured the city of Babylon. He died in 529 B.C. while fighting
against the barbarian tribes. He was not a ruthless destroyer but respected and preserved
many of the ideas of the conquered states.

groups and was finally acknowledge king. He was the great Persian ruler and the real organizer

c) Darius, the Great (521-486 B.C)
Darius was a great soldier, conqueror and also a great administrator. He ruled for 35
years during which period, he expanded the Persian Empire as well as organized its
administration. He conquered Babylon and “pacified” one after another, all the rebellious states.
Realizing that such a vast empire can fall to pieces very easily in a crisis, he took up the task of
consolidation. He thus became one of the wisest administrators in history. His rule gave western
Asia a generation of order and prosperity. He also conquered territories of Southern Russia,
then crossed into Afghanistan and reached the valley of the Indus. He managed to reunite the
old empire of Cyrus and extended his realm into India and Africa, and across the Bosporus to

Thrace. His activities on the Thracian coast aroused the hostility of the Athenians. When lonia
revolted and received help from Athens, Darius decided to punish the Athenians. This resulted
in his war with Greece and he met his first reverse at the hands of the Greeks at Marathon, in
490 B.C.
His successor Xerxes (485 – 465 B.C.) held the Empire in a state of equilibrium. He
continued the struggle of Darius, but reverses came thick and fast from the rising power of the

93
Greek city-states. His successors were not able to continue Persian success. The nation
slowly began to decline the frequent revolts of provincial governors and barbarian invasions
weakened it further. Finally in 331 B.C. Alexander, the Great put an end to the Persian
independence and made it a province of his Macedonian Empire.
6.2.3 Extent of the Persian Empire
At the height of its power, the Persian Empire under Darius included 21 provinces of
“satraps”. His vast empire comprised of two kingdoms: Egypt and Babylonia and following
territories from west to east Palestine, Syria, Phoenicia, Lydia, Phrygia, Cappadocia, Cilicia,
Armenia, Assyria, Medes, Persia, Afghanistan, Baluchistan and India west of the river Indus,
other regions were Sogdiana, Bactria and the regions of the Massagetae and other central
Asiatic tribes.
6.2.4 Persian Government

The Persian governmental structure was based on the Assyrian model, but they were
more efficient. The imperial system designed by Cyrus, the Great was completed by Darius,
the Great. The king was the head of the administration in theory. He was an absolute monarch
ruling by the grace of the god of light. His word was law in practice he was required to act on
the advice of his Council of Ministers, who was his chief nobles. The king had also to respect
the ancient customs and the traditional laws of the Medes and Persians. Even though the king
had power to nominate his successors there was no law of succession and so succession was
generally decided by assassination and revolution. The king’s power depended on his army
military service and was compulsory for all able bodied Persians between 15 and 50 years of

age. The most important part of the army was the Royal Guard consisting of 2000 cavalry and
2000 infantry all drawn from the nobility. The king’s will was law. All royal decrees were supposed
to have been inspired by God. Law was harsh and punishments were cruel and barbarous.
Death penalty was common and is the Persian legacy to posterity.
6.2.5 Provincial Administration
For administrative purposes the Empire was divided into 21 provinces of Satraps, each
governed by a provincial governor called a satrap. Four capitals, Susa, Ecbatana, Babylon
and Persepolis were established in different parts of the empire. The king himself ruled Egypt
and Babylon and divided the rest of the empire into 21 provinces. The Satraps were
administrators, and chief judges in their provinces. The satraps were also ambassadors and

94
imperial representative performing liaison function between the king and rulers of neutral
kingdoms bordering on their provincial territories. But strict supervision was maintained on
them and their activities.
This supervision made the governors serve the king well and loyally. One of their most
important duties was to collect annual tribute from their respective territory. Taxation was heavy
and some provinces like India paid nearly one-third of the total tribute. In the time of Darius, the
total annual tribute has been estimated at 14,500 gold talents (about Rs.50,000,000). People
had to maintain the satrap and his establishment. In fact, Darius was called the ‘shop-keeper’
because he stimulated trade by maintaining peace, constructing good road any by introducing
a system of gold and silver coinage on the Lydian model.

Administration was also facilitated by the use of one official language Aramaean, which
was very widely used in the whole Empire, particularly for business purposes. Realizing the
need for good communication, the Persians improved communications and transport. Great
imperial post roads, the best ever built before the Romans, were constructed. At each station
a fresh relay horses was maintained to carry on the mail. The highways were maintained so
efficiently that the royal messengers, travelling day and night could cover the entire distance
within a week. But they also served to stimulated trade, commerce and exchange of customs
and ideas of different peoples.
The aim of the Persian government was achievement of military efficiency and political
security. Darius believed in a good law for the good government of the Empire. His digest of

laws called as the ordinance of good regulations was based on the Hammurabi Code. He also
used religion, Zoroastrianism to consolidate his empire. He inspired in them qualities of austerity
loyalty and honour and tried to protect them from luxury and vice. Thus, by the use of one
system of coinage, one official language a good system of communications, a good law and
religion in the form of Zoroastrianism, the Persian ruler tried to consolidate the varied and
heterogeneous populations into one Persian Empire.
6.2.6 Estimate of the Persian Government
Persian Empire was the first to attempt governing many different racial groups on the
principle of equal responsibilities and right for all people. It was an example of one man
government which many rulers of later generations tried to follow. The Persian law, religion
and system of coinage did much to weld the empire together. The estimates of Persian

95
administration were due to the religion which taught that they were responsible to God and that
they could attain salvation only if they governed wisely justly and piously.
6.2.7 Defects of Persian Administration
Persian government had some very important defects. The Persian administration was
elaborate and expensive. But being a one man government, success depended on the
personality of the ruler. If the ruler was not strong (as it happened after the death of Emperor
Xerxes) the provincial Government failed and provincial governors repeatedly revolted. Thus
administrative irregularities and heavy taxation made the Persian rule very oppressive and at
the slightest opportunity, revolts broke out everywhere. This affected the permanency of the
empire. However, in spite of the serious defects, Persian administration forms a successful
experiment in imperial government.

6.3 Persian Society and Economy
The Persian society was feudal in character. They considered family as a holy institution.
Celibacy was discouraged. Polygamy and concubine were legalized were legalized and women
occupied a high position in society. They owned and managed property. They believed in
cleanliness. Eating and drinking in the street was considered as unhygienic and they punished
those who spread contagious diseases. They wore long robes and were found of cosmetic.
They were people with good manners, outspoken, generous and hospitable.
Agriculture was the main occupation of the people. Feudal economy was the order of the
day. Slavery was common and slaves were used for cultivation wheat and barley were the
main crops. Meat and wine were very popular. The Haoma juice, an intoxicating drink, was

used mostly for offering sacrifices, while the common than had his browned beer from corn.
They hated trade as they considered the market as a place of “breeding ground for lies”.
6.4 Persian Culture
Persian culture was eclectic in nature. It was mostly borrowed from earlier civilizations
and there was nothing original about it. They borrowed from Mesopotamia, Egypt, Lydia and
northern Palestine. Persian architecture was a mixture of Babylonian, Assyrian, Mesopotamian
and Egyptian architecture.

96
6.4.1 Education
Education was the privilege of the rich. It was managed by temples and imparted by
priests. Zend Avesta and commentaries on it, law and medicine, formed the curriculum. The
method of study was memorizing passages. Higher education was also provided and consisted
of training for public office or provincial administration.
6.4.2 Writing
Initially Persians had no writing and adopted Aramaic for business correspondence. The
old Persian language was closely related to Sanskrit. The Persian in course of time developed
an alphabet of 39 letters based upon the alphabet of the Arameans. They considered writing
as a feminine activity and so they did not produce great literacy masterpieces.
6.4.3 Literature and Learning
In literature, Persian contribution was not much. They loved poetry and almost all their

lyric poetry is found in the Zend Avesta, a collection of Zoroastrian songs and prayers.
Persian learning was mostly a branch of religion and they paid great attention to
metaphysics. Learning was considered important but not pursued with zeal. Medicine was
practiced through prayers, penance and acts of purification. They resorted more often to spells
and magic man to drugs.
6.4.4 Arts
They did not contribute much to fine arts. Their all important religion was not conducive
to the development of art. War was their pastime and they depended on import for many of
their luxuries.
6.4.5 Architecture
Architecture is the best example of the eclectic character of Persian art. They copied the
raised platform and the terraced building style of Babylonia and Assyria and the
winged bulls, the brilliantly coloured glazed bricks and other decorative motifs of Mesopotamia
architecture.

6.4.6 The Persian Religion – Zoroastrianism
A permanent contribution of the Persian to civilization was their religion Zoroastrianism.
It was of ancient origin and was highly developed. When the Persians began their conquests
very soon it became very popular and spread through most of Western Asia. Its origin can be
traced as far back as the 25th century B.C. its real founder was Zoroaster, from whom the
religion derives its name. His main aim was to purify the traditional beliefs of his people to

abolish polytheism, animal sacrifice and magic and to establish their worship on a more spiritual
and ethical plane.
Zoroastrianism had four unique characteristics:
1. Dualism, it was dualistic in which the same gods were capable of both good and evil. The
two were engaged in a desperate struggle for supremacy in which ultimately the god of
light (or Good) would emerge successful. Ahura Mazda represented the good, the
righteous and the just. ‘Ahriman’ represented forces of evil and darkness.
2. Zoroastrianism was religion believing in final things. It believed that the world would endure
for 12,000 years after which god of light will finally emerged successful. It believes in the
doctrine of last judgment and the coming of a Messiah.

98
3. Zoroastrianism was an ethical religion prescribing the code of good conduct and life and
also laid down a list of difference sins. He prescribed moderation in life and behaviour and
condemned the ascetic way of life.
4. Finally, Zoroastrianism was a revealed religion. This was perhaps the first of its kind in the
Western world. Revealed religions are not common in the Western world. While this
factor has contributed to their strength it has also contributed to their dogmatism.
Soon Zoroastrianism declined. It was corrupted by the persistence of old beliefs
superstitions and magic. As the religion spread, influence of other religions also affected it.
Finally the priests became more powerful and gained complete control over it. Most important
cults were (i) Mithraism (ii) Manicheism and Gnosticism.
Mithraism was a degenerate for of Zoroastrianism and a revival of pre-Zoroastrian

practice. It was the worship of young sun hero similar to the Neolithic solar god. It had an
elaborate ritual. It became a definite cult in around the 4th century B.C. and became very
popular soon after Alexander’s death and the consequent break-up of the Empire and the
disorder which followed it was introduced into Rome in the 1st century B.C. its appeal was
mostly to the lower classes from the ranks of soldiers foreigners and slaves. After 275 A.D. it
declined rapidly. It was a connecting link between Christianity and Zoroastrianism.
Manicheism was formulated by the principal successors of Mithraism in transmitting the
Persian legacy. It was founded by Mani, a highborn priest of Ecbatana about 250 A.D. He also
aimed to reform the religion but did not receive much support. So he confined himself to
missionary activities in India and Western China. In about 276 A.D. he was condemned and

crucified by his Persian enemies. About 330 A.D. a number of Manicheans including Augustine,
later became Christians.
Manicheans were greatly impressed by the dualism of Zoroastrianism and adopted it as
their central doctrine. In pursuance of it, it laid down a strict ethical code. He prescribed strict
celibacy and self-control by prolonged fasting and infliction of pain on the body. Mani divided
making into two sections the perfect and the secular. Only the “perfect” had to follow the code,
while the later had to give up dilatory, greed, adultery, falsehood and eat vegetarian food.
The influence of Manicheism was considerable. It became popular in Italy and Rome. It
contributed to the ascetism of Christianity. It strengthened the doctrines of original sin and the

99
total depravity of man. The third most popular cult which developed as an element in the
Persian heritage was Gnosticism. The term has come from the Greek work Gnosis meaning
knowledge. The date of its origin and the name of its founder are not known, but it prevailed in
the first century A.D. and had become very popular in the 2nd century A.D. it had little success
in Italy, and its influence was mostly confined to the Near East.
Persian heritage contained few elements of a secular nature. Their form of government
was adopted by the Roman monarch not in its political aspect, but in its character of divine right
despotism. Similarly, some Hellenistic philosophies were influenced by Persians from the
religious point of view.
6.5 The Hebrew Civilization
Of all the peoples of the ancient orient the Hebrew are of great importance next only to

the Egyptians. The origin of the Hebrews and their name is doubtful. One version says that
their name was derived from Khanbiru or Habiru, a name invented by their enemies and meaning
alien “outcast” or “nomad”. Another version says that the name is related to the term “Ever” or
“Eber” referring to those who came from the other side of the Euphrates. Whatever the truth, it
applied originally to immigrant people and was later on restricted to the Israelites. Through the
Hebrews provided much of the background of the Christian, their religious ideas were derived
from Egyptian and Mesopotamian source.

6.5.1 Political and Cultural History
The Hebrew seems to have originally come from the lower Euphrates-valley, but for
centuries they wandered in search of homeland. Finally they entered into the land of the Canaan.
Their conquest was a slow and painful process. Initially they had to fight and conquer the
Canaanians (a mixed Semitic and Hittite people) who were defeated. Later they had to fight
against the Philistines, who had entered the land from Asia Minor and from the islands of the
Aegean sea. It is from the Philistines, Palestine got its name.
Palestine was a very small region only 150 miles long and very narrow and was tucked
between the capitals of the Nile and those of the Tigris and Euphrates. This geographical
factor brought in trade as well as war, and repeatedly the harassed Jews were forced to take

sides in the struggle of the empires, to pay tribute or be overrun. This perilous geographical
position between Mesopotamia and Egypt shaped their civilisation.
For centuries the Hebrews gradually filtered into Palestine the desert and for a long time,
they did not have any centralized political institution. The Philistines prevented their unification
for quite some time. There was no unity in political administration. The 12 tribes were independent
and were administered as families by patriarchs. There was no king as such in lsrael. Saul
(1028 - 1013 B.C.) first united the Hebrews. David (1013 - 973 B.C.) the next ruler of the
Philistines, united the 12 tribes into a consolidated State under an absolute ruler and constructed

101
a magnificent capital at Jerusalem. But strong government, material and military glory also
meant heavy taxation and conscription. This resulted in popular discontent which was evident
in the closing years of David’s reign discontent increased in the time of his successor Solomon.
In spite of Solomon’s fame for wisdom, fairness, justice and enlightenment, his rule was
oppressive. Taxation was heavy. As a result soon after his death in 935 B.C. popular discontent
resulted in revolt and division of the Kingdom into two-the differences also between these two
divisions. The northern part of Israel had some fertile valley and people were comparatively
prosperous. In the Southern part, Judah, difference was reflected in the lives of the people.
The northern Israelites were worldly and materialistic in their philosophy and religion. They

were used to urban living and exposed to foreign influences. The Southern Judeans were
mostly pastoral and agricultural, traditional in their religion and hated the foreigners and their
ways. The glorified a life of suffering and privation and immortalised the shepherd and his
flock.
For more than two centuries they maintained their separate existence. But division
weakened them and exposed them to attack and invasion. In 722 B.C. the Assyrians conquered
lsrael, scattered ‘the Hebrews throughout their empire and finally were absorbed by the
population around them’. Since then they are referred to as the lost ten tribes of lsrael. Judah
was conquered in 586 B.C. by the Chaldean Emperor, Nebuchadnezzar. He captured Jerusalem
and carried all the inhabitants into captivity. When the Persians conquered the Chaldeans in

the 6th century, the Hebrews were permitted to return to Jerusalem and restore the temple of
Jerusalem. From 539 to 322 B.C. they were under the Persian rule. In 332 B.C. they were
conquered by Alexander, the Great. After his death, they passed under the control of the
Ptolemies of Egypt. Palestine became a Roman Protectorate. Its political history as a Jewish
Commonwealth ended in 70 A.D., when the Hebrews rebelled against the Roman emperor.
The Romans put down the revolt, destroyed Jerusalem, annexed their territory and made it a
province of the Roman Empire. The Hebrews were driven from Palestine and scattered to all
parts of the world where they were absorbed by the surrounding people. This dispersion of the
Hebrews from Palestine is called as Diaspora. Their wanderings and sufferings helped them

to develop a religion which provided the basis for Christianity. Their dispersion helped them to
promote a fusion of Greek and Oriental ideas. It was Hellenized Jew, St.Paul, who remoulded
Christianity on the basis of Greek philosophical doctrines.

6.5.2 Hebrew Government
Their central Government was ore an ecclesiastical organisation, where God was the
source of all political and religious authority. A king was considered as a necessary evil, to
maintain order, protect freedom of speech and encourage trade.
6.5.3 Religion
The Hebrew religion was the consummation of their ideals and the embodiment of most
of their activities. Originally the Hebrew religion was primitive polytheism, worship of spirits that
dwelt in trees, mountains and springs. Various forms of magic were practiced.
The 2nd stage which lasted from 12th to 9th century B.C was the stage of national monolatry
when there was exclusive worship of one God called Yahweh but without denying the existence
of other gods. This evolution was chiefly due to Moses who gave the Hebrews their loving all

powerful and ever-just God. They considered him as their only guide and deliverer, the protector
of the weak and the avenger of the nation’s wrongs. He was worshiped as a supreme law giver
and as the stern upholder of the world’s moral order. According to the Biblical account he gave
the Ten Commandments to Moses on top of Mt. Sinai. The Hebrews religion at this stage was
neither ethical nor spiritual.

103
By 9th century the Hebrews religion was in great need of reform as superstition and
idolatry had steadily increased with the passing years. The really important work of religious
reform carried out by the great prophets formed the third stage in the evolution of the Hebrews
religion. A great many of the characteristics of the Hebrew reflected their natural surroundings
and experience. But much the formulation and codification of the faith was the prophets purged
the Hebrew thought and religion of all corrupting influences, elevated and dignified the concept
of Yahweh to the exclusion of other Gods ad established a monotheistic religion.
Prophets like Amos, Hosea, Isaiah and Micah taught that God was a loving Father and
that He alone was the true God of the Universe. The period of the prophets was 8th and 7th

centuries B.C. They were men of the broader vision and three doctrines served as the substance
of their teachings. These three doctrines were monotheism that Yahweh is a God of
righteousness and that the aims of religion are chiefly ethical. These doctrines repudiated
everything that the aim of religion to its ancient purity. Their success was so great that they
achieved almost a religious revolution. As a result most of the barbarities which had entered
the Hebrews religion from foreign sources were removed. Its purpose still continued to be
social and ethical and not to confer individual salvation in an after-life.
The ideals of the prophetic revolution represented the highest perfection of the Hebrew
religion. The prophets rendered a great service to the Hebrew religion, and to other religions
which developed from it. They associated Yahweh’s law with a just society and concluded that

under a just God, social injustice comes only though the mistakes of man. So, the sufferings of
people were due to the sins of the wealthy and powerful classes. While they did not succeed in
reforming the social order, they gave ethical attributes to a deity. To the Hebrews justice meant
the reign of Yahweh’s law. Gradually, “the conception of one God” whose concern in the mortal
regeneration of mankind, was developed into an ethical monotheism.
Hebrew religion continued to develop after the days of the great prophets. Once again
they responded to outside influences. The first of these influences was during the period of the
Babylon captivity from 58 to 589 B.C. which constitutes the 4th stage in the evolution of the
Hebrew religion. They adopted the Babylonian’s ideas of pessimism, fatalism and transcendence

of God. Yahweh now became “omnipotent, unapproachable and holy”. At the same time the
forms of religion were changed. To preserve the identity of the Jews as a nation, their leaders
adopted or revived customs and observances which would serve to distinguish them as a
distinct people. Great importance was given to the institution of Sabbath, the forms of synagogue

104
worship, the practice of circumcision and distinction between clean and unclean food. The
growth of rituals increased the power of the priests. Judaism gradually transformed into
ecclesiastical religion.
The final stage in Hebrews religious evolution took place in the period of Persian influence
which covered the period from 539 to about 300 B.C. As a result of the influence of
Zoroastrianism, they adopted a belief in Satan as the great Adversary and the auto of all evil.
They also developed beliefs of the coming of Saviour, the resurrection of the dead and a last
judgment. They believed attainment of salvation as one important than enjoyment of the life on
earth. Lastly they accepted the conception of revealed religion and that different Books, like
the Book of Ezekiel were dictated directly by Yahweh to some of His followers. With these

beliefs the simple, ethical and monotheistic religion preached by the prophets underwent a
complete change.
6.5.4 Art
In some respects Hebrew genius was limited. They had no interest or talent for scientific
knowledge. They also did not have any artistic skill. They did not contributed to architecture,
sculpture or painting. The famous temple of Jerusalem was the work of the Phoenicians who
were commissioned by Solomon, the Hebrew king. Their temple was a simple uniform sanctuary
without many decorations. The priestly procession, the music and the recitation of their ritual
were the only decorations they wanted. Their religion was responsible for the absence of any
progress in architecture, painting and sculpture. In 62 B.C. the prophets advised them to destroy
all images and during the period of their exile their leaders told them not to portray any object

in artistic form. As a result, their cultural life was neglected. The only objects of art produced by
them were engraved seals.
6.5.5 Music
They used music extensively in their religious ceremonies. The melodies probably
developed from the rhythmical chanting of their religious verses. They used musical instruments,
especially the harp, as accompaniments to voices. An orchestra and the choir were also used
during service at the Temple. But neither the music nor the directions have been deciphered so
far. The Hebrew genius expressed itself in their law, literature and philosophy.

105
6.5.6 Law
The best example of Jewish law was the Deuternomic Code. In general this code was
more enlightened than the Hammurabi Code. Its authors were not interested in abstract
principles. Their aim was to infuse into Jewish society a more democratic and political democracy.
Some of the important provisions of the code were:
 Liberty to the poor and the stronger.
 A Hebrew slave after a service of 6 years should be set free and he should not be sent
empty handed.
 Judge and other officers were to by the people. They were not be accepted gifts or show
partiality in any way.
 Children should not be punished for the guilt of their fathers. Individual responsibility for
sin was affirmed.
 A Jew should not take from another Jew interest on any kind of loan.
 At the end of every seven years there should be a “release” of debts.

 The king’s power was limited. The king was not to accumulate huge wealth nor indulge in
luxury. He was not above law but subject to it. No military despotism was to be tolerated.
 The administration of justice was left in the hands of the people, cases of disputed guilt
were to be decided by the city’s elders and the punishment was to inflicted by the victims
family or by the community at large.
 Finally conscription of labour for Foreign Service was prohibited.
6.5.7 Literature
The Hebrew literature was the best of the ancient world. The greater part of it deals with
religion. Almost all of it is preserved in the Old Testament. And it is one of the greatest and
most beautiful pieces of literature produced by any people of any time. As history it ranks with
the works of the great historians Herodotus and Gibbon and as poetry it ranks with the works
of Shakespeare and Goethe.

The best Hebrew literary achievement is the Book of Job. It is a drama of the tragic
struggle between man and fate, with the problem of evil as its central theme. The most beautiful
of Hebrew love lyrics is the Song of Songs or the Song of Solomon. The Book of Psalms
contains excellent Hebrew poetry.

106
Besides the Old Testament there is in Hebrew literature a collection of laws and
commentaries known as the Talmud. It embodies the wisdom of the finest thinkers of the
Jewish people. It is an authoritative work of the Jews and included a record of debates and
decisions, poetry and philosophy and wisdom and mysticism. It covers a period of more than
800 years and exercise influence on Jews.
However, not all Hebrew writing was of high literary merit. A good part of it was dull and
repetitious Chronicles. Still, most of them, whether in the form of battle song, prophecy, love
lyric or drama, “were rich in rhythm, concrete images and emotional vigour”.
6.5.8 Philosophy
Hebrews were very good in philosophy. They dealt mostly with problems relating to the
life and destiny of man. Their thought was personal and not abstract. Their philosophic writings

which are mostly ethical in nature are to be found in the Book of Proverbs and the Book of
Ecclesiastics. The Book of Proverbs advocates moderation hard work, wisdom and honesty,
for a good, long and prosperous life. The Book of Ecclesiastics is more profound and critical.
The basic ideas of its philosophy are fatalism, skepticism, pessimism, moderation and the
belief that the Universe is a mechanism of recurring cycles.
To sum up, Persian’s outstanding achievement was that they succeeded in bringing the
various civilization centres under one rule which worked towards the development of a more
cosmopolitan culture. It had within its territories as many as nine mature civilizations – Egyptian,
Sumero-Babylonian, Assyrian, Syrian, Hebrew, Lydian, Phoenician, Median and Indian. It made
it possible for exchange of cultural elements, trade and commerce. It made possible for

Aramaean to serve as a lingua franca for a long time. Thus Persia served as a cultural and
commercial bridge between West Asia and East Asia. This was its important mission on which
she won great success. Finally, Zoroastrianism their most original accomplishment was their
gift to the world. It marked an important step in the attempt to satisfy man’s spiritual desire
further and more important is that it served as a unifying force for the Persian Empire.
The Hebrew influence was chiefly religious and ethical. The Old Testament is the most
precious legacy to Western Civilization. It formed the principal foundations of Christianity.
From the Hebrews, Christianity got its theory of the origin of the Universe, the Ten
Commandments and a large portion of its theology. Even Jesus only condemned their legalism
and hypocrisy, but did not oppose all their teachings. Thus, he respected and honoured the

107
Prophets, believed in rewards and punishment after death and considered the Jewish people
as the chosen people of God.
6.6 Summary
 The Persians set up a vast empire and an efficient administration which provided peace
and security for nearly two centuries.
 This was not equaled until the rise of the Roman Empire.
 It had a fundamental weakness in that.
 Its Government was not based on institutions but depended on persons.
 It lasted for nearly two centuries and provided as model to future peoples who wanted to
establish vast empires.
 The ethical and political influence of Hebrews was great.
 Their moral conceptions were responsible to a great extent for the development of a
negative approach towards ethics in western countries.
 As regards political influence, their ideals of limited government, the sovereignty of law

and their regard for the dignity and worth of the individual were the major formative
influences, which shaped the growth of modern democracy.
 Hebrew traditions contributed equally with the influence of Christianity and the stoic
philosophy in fostering recognition of the rights of man and in promoting the development
of free society.
