7.1 Introduction
Greece is a country in southeastern Europe, known in Greek as Hellas or Ellada, and
consisting of a mainland and an archipelago of islands. Ancient Greece is the birthplace of
Western philosophy (Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle), literature (Homer and Hesiod),
mathematics (Pythagoras and Euclid), history (Herodotus), drama (Sophocles, Euripedes,
and Aristophanes), the Olympic Games, and democracy. The concept of an atomic universe

was first posited in Greece through the work of Democritus and Leucippus. The process of
today’s scientific method was first introduced through the work of Thales of Miletus and those

112
who followed him. The Latin alphabet also comes from ancient Greece, having been introduced
to the region by the Phoenicians in the 8th century BCE, and early work in physics and
engineering was pioneered by Archimedes, of the Greek colony of Syracuse, among others.
Mainland Greece is a large peninsula surrounded on three sides by the Mediterranean
Sea (branching into the Ionian Sea in the west and the Aegean Sea in the east) which also
comprises the islands known as the Cyclades and the Dodecanese (including Rhodes), the
Ionian islands (including Corcyra), the isle of Crete, and the southern peninsula known as
the Peloponnese.
The geography of Greece greatly influenced the culture in that, with few natural resources
and surrounded by water, the people eventually took to the sea for their livelihood. Mountains

cover eighty percent of Greece and only small rivers run through a rocky landscape which, for
the most part, provides little encouragement for agriculture. Consequently, the early ancient
Greeks colonized neighboring islands and founded settlements along the coast of Anatolia (also
known as Asia Minor, modern day Turkey). The Greeks became skilled seafaring people and
traders who, possessing an abundance of raw materials for construction in stone, and great
skill, built some of the most impressive structures in antiquity. Hardly there is anything modern
western culture does not owe its origin to Greece. The civilization of the Greeks was founded
upon ideals of freedom, rationalism, secularism, moderation and a high regard for the dignity
and worth of the individual man.
The Greek civilization has two phases (1) the Hellenic phase starting with the advent of

the Greeks and ending with the advent of Alexander the Great a period during which the
Hellenic Civilization in all its essential aspects was evolved and (2) the Hellenistic phase
covering the period from the advent of Alexander to the 1st century A.D. when the Greek culture
bursting its narrow bounds of the Greek peninsula overflowed into the countries of the orient,
got itself exposed to new ideas and was considerably influenced by them. The Greek immigrants
who came and settled in Greece called themselves as Hellenes, for, they regarded themselves
as descendants of a common ancestor Hellen. So the people were Hellenes, the land occupied
by them was Helias and their culture Hellenic. Naturally the Greeks borrowed many of their
ideas and thus Greek culture was shaped by Aegean influences.
7.2 Early History of Ancient Greece

Ancient Greek history is most easily understood by dividing it into time periods. The
region was already settled, and agriculture initiated, during the Paleolithic era as evidenced

113
by finds at Petralona and Franchthi caves (two of the oldest human habitations in the world).
The Neolithic Age (c. 6000 - c. 2900 BCE) is characterized by permanent settlements (primarily
in northern Greece), domestication of animals, and the further development of agriculture.
Archaeological finds in northern Greece (Thessaly, Macedonia, and Sesklo, among others)
suggest a migration from Anatolia in that the ceramic cups and bowls and figures found there
share qualities distinctive to Neolithic finds in Anatolia. These inland settlers were primarily
farmers, as northern Greece was more conducive to agriculture than elsewhere in the region,
and lived in one-room stone houses with a roof of timber and clay daubing.
The Cycladic Civilization (c. 3200-1100 BCE) flourished in the islands of the Aegean

Sea (including Delos, Naxos and Paros) and provides the earliest evidence of continual human
habitation in that region. During the Cycladic Period, houses and temples were built of finished
stone and the people made their living through fishing and trade. This period is usually divided
into three phases: Early Cycladic, Middle Cycladic, and Late Cycladic with a steady development
in art and architecture. The latter two phases overlap and finally merge with the Minoan
Civilization, and differences between the periods become indistinguishable.
The Minoan Civilization (2700-1500 BCE) developed on the island of Crete, and rapidly
became the dominant sea power in the region. The term ‘Minoan’ was coined by the archaeologist
Sir Arthur Evans, who uncovered the Minoan palace of Knossos in 1900 CE and named the
culture for the ancient Cretan king Minos. The name by which the people knew themselves is

114
not known. The Minoan Civilization was thriving, as the Cycladic Civilization seems to have
been, long before the accepted modern dates which mark its existence and probably earlier
than 6000 BCE.
7.3 Contributions of Ancient Greece
The Minoans developed a writing system known as Linear A (which has not yet been
deciphered) and made advances in ship building, construction, ceramics, the arts and sciences,
and warfare. King Minos was credited by ancient historians (Thucydides among them) as
being the first person to establish a navy with which he colonized, or conquered, the Cyclades.
Archaeological and geological evidence on Crete suggests this civilization fell due to an overuse
of the land causing deforestation though, traditionally, it is accepted that they were conquered
by the Mycenaeans. The eruption of the volcano on the nearby island of Thera (modern day

Santorini) between 1650 and 1550 BCE, and the resulting tsunami, is acknowledged as the
final cause for the fall of the Minoans. The isle of Crete was deluged and the cities and villages
destroyed. This event has been frequently cited as Plato’s inspiration in creating his myth
of Atlantis in his dialogues of the Critias and Timaeus.
7.3.1 Political History
Originally Crete consisted of numerous warring clans living in independence village under
their own chief. Finally Cnossus succeeded in merging all these class under its relationship
and the king known as ‘Minos’ succeeded in establishing extensive maritime empire.
7.3.2 Society
The Cretans led an urban life. They lived in cities with their teeming population paved
and guttered streets, intersecting lanes and countless shops and houses. They were built with

sun-dried bricks while stones were used for the foundation. They knew the use of limestone,
gypsum and cement. The fresco paintings in the palaces show that Cretans led a happy and
care free life. They depict gay groups of men and women enjoying themselves. The men were
slim and graceful and they were a short waist cloth which was held by a tight belt. Women
enjoyed much freedom. We see them sitting in the balconies enjoying their leisure or in theatres
enjoying public entertainment.
Their chief amusements were bull-fighting and wresting. They also played a game similar
to chess. An exquisite gaming board made of ivory found in the royal palace and perhaps this

115
was a favourite pastime of royalty bull-fight seems to be the most popular game in which both
men and women participated in one of the frescoes paintings a woman is shown in the air
caught between the horns of a bull.
7.3.3 Economic Life
The Cretans were engaged in all the three economic activities viz. agriculture, industry
and trade. They cultivated what, barley, flax, olive and wine. Manufacturing olive oil and wine
were their important industries, besides pottery of exquisite workmanship. Manufacture of textiles
and metal goods, gem setting, carpentry and jewellery were other industries. Most of these
private industries were concentrated outside the capital, in cities like Gournia, Thrasia, Phaestos
etc.
The factories were run with the help of human labour and large numbers were employed.
There was division of labour and centralized control and supervision of workers. Even women

were employed in these factories. There was not only internal trade, but trade with the
neighbouring countries also. The Cretans were skilled navigators and traded with Egypt, Asia
Minor, Spain and other countries of the Mediterranean. Their chief articles of export were olive
oil, horse and metals of various kinds. They seem to have known the art of book keeping, for
a number of documents bearing mathematical symbols like decimals and fractions have been
discovered in Crete. This active business life of the Cretans accounts for their material prosperity.

116
7.3.4 Religion
The chief deity of the Cretans was not a god but a goddess who represents the source of
all life and who rule the entire universe. The serpent and the dove are her constant companions.
The Cretans called her Rhena. Originally no male deity was worshipped but late a male god
was associated with her as her son and lover but he occupied only a subordinate position. The
goddess and the god were represented by a double axe known as ‘labyrs’. No temples were
built for the divinities but there were domestic shrines in palaces, and houses where offerings
were made to them. They also worshipped animal like bull, stage, minotaur, (half bull-half man)
and trees and symbols like double axe, pillar and cross.
7.3.5 Art of Writing and Science
The Cretans knew the art of writing and first they used a pictographic script and later

developed two linear signs. Most of the records relate to business transactions and no literary
texts have so far been discovered. They constructed broad roads of concrete and from the
amenities available in the palace of Knossos like bath, drainage, etc., we may infer that they
knew all the basic principles of sanitary engineering.
7.3.6 Art
In the field of art the Cretans made significant achievements. Unlike the art of other
Oriental cultures, it was free from the retarding influence of tradition. Of the different arts,
architecture was the least developed. Their palaces, houses and other structures did not have
an aesthetic appeal and they were constructed with an eye on utility.
7.3.7 Other Centres of the Aegean Civilization – Troy
In 1870 Dr. Schliemann, conducted excavations at Hissarlik in Troy and brought to light

ruins of six cities. The second city often called the burnt city shows a decided advance. There
is a fortress in the centre of which there is a palace. In the great hall were found a heap of gold
and silver ornaments and copper and bronze. The gradual advance in civilization culminates in
the sixth city, surrounded by a strong wall of stone with several gates.
The remains at Mycenae were unearthed in 1876 by Dr. Schliemann. It is situated in
Argolis in the mainland of Greece on a hill top and it was surrounded by a wall. The main
entrance to the citadel is the celebrated ‘Lion Gate’. Inside it were six graves in one of the

117
which were found 19 skeletons of men, women and children with profuse ornaments of gold
like necklaces, bracelets, rings, sword-hilts etc., Mycenae civilization reached its most advanced
stage and the invasion of the mainland by the Achaean Greeks must have led to its destruction.
Tiryns another centre of this civilization was brought to light in 1885. This city is also
situated on a small hill in Argolis and is surrounded by a wall built in the Cyclopean style and
hence called the ‘walled city’. Within the city there are long galleries with doorways leading into
separate apartments for men and women. The walls are decorated with paintings. A fire might
have caused the destruction of the city.
7.3.8 Importance of the Aegean Civilization
On the basis of some similarities between the Aegean and Egyptian civilizations some

scholars, regard the former as an offshoot of the later. Through the Philistines who came from
the Aegean world, the Aegean’s influenced the later Hebrew and Phoenician cultures.
Notwithstanding its limited impact, its importance consists in the fact that it was one of the very
few ancient civilizations which secures even for its humblest citizens a degree of happiness
and prosperity. In its love of comfort and amusement, in its individualism and courage for
experimentation the Aegean culture breathes a modern sprit.
7.4 Hellenic Civilization
The Acheans and the Dorians, the earliest of the Greek invaders who descended on the
mainland of Greece were transformed into a civilized people by the Aegean’s who had earlier
settled in Greece and had evolved a highly advanced culture. The Homeric Age (1200-800

B.C) constitutes, the first period of the history of the Greeks. By the end of this period the old
village communities were replaced by larger political units, the city states chief of them being
Athens, Sparta, Thebes, Corinth and Megara. Under the leadership of Lycurgus and Solon
respectively Sparta and Athens became pre-eminent states of Greeks.
The 8th and 7th centuries B.C. saw a great movement of expansion of the Greeks towards
Western Asia, Black Sea, Africa, Italy and Sicily thus creating Hellas, Greece in its widest
sense, Greek democracy and Greek freedom were in grace peril when Greece, thanks to
Athenian leadership. After the war Athens refused to dissolve the offensive and defensive
alliance she had concluded with a number of Greek states, (the Dulian League) and gradually
she transformed it into a naval empire for the advancement of her own interests. During this

118
period Greece reached unprecedented speaks in poetry, drama, philosophy, history and art.
The Peloponnesian War brought this Golden Age to a suicide end. Finally came Phillip and
Alexander who succeeded where the others had filed in the past, viz., to politically unify the
whole of Greece under the leadership of a single state. Under Alexander the Hellenic culture,
too powerful to contain it within the narrow bounds of Greece overflowed into Asia, Africa,
Egypt and other parts of the Orient and influenced the cultures of those regions. With the
fusion of Oriental elements the Hellenic culture assumed a new form in which it is called the
Hellenistic culture.
7.4.1 Social Institutions
Society during the golden age consisted of three distinct groups the citizens, the metric
or resident foreigners and the slaves. In the first were included only those born of citizen

parents. The second consisted largely of persons who did not belong to the particular city but
who were Greeks. The citizens attended to their public duties relating to the state and government
so much and so they had little time to devote to agriculture, industry or trade. For all these they
depended on the metrics and slaves. Slaves did most of the manual labour and women slaves
did most of the domestic work. They also did a great part of clerical and executive work in
industry, commerce and finance.
On the whole they were well treated and were rewarded for faithful service by being
liberated. They were allowed to own property. An amazing degree of social and economic
equality prevailed among these classes. The mass of the people had a low income and led a
simple life. A larger piece was draped around the body as an extra piece particularly when

going out door. Few wore sandals. Each citizen wanted to have a reasonable income and
abundant leisure for politics and for intellectual and artistic activities. Education which was
largely in private hands consisted of not only learning the three R’s but also drawing, music
and gymnastic, Higher education was provided by professional teachers called sophists.
Both sexes wore long hair and men grew moustaches and beards. They used various
kinds of perfumes and cosmetics. Women wore ornaments like bracelets, necklaces and ear
rings. A man is permitted to take a concubine. Divorce was permissible under certain conditions.
Woman was not accorded a high status in society and she was a subordinate to man.

119
7.4.2 Economic Life
The basic economic activity of the Hellenic society was agriculture. Nearly all the peasants
owned the land they tilled. Clan control of land disappeared and private ownership was firmly
established. Since the soil was poor and rainfall meagre the agricultural output was generally
inadequate to sustain the population and without imported food Greece would have starved.
This was one of the factors that prompted colonization in the early stages. Olive and grapes
were grown in plant, cattle rearing were another occupation, horses, sheep, goat, asses and
mules were reared. Bees were kept as providers of honey. Vegetables and fruits were grown.
Industry was not highly developed. Mining was one of the important industries which
absorbed a large labour force. But mines were mostly owned by the state. The silver mines of

Laurium were well known. Most of these industries were organized on a small scale tanning,
shoemaking, ship-building, black-smithy, carpentry were other industries. Common textiles for
the most part were produced in homes. From the age of Pericles this system of domestic
production was replaced by the factory system.
Surplus production led to trade; but in the early stages it was not brisk because transport
was difficult. Sea transport was easier and cheaper. Harbours like the Piraeus offered all facilities
for export trade, warehouse, banks, etc., olive oil, wine, pottery, minerals, marble tin and some
of the articles of export while grain, fruits, cheese, meat, fish, copper, iron, tin and timber were
articles of import. Greece had trade connection with the Propontis, Hellespont, Italy and Sicily,

Egypt, Syria and Phoenicia. It is this maritime trade of Greece that made her prosperous and
provided her with the news of cultural development.
7.4.3 Greek Religion
Greek religion which was polytheistic was free from dogmas, complicated rituals and
sacraments. Greek religion did not develop a separate class of priests. Just as the father acted
as the priest in the family, the chief magistrate of the city was the high priest of the state
religion. The Greeks endowed their gods with attributes similar to their own, human bodies,
human weaknesses and wants.
The Greeks believed that their Gods dwelt not in the sky but on the summit of Mt. Olympus
in northern Greece. The Greek pantheon consisted of deities like Zeus, the sky god, Poseidon
the sea god, Aphrodite goddess of love, Thena goddess of war and the presiding deity of the

120
city of Athens Apollo the sun god and Hades, the guardian of the realm of the dead. The
Greeks did not worry about the life after death and so they did not preserve their dead bodies.
Sacrifice was an important part of worship. Offerings were made to please the gods and
to get favours from them. Their religion was devoid of any ethical content. The primitive religious
beliefs of the Greek of the early period continued in the later periods also, though some changes
came at least among the intellectuals. The orphic cult and the Eleusinian cult came into vogue
in the later days.
7.4.4 Greek Philosophy
The word philosophy is derived from a Greek word which means love of wisdom. The
Greek thinkers brought all branches of knowledge under philosophy. They attempted to find
answers to every problem like the nature of the universe, truth, meaning and purpose of life
etc.
a)The Milesian School

It was in the 6th century B.C. that Greek philosophy and its beginnings in the commercial
city of Millets on the shores of Asia Minor. Here for the first time thought became secular and
sought rational and consistent answers to the problems relating to world and man. The founder
of this school was Thales. He was called ‘sophos’ or sage by the Greek people and was placed
first among the Seven Wise men of Greece. His work was continued by his pupil Anazimander
who said this primary substance could not by any particular thing like water but some substances
which he calls indefinite or boundless. Another member of this school, Anazimenes declared
that the original matter of the universe is air and maintained that the essential difference between
things consists merely in the amount of the basic substance they contain. The significance of

the Milesian school consists in the fact that it repudiated the mythological beliefs of the Greeks
about the origin of the universe and substituted a purely rational explanation.
b)The Pythagorean School
Before the end of the sixth century we see a new trend in Greek philosophy which no
longer concerned itself with the problems of the physical world but began to deal with abstract
questions like the nature of being, meaning of truth and position of the divine in the scheme of
things.

121
c)The Atomist School
The debate regarding the nature of the universe was brought to a close by the Atomists,
the chief among who were Leucippus and Democritus who held that the universe is made up
of an infinite number of indivisible atoms, differing in size and shape. The only difference
between a man and a tree is the difference in the number and arrangement of their atoms.
d)The Sophists
About the middle of the 5th century there was a reaction against the old ways of thinking
and a new school of philosophy came into existence which was no longer interested in the
study of the nature of the universe but turned its attention to problem more intimately related to
man. They are said to have charged heavy fees for the instruction they gave. The greatest
among them was Protagoras of Abdera who sums up the essence of sophist philosophy in the

words ‘Man is the measure of all things’. All truth, goodness and beauty are relative to the
needs and interests of man. The scepticism that is implied in their doctrine was perverted by
some of the later Sophists like Gorgias. The Sophists held progressive views on various issues.
They condemned was slavery and the racial exclusiveness of the Greeks. The Sophists, like
the thinkers of enlightenment were the instrument of this re-examination. They provided powerful
stimulus to the pursuit of knowledge and made it fashionable to think.
e)Socrates
The highly relativist and individualistic ideas of the Sophists produced a strong reaction,
for it was felt, that it left unchallenged. It may lead to atheism and anarchy. A new school of
philosophy rose based on the conviction that truth is real and those absolute standards exist.

Socrates, Plato and Aristotle are the three distinguished representatives of this school.
Socrates, was born in Athens, his father being a sculptor and mother a mid-wife. It used
to be humorously said of him that he merely continued his mother’s trade, but in realm of ideas
helping other to deliver themselves of their conceptions. This greatest teacher of Greece
resembled the Sophists in so far as he questioned every common belief and superstition but
unlike them received no pay for his teaching. He was considered a rebel and was accused of
corrupting young minds. The Athenian government condemned him to death. As a law-abiding
citizen he drank the poison (hemlock) and died fearless.

122
f)Plato
Socrates a most distinguished disciple was Plato, who unlike his master was a prolific
writer. Some of his important works are the Apology, the Republic and the Laws. Plato
propounded the doctrine of ideas. The world we perceive without senses is constantly changing.
As a political philosopher he had no faith in democracy and in his Republic he described an
ideal state where wise men rule. He described an Utopian state where philosophers were
kings. Plato started his academy where he taught his ideas to his disciples.
g)Aristotle
One of Plato’s worthy disciples was Aristotle who became the tutor of Alexander the
Great. Like his teacher he too started an institution to teach his ideas called Lyceum. He was a
master of many subjects, logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics, natural science, etc. He agreed

with Plato that ideas (from as he calls them) are real but he asserted that ideas cannot exist
independently. He classifies different forms of government like monarchy, aristocracy, democracy
and considers polity (which is midway between oligarchy and democracy) as the best.
7.4.5 Literature
In the evolution of Greek literary forms four stages may be noted-epics, elegies, lyrics
and dramas. In the early stages the most common form of literary expression was the epic,
narration of heroic deeds. The well known of the Greek epics are the lliad and the Odyssey of
Homer which exerted a powerful influences on later writers, particularly the tragedians of the
Golden Age. The age following Homer saw tremendous social and economic changes and
these were reflected in the new forms of literary expression the clergy. Though elegies, had

various themes, generally they were devoted to melancholy reflection.
Well known among the elegie writers were Solon and Theognis. In the 6th and 5th centuries
the elegay was replaced by the lyric which is usually sung to the music of the lyre. The founder
of Greek tragedy was Seschylus who is said to have written eighty plays of which about eight
only are existent. Sophocles was the greatest among tragedians who had written about one
hundred plays of which only a few are available Oedipus Rex, Antigone and Electra are some
of them. Euripides was the first to give even the ordinary man a place in his drama.
An account of Hellenic literature will be incomplete without a reference to historical prose
literature. Herodotus is the famous historian of Greece who in the course of his extensive

123
travels in Persia, Egypt, Sicily and Southern Italy gathered materials for his great history of the
Persian Wars. In spite of his imperfections as a historian, he is regarded as “the father of
history”. Thucydides is another historian who wrote about the Peloponnesian War. Hence he
is regarded as the first scientific writer of history. But one defect in his work is that he over
emphasizes political events and ignores social and economic factors.
7.4.6 Art
Form and rhythm, precision and clarity, proportion and order are the essential qualities of
Greek art. ‘Beauty without extravagance’ was the watch word. Their works of art were produced
not only with an aesthetic sense but with an eye on utility and were known for their simplicity
and restraint. Their sculpture and painting depicted human types rather than individuals.

The evolution of Greek art may be studied in their stages; (1) the archaic (7th and 6th
centuries) when art was under Egyptian influence; (2) the idealistic (5th century) when art reached
its perfection and (3) realistic (4th century B.C) when sculpture dominated and art became
individualistic.
7.4.7 Architecture
Three distinct styles of architecture developed the Dorian, the Ionic and the Corinthian,
though actually the last belongs to the Hellenistic period. The Pantheon in Atheas, the temple
of Athena, the best example of Greed architecture is the Propylael which is a new and finer
gateway to the Acropolis. The Greek gods situated on the Acropolis, Phidias and Callicrates
were the two artists who were entrusted with the construction of the Parthenon and other
temples.
7.4.8 Sculpture
Phidias was the greatest sculptor of Greece to whom Pericles entrusted the execution of

all the works of art in Athens. His greatest work was the gigantic statue of Athena made of ivory
and gold. His masterpiece is the statue of Zeus at Olympia. Myron was another great sculptor
of the period, famous for his statue of the Discus Thrower. The maker of the statue of Hermes,
Praxiteles was another well known sculpture, the works of Lysippus exhibit qualities of realism
and individualism.

124
7.4.9 Painting
Greek painting in the early stages was devoted to the adornment of wares. In the next
stage it was architectural when colour was given to public buildings and statues. Then they
started decorating dwellings and making portraits. Polygnotus was a great painter of the 5th
century who adorned several public buildings with murals. ‘Sack of Troy’ and ‘Odysseus in
Hades’, are some of his well known frescoe paintings. Panaenus was another painter who
painted the ‘Battle of Marathon’. Phidias was also a great painter.
7.4.10 Science
The Hellenic period was not marked by any great development in the field of science.
That was naturally so because the interests of the Greeks in the Hellenic period were chiefly
speculative and artistic. Most of the scientific achievements that are ascribed to the Greeks

were those made during the Hellenistic period. With the exception of some developments in
mathematics, biology and medicine, scientific progress was very little. In the field of Mathematics,
Thales of Miletus originated many theorems. Pythagoras developed a theory of numbers
classifying them into odd, even, primer composite, etc. He discovered the theorem that the
square of the hypotenuse of any right angled triangle is equal to the sum of the squares on the
other two sides. Hippocrates of Chios was the first to develop geometry as a science.
Anaximander evinced keen interest in the science of biology and developed a crude theory of
organic evolution. It was Aristotle who made a rich contribution to the development of biology.
A pioneer in the field of Medicine was Empedocles but more important was the work of

Hippocrates of Cos. He was the first to reject a supernatural cause. He had a wide knowledge
of drugs but he relied more on rest and diet as cure for diseases. He improved the practice of
surgery.
7.5 Hellenistic Civilization
Before we proceed to examine the salient features of the Hellenistic civilization we should
understand the difference between Hellenic and Hellenistic. The dividing line between the
Hellenic and the Hellenistic civilization is 323 B.C. when Alexander the Great died. With this
the old Hellenic civilization comes to an end and a new pattern of culture, different from the
previous one emerges. This new culture is a result of the fusion of Greek and Oriental elements
which was made possible by Alexander’s conquests in the East. This brought Hellenic culture
face to face with the cultures of the East. This resulted in intermingling of peoples and fusion

125
of ideas and most of the ideals represented by the Greeks were thrown overboard by the new
ideas from the Orient.
It is to this new civilization which lasted till the beginning of the Christian era, the term
Hellenistic is commonly applied. Though the Greek language and Greek nationals continued
to dominate many fields the culture of this period was basically oriental in spirit. For example
the Greek idea of democracy and the love for it were superseded by despotism of the oriental
type. The classical Greek love for simplicity and moderation were replaced by love for luxury
and excess. The economic organization underwent a market change. Small scale production
gave place to big business. In the realm of thought the robust confidence of the earlier period
in the power of the mind gave place to defeatism ultimately leading to the sacrifice of logic to
faith.

7.5.1 Political Institutions
Oriental monarchy proved more powerful than Greek democracy and impressed its form
on the west. The dominant form of government in the Hellenistic age was despotism and the
successors of Alexander who ruled the Greek states were deified and claimed divine right to
rule. They formed themselves into associations and two such associations came into existencethe Achaean league consisting of all the states of Peloponnesus except Sparta and Aetonalian
league consisting nearly of all states of Central Greece excepting Athens.
7.5.2 Society
Society during this period enjoyed a high degree of prosperity though occasionally there
were periods of economics crisis. But this prosperity was confined to the ruling class and the
upper classes. The Hellenistic age saw the emergence of many big cities like Alexandria,

Antioch, Seleucia etc. and cities like Alexandria with its public buildings, parks, museums,
libraries, etc, became the centre of Hellenistic culture. Women of all classes moved freely
through the streets doing shopping.
7.5.3 Economic Life
Under the successors of Alexander vast changes took place in the economic life of the
Greeks. We see far-reaching changes taking place in agriculture. There was concentration of
land holdings. Small farmers found it difficult to compete with large estate holders. Industry
also was brought under strict state control and regulation. The Ptolemies and Seleucids for

126
example established factories and shops in every village and town. These brought huge profits
to the government. Besides, privately owned enterprises were also fixed by the government.
Alexandria became a flourishing emporium of trade. To facilitate commerce an inter-national
money economy based on gold and silver coins came into existence. Banking institutions also
appeared making available credit facilities to businessmen and traders. Because of the large
availability of capital interest rates came down from 12 per cent to 7 per cent. As a corollary to
all these developments, big business houses came into existence, speculative trading intense
competition, development of insurance and advertising were other important developments.
7.5.4 Religion and Philosophy
The religious beliefs of the Greeks of the pre-Alexandrian days disappeared yielding

place to new trends. The mystic cults like the Orphic and the Eleusinian became popular. The
cult of the Egyptian Mother Goddess and the astral cult of the Chaldeans spread rapidly.
Mithraism and Gnosticism which were offshoots of Zoroastrianism led to the dispersion of the
Jews in the Hellenic land and their religious beliefs had considerable influence on those of the
Greeks. Some of the philosophical schools that flourished during this period are Stoicism,
Epicureanism and Skepticism. Zeno, the founder of Stoicism taught that all things happen in
accordance with a predetermined pattern with a national purpose and that man is not a master
of his fate.
7.5.5 Literature
Greek language became the common language of the Hellenistic world. Writing became
a profession and a large number of intellectuals and schools produced many works but they

were of mediocre quality. A few works of high standard were also produced. Drama, Pastoral
and Mime were the three forms of poetry. But the poets of the period preferred to write comedies
only. The new comedies have as their theme romantic love, its pains and pleasures. Philemon
and Meander were two of the great writers of comic drama Theocritus was a writer of pastoral
and mimes. The Hellenistic age produced a variety of prose literature essays, biographies,
encyclopaedias, novels and histories. Historiographical tradition was established by Ptolemy
and Pyrrhic of Equities which culminated, in Caesar. The greatest of the Hellenistic historians
was Polypus. He wrote his history with a wide background of education, travel and experience.
From the standpoint of his scientific approach and his zeal for truth he deserves to be ranked

next only to Thucydides. But unlike Thucydides he realized the importance of social and economic
forces. Other forms of prose writings that were popular were biographies and Utopias.

127
7.5.6 Art
In its fertility and originality Hellenistic art bears comparison with the earlier period. In the
place of humanism, restraint and balance of the art of the earlier period we find new exaggerated
realism, sensationalism and voluptuousness. Some examples of the architecture of this period
are the temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens, Apollo’s sanctuary at Delos, the many public
buildings at Alexandria, especially its Lighthouse.
Hellenistic sculpture also lacked restraint and grace. In the island of Rhodes a distinct
school of sculpture developed. The outstanding specimens of this school are the bronze statue
of the Sun God Helios, and the figure of Laocoon, the Trojan priest. The Hellenistic painters
brought nature into the art and anything human fascinated them. They chose themes from the

life of the common man. The walls of palaces and residences of rich were adorned with paintings.
The mosaic art also was developed during this age.
7.5.7 Science
Growth of scientific knowledge reached its climax during the Hellenistic period many of
the scientific achievements of today would not have been possible but for the work done by the
scientists of Alexandria, Rhodes, Pergamum and other cities. The sciences that developed
during this period were astronomy, mathematics, geography, medicine and physics. In
mathematics and astronomy the Greeks owed much to Egypt and Babylon respectively.
Aristarchus of Samos contributed much to the enormous size of the universe. Later Aristarchus
had to abandon this hypothesis. He is called the Copernicus of the ancient world. He laid the
foundations of the science of Trigonometry.

Ptolemy of Alexandria was another noted astronomer of the Hellenistic period. Though
he made few original discoveries, he systematized the works of others. His chief contribution
was the geocentric theory which assumes that the sun and other planets revolve round the
earth. The well-known mathematician of the period was Euclid who was the author of the work.
Elements of Geometry which is a standard work on the subject. Hipparchus was also a great
mathematician. Much of Hellenistic geography owes its development to Eratosthenes of
Alexandria. In his ‘Geographical’ he describes the earth depicts the physical features of each
region.
Herophilus was worked at Alexandria developed the science of medicine. He dissected
the eye and gave an account of the retina and optic nerves. He dissected the brain and described

128
its various parts. He discovered the significance of the pulse and its use in diagnosis. He
distinguished arteries from veins and studied the liver and pancreas. He is regarded as the
greatest anatomist of antiquity.
Erasistratus is considered as the founder of physiology as a separate science. He
gained a thorough knowledge of the various organs and their functions by practicing vivisection.
He conceived the art of medicine as prevention through hygiene rather than as cure through
therapy. Archimedes was responsible for making physics as separate science. He discovered
the law of specific gravity and formulated the principles of the lever, pulley and screw. Some
scientists like Heron of Alexandria devoted their attention to applied science and a number of
mechanical devices were invented.
