9.1 Introduction
The broad territorial expanse of China and the great number of people inhabitating the
land make it one of the most important countries in the world. China is one of the thickly
populated countries in the world. The country possesses a rich cultural heritage and hoary

past. It is one of the few countries which offered ready residence to the Stone Age man and
also yield human fossils belonging to that period. The finding of these fossils which is also

166
known as Peking Man proclaims that China served as one of the cradles of stone age man.
The country developed contacts with a number of other countries in the world, from very ancient
period and that is attested by the Chinese records or annals.
The climate is monsoonal, but in the northern part it is much colder than India. There are
deserts, mountain peaks, vast upland plateaus and many fertile river basins. Among the river
basins are the Yantzee Kiang, Hwang Ho and Sikiang. The rivers rise in the western highlands
and run towards east. There were no forests to clear for agriculture, and the level land made
transportation easy. The handicaps to agriculture are insufficient rainfall and the tremendous
amount of erosion that accompanies the seasonal downpours. Navigation also is hindered by
the excessive amount of sediment in the streams. But China possesses a large volume of

natural resources such as coal, iron and soil which were not important in the classical period,
but have become the source of attraction in modern times.
The above said topographical features made an impact on human life and contributed to
the development of culture and civilization from time immemorial. China is not easily accessible
because desert and high mountains make formidable barriers. In spite of these, she developed
contacts with many countries including India from very ancient times.
The Chinese belong to Mongolian race and there had been less racial mixing as it was
inaccessible to foreign people. As there were many types of Chinese, so there were many
cultures, which developed more or less independently of each other. Space does not permit a
description of each, but it may be possible to give a general impression of Chinese civilization.

The Chinese people developed a dynamic and rich civilization at the eastern end of
Eurasia. Geographically and politically united by Emperor Huang Di in the 200 B.C., China’s
civilization has alternated between times of political centralization with rule from a capital city
and times of fragmentation when local warlords dominated. Confucianism, a belief system
which supported centralized political power, a professional bureaucracy, and a hierarchy of
social relationships has remained influential in China for 2500 years.
With a dense population from early times, the Chinese have achieved high levels of
productivity and exported many sought-after goods such as iron, porcelain and silk. With a
common language, paper to print it on, and a varied and distinctive cuisine, the people have
been rightfully proud of their cohesive and distinctive culture. They have traditionally viewed

themselves as living in “The Middle Kingdom” – that is, the centre of the known world, but have
sometimes seen neighbours and outsiders as “barbarians” from whom they demanded tribute.

167
9.2 Political Institutions
China has few archaeological remains, but the Chinese have an abundance of historical
records. Each of the more important rulers appointed a board of historians to record the
important events of his reign. These writings were more than mere political annals, for they
contain accounts of agriculture, social and economic conditions, plagues and wars. It is
interesting to note that the Chinese always gave importance to actual history and preferred it to
epic poetry or mythological accounts. They were ardent believers in reality rather than mythology.
According to one account there were 13 celestial emperors who ruled China for about 18,000
years. This account is not dependable. However the political history of the country begins from
about the 8th century B.C and there are authentic records for the same.
9.2.1 Mythological rulers

The earliest political documents contain little more than a list of royal names. Chinese
mythology records the names of rulers as far back as 3000 B.C. Fu Hsi (2852 B.C. according
to legend) was the first civilized ruler and taught his people marriage, writing, fishing, music,
painting, and domestication of animals and the feeding of silkworms.

168
He was succeeded by Shen Nung who supposedly introduced cultivation, commerce
and medical science and technology. The later rulers are said to have slowly introduced compass,
wheel, built houses and invented the calendar, which contributed a lot to the development of
Chinese culture in the later period. Though these accounts are legendary, they throw some
glimpses into the revolutionary changes inject into the Chinese society and culture.
9.2.2 Early Dynastic Rulers
One of the earliest dynasties was Shang dynasty which held sway in and around Hwang
Ho Valley (from 1766 - 1122 B.C.) then it was followed by Zhou (1122 - 221 B.C.). Chinese
were ruled by king-saint functioning as a royal priest as well as secular head of the government.
He was considered as an appointee of God. Government officials were carefully selected on

the basis of their qualification and experience in horsemanship, writing and fine arts. The king
was expected to identify himself with the people sharing their joy and sorrow in equal terms.
After the fall of the Chou rule the empire was split into a number of small feudal states and that
heralded the “age of the feudal” in China.
9.2.3 Feudal Age
During this age the king became weak and the nobles became strong and powerful and
worked for the creation of feudal states. It was the age of countless wars, treacheries, deeds of
heroism and adventures. Great emphasis was laid on the army. Soldiers became heroes and
highly respected by the people. There were number of self-styled war lords and they waged

169
war on each other, entered into alliances against a powerful lord and lastly fought among
themselves over the ruins. Hence there was a continuous struggle for capturing Central authority
and that was achieved by one Shih Huang-Ti (246 - 210 B.C.) in the province known as Chin.
The name China is said to have come from the word chin. He was considered to be the first
Emperor of China and he was a friend of the poor.
After his death Hang dynasty took over the administration and established its authority in
a greater part of China. Wen Ti (179 - 157 B.C.) was the greatest ruler of this dynasty. He took
steps to spread literacy among the people and reformed the penal code. Then came Wu Ti
(140 – 87 B.C.) who made an attempt to establish centre authority. He divided the country into
provinces and they were administered by his Governors. He patronized art and architecture.

Libraries were set up to preserve records and literary works. There was an Imperial Library
with thousands of volumes of books and manuscripts. There were books on medicine,
mathematics, astronomy and war. China saw progress in all walks of life and there was peace,
plenty and prosperity. Chinese call this period as “the Golden Age” and call themselves “sons
of Han”.
9.2.4 Tang and Song Dynasties
The rule of the Hans dynasty ended by about 221 A.D. and there arose two great dynasties
during the beginning of 7th century A.D. They are known as Tang and Song dynasties. The
Tang dynasty expanded the empire and reunited China after the fall of Hang dynasty. Emperor
Tai Tsung (627 - 649 A.D.) was one of the ablest rulers. He introduced many reforms in the
fields of education and civil code acts.
Another Tatar invasion ended the Tang rule but upon the ruin arose the Song dynasty

(960 -1279 A.D), Tai Tsu (960 - 976 A.D), the solider emperor, attempted to restore civil service
on the basis of Confucian principles. Economic life was carefully supervised by the state.
Another great ruler was Wang An-Shih (1021 - 1086 A.D.) who had made many
administrative reforms. He was more concerned with the upliftment of poor-working classes.
He desired to nationalize the big commercial establishments, industries, and agriculture
operations with a view to helping the working class. He enforced strict laws to protect the poor
from the clutches of the rich. He was opposed by the conservations. There were violent invasions
which posed danger to the security and unity of China.

170
Wang was thrown out of office and Chinese Government fell back into chaos and disorder.
In 1279, the last Song prince was murdered and the country was passed under the control of
the Mongols.
From the above, it can be summarized that the main political characteristics of Chinese
civilization are:
 Pervasiveness of authoritarian rule and hierarchy.
 Pattern of decentralized domains ruled by lords alternating with centralized rule by an
emperor in a capital city.
 Political centralization made legitimate by the theory that the Emperor had the Mandate
of Heaven to rule.
 A scholar-civil servant class who took a rigorous exam which tested, among other things,
knowledge of Confucian classics.
 A system of relationships established by Confucianism where the nation was pictured as
a family with the father, or Emperor, at its head. Social harmony meant centralized rule

with a strong father-figure at the top.
9.3 Social Conditions
The social structure of Ancient China was the key to determining who was the more
important and most respected people of ancient times in China. The King and his family were
placed on the topmost level of the ancient Chinese social pyramid. Five groups such as the
Shi (gentry scholars), the Nong (peasant farmers), the Gong (craftsmen and artisans), the
Shang (traders and merchants) and the Nubi (slaves). During the early centuries of the Christian
era, the nobles and the priests wielded tremendous influence in society and were highly
respected. They enjoyed most of the social privileges. But as centuries rolled on, common
people received the attention of the rulers and nobles. They were included in the army and
even the peasant population joined the army. The merchant class also gained more and more

importance particularly during the Chin period. During the first few centuries after the Christian
era, certain social and economic reforms were set in motion. For example, every man and
woman had a right to receive certain amount of land for life time. In addition to this, ‘personal
land’, ‘mulberry land’ was also given to the farmers.

171
9.3.1 Family Life and Women
Father was the head of the family, there was no family priest and the head of the family
performed the religious rites. The tradition of male superiority in China was part of Confucian
belief, and it continued from ancient times to the 20th century. The eldest male in the family
ruled as an autocrat. Women were expected to be devoted to parents in their youth and to
husbands and husband’s families thereafter. Fidelity, chastity and modesty were ideal feminine
qualities. A woman’s family provided a dowry to her husband’s family when they married.
Female infanticide was common in times of famine. The female members of the ruling family
and wealthy class received education and training in various fine arts and useful crafts. In 960
A.D. during the Song dynasty the practice of foot-binding began. This meant a woman would

have an odd, stilted walk and a minced gait which men found attractive. In addition to footbinding, another sign of double standards could be seen with emperor’s possessing concubines,
sometimes hundreds of them.
9.3.2 Food and Drink
Rice and wheat were used for preparation of food from the early times. Millet became the
chief Chinese cereal from the early period. Soya beans, buck wheat and tea were very commonly
used during that period. Drinking was popular among the people from the beginning. Wine was
made from a special variety of millet and it was a popular drink. Numerous wine jars were
discovered in the excavations of sites belonging to the Shang dynasty.
9.3.3 Towns, Places and Houses
Numerous towns were created. Each town was surrounded by a moat and provided with
gateways. A mud wall was built to protect the city from invaders during the Shang dynasty. The

places were located at the centre of the city. There were separate quarters for artisans, close
to the palaces. Houses were built of mud and burnt bricks. They were either in square or
rectangular plan but Chinese preferred wood to brick and stone. Bamboo was imported from
India. Varieties of furniture such as tables, and chairs couches were produced. From the period
of Han-dynasty glass was made as early as 2nd century B.C. numerous vessels of bronze,
silver, copper and iron were unearthed from excavations belonging to a period ranging from
1600 B.C. to the medieval times. These vessels throw a flood of light on the status and diet
habits of the Chinese at different periods. Among the vessels, these of celadon ware deserve
special mention. They bore glossy green surface and thin, brittle walls incised and painted

172
designs were executed on-these vessels. They also bore stamped decorative features. These
vessels were used both by the rich and the poor.
9.3.4 Slavery
Slavery was a well known institution particularly in the early medieval times. The slaves
were owned both by the State and the private owners. These unfortunate people belonged to
the peasant community. They were regarded as pieces of property according to the law.
9.3.5 Marriage
There were different groups of people or families such as peasant families, shepherd
families, kiln families, sooth-sayer families, medical families, musician families, etc. They have
to marry within their category and no inter-caste marriage or adoption was allowed.
9.3.6 Sports and Leisure
Hunting, fishing, riding, wrestling, boating were some of the outdoor games favoured by
the Chinese. Chess was also a favoured game.
9.4 Economic Developments

The great floods and extreme droughts in China necessitated centralized supervision of
economic activity. Irrigation was developed very early, the work being supervised and financed
by the rulers. Great canals were constructed; which were used for both drainage and irrigation
purposes. The Han emperors undertook at least 56 water-control projects. By the 6th century
of the Christian Era, the elaborate water-control projects in the Yangtze Valley were completed.
9.4.1 Agriculture
The Chinese showed great aptitude for the development of agriculture as it was the
mainstay of the people. Irrigation was a boon to agriculture and therefore much attention was
paid to improve irrigational facilities. China was threatened by natural calamities like floods
and droughts very often and hence great care was shown to water-control projects in all periods

of Chinese history. Millet, rice, wheat were the chief crops cultivated from the very beginning
soyabeans, buck wheat and tea were other items in Chinese trade.

173
9.4.2 Industries
Besides agriculture there were other major industries which contributed to the development
of Chinese economy. Chief among them were carpentry, textiles, pottery, metallurgy, glass
and ship building. It was an attractive craft as the Chinese liked wooden houses than those of
brick and stone. Besides loval wood, bamboo was introduced from India and it was used along
with the former in the construction plenty of furniture made their appearance during Han dynasty.
The furniture such as coal, couches, chairs and tables were beautifully decorated with carving.
Both cotton and silk were produced in large quantity. However, Chinese silk earned a worldwide fame and was exported to a number of countries including India. The art of pottery was
practiced as a village or cottage industry and a very fine variety known as celadon was

manufactured from the very early days. It has a green glossy surface and made of fine clay. It
was exported to foreign countries on a large scale vessels of various kinds were made.
Decorative designs were executed on the vessels. Stamped designs were also seen on them.
The findings of this pottery beyond the frontiers of China indicate her trade contacts with those
countries.
Metal objects, weapons and agricultural equipment and ornaments were made from the
beginning of 2nd century B.C. Bronze and copper were used for making utensils and ornaments.
While iron was used for making of warfare and agricultural equipments like knife, sickle, etc.
Gold and silver were used for making jewellery and ornaments like bangles, beads, studs, ear
rings, etc. These have been found in large numbers in the excavations of China dating from

1000 B.C. onwards. Chinese knew the technique of identifying the ores and smelting the same
from the very early times special furnaces were preserved into service for melting the metals
and casting the same into required shapes.
Glass was produced in China as early as 200 B.C. and therefore glass objects and
ornaments were very popular. Ships were built in China during the 2nd century A.D. and that
helped them to develop overseas contacts with their neighbours. New trade routes were
discovered. Chinese craftsmen were great experts in wood work and they knew not only to
build ships of various kinds but also repair them.
9.4.3 Trade and Commerce
It is known that trade began as early as the Shang dynasty because sea shells from the
south China coast and the Malay peninsula have been found in tombs. The Chinese transported
goods across the Silk Road in a relay trade conducted by middlemen who bought and resold

174
goods in a series of short stages without going too far from home. Goods moved through the
rugged Kunlun Shan and Tian Shan, mountains and through deserts like the Takla Makan and
Gobi. Merchants sold silk lacquer ware, ironware, and spices and the Europeans sold woolen
and linen textiles, coral, pearls, statuettes, amber, glass and precious gems. Han China and
the Roman Empire were two of the most commercially active empires in the ancient world.
The Parthians in-between took a large share as middlemen in the trade. They exported fruit,
rare birds and ostrich eggs.
Thus, both inland and foreign trade made tremendous progress, roads and water ways
helped the growth of inland trade and smooth flow of commodities from the production centres
to markets. Agricultural products as well as items like silk, cotton, iron, glass and wood were

the articles involved in the local trade transactions. Paper was also a popular item. China
developed intensive trade contacts with a number of countries in Asia and Europe. The art of
ship building and navigation were well known to the ancient Chinese and that knowledge helped
them to develop the foreign trade contacts. The items of export included silk, salt, metals like
iron, paper, jade, lacquer besides porcelain, imports included bamboos, cotton, raw silk from
India. The traders and businessmen were highly respected in society and enjoyed special
status. They were wealthy people and have wielded considerable influence in the administration.
9.4.4 Medium of Exchange
Coins as well as barter were in vogue in the business transaction. During Zhou dynasty
a metal medium of exchange was introduced and later a money economy was developed

along with increased trade transactions. A round coin with a square perforation was treated as
the official money even as early as 3rd century B.C. and copper coins were introduced at the
same time. Money lending and banking were practiced extensively during the 4th century B.C.
9.4.5 Weights and Measures
Several kinds of weights and measures were in vogue from the beginning and the weights
made of terracotta, stone and metals were obtained from the excavation.
9.5 Cultural and Religious Developments
The Chinese, unlike the other peoples we have studied, put little emphasis on art, and in
spite of their long unbroken line of cultural development, there are periods from which there
are no artistic remains. The artistic remains of the ancients are not many however there are
certain periods for which we have enough material.

175
9.5.1 Chinese Art and Sculpture
The Chinese preferred the picturesque art to the monumental. They worshiped their
ancestors with continuous elaborate funeral rites, but they did not raise enduring tombs or
monuments as the Egyptians did therefore we cannot expect much material or existing
monuments to throw light on this vital aspect of their social life.
There are both stone and bronze figures, vessels and other objects unearthed from the
excavations and chance diggings, dating back to the beginning of the Christian era. The stone
sculptures, in round and relief sculptures representing deities, men, women and animals
belonging to the Tang dynasty deserve special mention. They are beautifully executed with life,
rhythm. The deities particularly the one representing Bodhisattva Avalokiteshwara exhibit the

scholarship of the sculptures and their mastery of human anatomy. There are miniature carvings
which represents dancing girls, warriors and wrestlers which throw a flood of light on the
contemporary social and cultural activities. We can infer and form an idea about the dress and
decoration of the ancient Chinese with the help of these carvings and sculptures. These artistic
specimens not only contain religious them but also social scenes such as processions, battles,
entertainments, display of movements and mastery of form.
9.5.2 Architecture
Both secular and religious architecture made rapid strides, however secular architecture
received greater attention. Stone, wood, brick, mud and metals were used in the construction
of such structure. Among the remains, mention may be made of “the Great Wall of China”. It

is one of the most impressive models of Chinese architectural accomplishments. It was built by
King Shih Huang Ti (246 B.C.) for a purely utilitarian purpose. But the wall exhibits the salient
features of the Chinese architecture: the simplicity, grandeur and beauty deserve appreciation
and admiration from the modern architects and civil engineers. The wall runs for several miles
over regions covering plains, deserts and mountains. It has gates with valuated roofs with end
bearing massive square lowers which dominate the landscape.

176
The Great Wall of China
Huge and beautiful palaces constitute the major part of Chinese architecture. For instance
the palace of the King Shih Huang Ti was described by the poets as one of the wonders of the
age (3rd century B.C.). The Chinese buildings were mostly built of wood. The roof was shaped
with a curved tilted top. Similarly, the popularly known – pagoda towers were associated with
the Chinese architecture. The Chinese paid attention not only to the architecture designs but
also to the landscape surrounding the buildings. This is one of the salient features of ancient
and medieval Chinese architecture.
9.5.3 Paintings
Chinese art reached a much higher plane in painting; the later works were executed in
water colours on woven silk. To the Chinese painting was a branch of calligraphy, or beautiful

penmanship. They painted their pictures for their own enjoyment and only infrequently displayed
them. Paintings were executed on wooden boards and clothes. It was practiced to satisfy the
aesthetic thirst. The painted pictures were retained as art specimens. They were not meant for
display. The knowledge of this art was considered as one of the pre-requisites of Chinese
society.
The theme of the paintings varied in different periods. However, the themes included
natural scenes and settings, landscape portraiture and historical events. But theme was by
and large secular in nature. The paintings exhibited perceptiveness, light and shade and
naturalism. These features enhanced the status of this art in Chinese society.

177
Among the painters, Wang Wei (699 - 759 A.D) was considered as a great master of this
century. He was not only a painter but also an author of a treatise on the subject. He was also
a poet. His manual was considered as a standard work in those days. His poems were told in
painted designs as narrative pictures. This suggests the high standard. The Chinese paintings
bore a dreamy effect. Most of the paintings were imaginative but thought provoking. The other
painters of the times were Mu Hsi and Laing K Uel. They were masters in the production of
black and white pictures. Their works exhibited natural objects like mountains, rivers, tree tops
and roofs covered with heavy mist. There were portraits representing priests, sages, saints
and laymen including famous poets.
9.5.4 Chinese Porcelain
The porcelain of the Chinese, one of the greatest of their arts, reached its height in the

Song dynasty. It was green in colour and cannot be reproduced. Various types of vessels such
as plates, cups, bowls, beakers, vases, bottles, jars besides chess boards. Boxes and candle
sticks were manufactured. The study of the vessels gives us some ideas about the diet and
eating habits of the ancient Chinese. The Chinese pottery of early and medieval periods is still
considered to be a sophisticated ceramic tradition ever known in that country. It is known as
celadon water and it was considered to be one of the greatest of their arts and was well known
to the outside world in medieval times. This pottery has also been found in the excavations at
Kanchipuram, Uraiyur and other numerous sites in Tamil Nadu and this fact bears testimony to
the trade and cultural contacts. The Chinese celadon ware serves as one to the criteria to

identify and locate the areas or countries where the Chinese culture made inroads.
9.5.5 Education and Learning
Education was for knowledge sake and was considered to be an essential qualification
for the princes of the royal family. However, education was imparted to one and all who desired
to acquire it. Educational qualifications were prescribed for persons to become government
officials. The aim of the education in those days was to create a thirst for knowledge and to
suppress appetite and hunger. It was taught through models. Both theory and practical were
included in the curriculum. The subjects taught included politics, history, logic, ethics and nature.
Education was not under state control and Confucius, who was a dominant figure in the field of
Chinese education, advocated the above said policy. He was not only a philosopher but also a

great patron of education and learning. Chinese made a tremendous progress in the field of
science, mathematics, astronomy and astrology.

178
The Chinese were aware of the theory of geometry. Eclipses were correctly predicted
and a lunar calendar was devised during the time of Confucius. Careful observations were
made of the location and movements of the clouds and winds. A careful study of the different
stars in the sky was made a map locating as many as 320 stars was prepared during the first
century A.D. Astronomy became a very popular subject and the rulers evinced keen interest in
the study and progress of the subject. The astrologers wielded tremendous influences in the
royal court. Astronomy became a very popular subject and the rulers evinced keen interest in
the study and progress of the subject. The astrologers wielded tremendous influences in the
royal court and they seem to have been consulted in matter of importance. The priests were
the masters of astrology.

Sciences like Chemistry, Physics, Zoology and Medicine were very well known to the
scholars. Chinese believed that earth, water, fire, wood and bold were the basic “elements”.
They also believed that life originated in water and man evolved from the primitive marine life.
Medical science received greater attention; primitive or aboriginal methods as well as
modern scientific methods were put into practice. Magic and superstition in the world of medicine
were not unknown. Treatises on medicine were brought out which mentioned not only diseases
but also methods of treatments. The various organs of the human body such as heart, liver,
kidney, lungs and their functions were thoroughly studied by the physicians of those days.
Diseases such as fever, lung and throat infection and skin diseases were very common. The

medical science received greater attention even during the second century A.D and among the
medical luminaries of the age was one Chang Chung Ching who did a lot of ground work for
the eradication of typhoid fever. He was popularly unknown as the “Sage of Medicine”. Surgery
was also practiced and Hua T’o was the most famous surgeon of ancient China (2nd century
A.D.). He is said to have used anesthetics and performed many operations.
9.5.6 Language and Literature
The Chinese written language has 40,000 characters which are used in the spoken dialects
with nearly 700 monosyllable sound words (vocables). Each vocable has six tones. Further
there are some 600 fundamental signs. The Chinese produced literature in different fields of
study such as History, Politics, Religion, Philosophy, Warfare and Love. There were also
poems dealing with social and cultural life of people.

Confucius was an outstanding figure in the Chinese literature and was ranked as the
great contributor to its development. He was not only a philosopher but also a versatile writer

179
on war, love and history. Among his works mention may be made of the following: Shir Chings
(deal with various subjects like love, war, etc.); Lichi (records of rites); I chang (commentary
on metaphysics); Ch’ Un Ch’iu (spring and autumn annals) and She ching (books of history).
Confucius preserved the rich traditions of the earlier period in his book Chi Ching. This work
includes extracts from various works of the earlier period.
The bulk of Chinese literature is in the form of poems. During Tang period the Chinese
poetry reached a high water mark. Among the poets Lipo and Tu Fu (9th century A.D.) deserve
special mention. Lipo’s work “Wandering Guest” deals with dead heroes and ruined places
regaining their splendour. Tu Fu was called “Keats of China”. He wrote poems on sad theme
such as starvation and suffering.

Though there were numerous prose writer, they were not given due recognition. However
works on Philosophy and Encyclopedia were much respected.
9.5.7 Religion and Philosophy
The ancient Chinese offered worship to nature such as earth and heaven besides to the
sprits and ghosts of the dead. They believed that heaven was the main nature spirit and chief
of the ancestor spirits. Heaven was also considered as a forefather of the ruler. It was not
considered as a sacred place or abode of gods but as the will of the almighty. The king claimed
descent from the heaven and therefore he offered worship to heaven as well as earth once in
every year.
Ordinary people were not able to worship heaven as the king did and therefore they
worshipped the spirits of their ancestors. They believed that there was life after death and

thought that the spirit of the dead reside somewhere and it might come down to the earth to
guide them. Therefore they offered worship to the spirit. No prayer was direct and personal
without manifestations of fear.
Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism were the chief religions in China.
a) Confucianism
Confucianism was a philosophy and not a religion. But the Chinese treated the philosophy
as their religion. During the rule of Zhou dynasty, there were confusion, chaos and social
disorder. The learned men of those times devised some kind of philosophy to achieve social

180
order and stability. These men went from city to city meeting people from different walks of life.
They also approached wealthy and business people for financial support and the later readily
responded and assisted the philosophers in the crusade against poverty, social disorder and
exploitation of the poor. Confucianism was the most outstanding among such philosophers
(551 - 478 B.C.) He was originally known as K’ Ung Ch’i.
Confucius was not the founder of any religion nor the reformer but a great teacher. He
led a luxurious life in his early years and later came to realize that desire or fame was the cause
of suffering. He was more concerned about the character and discipline of the people than
anything else. He was not only a philosopher-teacher but also a good administrator. He served
as a magistrate of a city and that gave him good opportunity to learn politics and political

theories. But he became unpopular because he stressed on good conduct, sincerity and loyalty.
He was driven out of the city by the selfish politicians. But later he became a philosopher. He
spoke nothing about gods and rituals. He did not believe in tales, legends, and spirits. He
preached that god or spirit resides in every man’s heart and therefore he advocated that people
should serve the need and not spirits. He asked “so long you are willing to serve men, how you
can serve the spirits”. Regarding the search for gods he asked “what a superman seeks is in
him”.
Confucius also put forth his views about life after death. He stressed that people should
first understand the life while they are alive. There is no point in trying to understand the life
after death. He was a strict disciplinarian. He wanted people to be kind and sympathetic towards

others. He also wanted them to be pure in their mind and cultivate good habits and conduct. He
was also very particular about observing rules and regulations. He was very punctual and strict
in adhering to certain principles in the day to day life. Much of his philosophy was directed
towards mortality and virtues of mankind.
After his death he was deified. He was canonized “Duke Ni, the All-Complete and All-
Illustrious” in the beginning of the Christian era. He was worshipped and sacrifices were
conducted for him. In 492 A.D. he was canonized the “Accomplished Sage” and later in 1907
the Empress Dowager ranked him with the deities of “Heaven and of Earth”.
Many scholars went round the country to spread his philosophy and established schools:
such schools served as great centres of intellectual activities and they have contributed a lot to

the growth of Chinese civilization during the periods of political vacuum of collapse. His
philosophy and moulded the Chinese mind for well over 2000 years.

181
b) Taoism
Taoism represents the radical beliefs of the Chinese. It was based upon the interpretations
of the teaching of Lao-Tse; who was also deified. Taoism was dominated by a priestly class
called “Professors of Taoism”. They claimed possessing some supernatural powers. They fooled
the Emperor and the people by their teachings which consisted of many superstitions.
c) Lao-tse
He was also a philosopher and wielded very great influence on Chinese society. He
advocated a policy of inactivity and ignorance which could alone save mankind from disaster.
He preached “abandon wisdom and discard knowledge”. But Lao-tse’s philosophy and Taoism
disappeared when Buddhism was introduced into China from India during the first century A.D.
d) Later Philosophers
There were other philosophers like Mencius and Hui Tzu of 3rd century A.D. Their
philosophies had also some influence of Chinese life.

The Chinese philosophy had influenced not only the Chinese, but also many renowned
scholars from the west and east; classical Chinese philosophy was distinguished by two important
concepts viz., life of man in the earth and tradition had a strong divine sanction.
To sum up, the Chinese civilization represents the longest unbroken chain of development
known. Voltaire remarked, “The body of this empire has existed 4,000 years without having
undergone any sensible alteration in its laws, customs, language, or even in its fashions of
apparel”. A tradition of poetry goes back to 1700 B.C. The Chinese, who were civilized when
Greece was inhabited by barbarians, have seen the rise and fall of countless governments and
civilizations. They possess a social organization that has included a greater number of persons
and has endured longer than has any other known to history.

The religious leaders and philosophers of China have hardly been surpassed in any age
or by any civilization. Confucius is outstanding among the philosophers of the world. The
Chinese produced ceramics and painting which, in their kind, are unequaled. The Great Wall
and the many irrigation projects demonstrate their skill in engineering. Until the recent intrusion
of Western imperialists, China remained comparatively free of outside influence. This may be
one reason why progress has been so slow in recent times, because new blood and new

182
ideas, even though they may be introduced by barbarians, give a stimulus to further progress.
The religion of the Chinese has been partly responsible for their backwardness. Ancestor
worship is not conducive to new ideas, but this is perhaps the fault of the people, not of the
religion. It has been a convenient excuse for their indifference to change.

Eurasia.

a capital city and times of fragmentation when local warlords dominated.
 With a dense population from early times, the Chinese have achieved high levels of
