10.1 Introduction
The history of medieval Europe includes the Byzantine and the Saracenic civilizations.
Both were contemporary civilizations having some common features both occupied on the
European continent but possessed vast territory in Africa. Both had Oriental features. In both,
religion was predominant but while Saracens were Moslems. Byzantines were Christians. Both

were theocracies and in both Government and religion were closely inter connected. Both
civilizations were characterized by pessimism, fatalism and mysticism. But while Saracens
made important contributions to philosophy and science, the Byzantines contributed to art and
preserved the legacy of Greece and Rome for posterity. Byzantine civilization lasted for eleven
centuries, while the Saracenic civilization lasted for seven centuries.
The term Saracen was originally applied to an Arab but later it was applied to any member
of the Muslim religion irrespective of his nationality. The Saracens included Jews; Persians
and Syrians. But the founders of the civilization were the Arabs. To the new religion, Islam was

188
the main driving force in development of their civilizations. The Saracenic or Moslem Civilization
was a composite product synthesis of the civilizations of India, Byzantium, Persia and Egypt.
The Moslem achievements were due to Moslem’s ability to synthesize the best in other cultures.
Under Harun-al-Rashid and his successors, Indian and Persian works were preserved and the
works of Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Archimedes were translated into Arabic and later transmitted
to Western Europe. They laid the foundations for the Renaissance.
10.2 The Byzantine Civilization
Traditionally, the Roman Empire disappeared in the 5th century. In 330 A.D Constantine,
the Roman Emperor made Byzantium his capital and called it Constantinople. But its earlier
name Byzantium continued and is used to designate the eastern culture which did not disappear

when the Romans conquered it, but dominated the Romans. The division of the Roman Empire
into Eastern and Western was because the two parts were never completely united. The East
remained basically Greek in culture and the cultural difference became more pronounced after
the decline of the political domination of Rome. Ultimately, two different types of Government
and cultures developed. The later Roman emperors gave up Rome for Constantinople and
adopted the oriental setting for their courts. The religious schism resulted in the establishment
of the Greek orthodox Church. This resulted in the complete separation of the East from the
West in about the middle of the 4th century. After the collapse of the Roman Empire, the East
differed from the West in culture, religion, philosophy, politics and geographical setting. The

Byzantine civilization represented a fusion of the late classical and oriental civilization and
made several contributions to the development of later cultures.
Byzantine culture was more oriental in character. The oriental character was because of
the following reasons. (1) Constantinople faced the orient and most of its territories were outside
Europe. Most important amount these territories were Syria, Asia Minor, Palestine and Egypt.
(2) Greek and Hellenistic elements entered Byzantine culture to a greater extent. (3) The
language was predominantly Greek. (4) Traditions such as literature, art and science were
largely Hellenistic. (5) Finally, Christianity of the Byzantine Empire different from that of Latin
Europe. It was more “mystical abstract pessimistic” and more completely subject to political
control.
10.2.1 Nationalities in the Byzantine Empire

The population of the Byzantine Empire consisted of a number of nationalities. The majority
of the people were Greeks and Hellenized Orientals-Syrians, Jews, Armenians, Egyptians and

189
Persians. The European sections of the population consisted of a number of barbarians,
especially Slaves and Mongols. The slaves came from the Caramathian Mountains in modern
South Western Russia.
The Byzantian Empire
10.2.2 Political History
The early history of the Empire mostly covers the struggles of the Empire with the Germanic
Barbarians and its ultimate success against them. This period lasted from 330-257 A.D. The
history of the Byzantine Empire for the next one thousand years can be divided into four main
periods such as: expansion, peril, recovery and disintegration.
In the 6th century the history of the Empire focuses on the reign of Justinian (527-567)
Justinian’s aim was to restore the Roman Empire to its ancient scope and grandeur. He undertook
a career of expansion and after many years of continuous warfare, captured a part of Spain

from the Visigoths and Italy from the Ostrogoths, Yet, Justinian Empire was smaller than the
Roman Empire at its height. A part of Spain, Gaul, Britain and Southern Germany were
independent of Justinian. Further, the Empire was weekend both militarily and financially.

190
In domestic affairs, as in warfare Justinian tried to restore the dignity and splendour of
the Roman Empire. In this area, his greatest achievements were the codification of Roman law
and the erection of the great Church of Hagia Sophia. With the death of Justinian, the first and
the greatest period of Byzantine history ended. The three centuries from 556-867 were the
centuries of peril (from the middle of the 6th to the middle of the 9th century) Justinian’s
concentrated increasingly upon saving the provinces in the East rather than fighting on both
Eastern and Western fronts.
The next important emperor after Justinian was Heraclius (610-614). When Heraclius
came to the throne, the empire was in a perilous position. The Slavs threatened from the north,
while the Persians and conquered Syria and Jerusalem. One Persian army conquered Egypt

while another advanced into. Asia Minor and reached right opposite to Constantinople. Heraclius
in three campaigns, between 622 and 628 defeated them decisively and regained Syria,
Palestine and Egypt.
While the Persian menace disappeared, a new danger appeared in the form of Muslims.
The struggle with Persia exhausted both empires and made them open to Saracenic conquest.
By the end of the century their armies had subjugated Palestine, Syria, Egypt, North Africa and
part of Asia Minor. While their navies seized Cyprus and Rhodes and harassed Byzantine
shipping in the Aegean, fleet and army were even besieged Constantinople annually for several
years and the distracted in modern Bulgaria. By 700 the eastern empire was threatened with
disintegration. The emperor’s power extended only to the environs of the capital and to a fringe

of ports in the eastern Mediterranean. While his power in the western Mediterranean,
disappeared, in the eastern Mediterranean his power was precarious.
The next great emperor was Leo III who ruled from 717 to 714. He restored order in the
Byzantine Empire. He defeated the Muslims on the sea in several engagements and also
drove them away from Constantinople in 717 and 718. This action of Leo prevented Muslim
capture of Constantinople for another seven centuries. On the domestic front Leo introduced
a new law code and an increased centralization of Government. However, his religious policies
resulted in widespread dissensions and caused the iconoclastic controversy.
The period between 867-1057 A.D was the last period of grandeur. During this period the
strong Macedonian dynasty protected the Empire from Muslim and other invaders. While the

Muslims were defeated in the Aegean, Byzantine armies defeated the Bulgarians who tried to
possess the Balkans, the greatest ruler of this dynasty was Basil II (976-1025). He incorporated

191
the Bulgarian kingdom into the Empire and maintained friendly relations with Russia and
converted the Russian rule to Christianity. The Byzantine customs learning, Christian beliefs
etc, spread all over Russian territory.
After 1057 the Byzantine sect decline was steady. This was chiefly due to the rise of
commercial rivals and to invasions by Muslims and Christians alike. In the 11th century the
Seljuk Turks attacked the eastern provinces, rapidly conquered them and in 1071 defeated a
Byzantine army. This ended with the crusades, plundering attacks upon Byzantine territory. In
1014, the crusaders captured and plundered Constantinople. These disasters did not prove
fatal as the Empire recovered to some extent its strength and prosperity in late 13th and early
14th centuries. Its history was finally brought to an end with the capture of Constantinople by
the Ottoman Turks in 1453.

10.3 Factors responsible for the stability of the
Byzantine Empire
The Byzantine Empire has lasted for a thousand years during which period political life
was not always smooth. It had experienced not only frequent foreign invasions, but also internal
disturbances as a result of place intrigues, mutinies in the army and violent struggles between
political factions. There were as many as 65 revolutions and abdications or murders of more
than 60 emperors. In spite of this political turmoil’s the empire survived for such a long time.
There were several reasons for this stability. They were as follows:
 The first important reason was that the Byzantine Civilization was largely oriental and
relatively static. There were no rapid social changes and Cultural Revolution was gradual.
The conservative aspect of their culture helped them to preserve the nation from rapid
decline.

 The location of Constantinople made it almost impregnable. Surrounded on three sides
by water and on the fourth by a high wall, the capture of the city was very difficult.
 It did not suffer any decline in industry and commerce. Its continuous use for money
economy facilitated trade and the payment of taxes.
 The Byzantine government had a well filed treasury which could always be used purpose
of defence. The annual revenues of the State have been estimated as high as 106 million
dollars.

192
 These riches helped the empire to maintain standing military and naval forces. Military
science was well advanced and the army was also good.
 Another important reason for the enduring character of the empire was the wholesale
loss of African, Italian and eastern territory by the year 700. As a result, the empire was
now more homogeneous.
 Another reason was its centralized system of administration. The Byzantines had a strong
monarchy and a well trained bureaucracy. By providing continuity of administration the
Bureaucracy helped the “empire to face political problems. The emperor was consecrated
with holy oil by the patriarch and thus claimed to rule by divine right. He regulated Church,
State, business and military affairs with an iron hand. He had such absolute control that
he was called as autocrat or which has been carried the English language as autocracy

meaning absolute supremacy.
10.3.1 The Government
The Government was despotic and theocratic. The emperor was an absolute order with
unlimited authority over every aspect of the national life. Empresses also have corresponding
feminine title and in general played an important role. Their images often appeared on the
imperial coinage. In Byzantine history there were impresses also who ruled alone. The emperor
was considered as the Vicar of God and enjoined spiritual dignity also. Even though individual
autocrats were ever thrown, autocracy as such was never challenged. An elaborate and rigid
code of etiquette governed every movement the emperor made every day of the year. He was
responsible for the preservation of the traditional Roman law. As defenders of the faith the
emperors fought against the enemies of the empire. Some emperors were very efficient and

carried out most of their duties personally. But generally the actual functions of the government
were carried out by an elaborate bureaucracy who was very efficient and highly trained. The
main sources of income for the state were land, booty seized in war, fortunes confiscated from
rich men and taxes on persons, sales, profits, import exports and inheritances.
10.3.2 Economy
The economic system was strictly regulated. In fact, the Byzantine Empire has been
described as a “paradise of monopoly of privilege and of paternalism”. The state controlled
every economic activity, workers, wages and prices of products were fixed by the state. In the
industrial field since the guild system operated effectively the individual worker had no freedom
to choose his own profession. Membership of the guild determined his status.

193
To provide for the cheap administration of the system, the emperors encouraged competing
businessmen and workers to act as informers against each other. The state also owned several
industrial fisheries, mines, armament factories and textiles. The Government also tried to
monopolize the silk industry but failed because the government factories could not supply in
accordance with the demand and so permission had to be given to private manufactures to
resume production.
In agriculture, the Roman model was generally followed. Most of the land was divided
into great estates. Only in the hilly and mountainous regions, there were a few independent
farmers. In the agriculture area the population was made up almost entirely of tenant farmers
and serfs. Another importance in the Byzantine Empire was that landed wealth was concentrated

in the hands of the church, especially the monasteries. As life conditions became more difficult
more and more farmers fought for their lands to the monasteries and entered them. The church
lands were cultivated by the serfs. In the 7th and 8th centuries when the economic conditions
improved, several serfs gained their freedom and became owners of the lands they cultivated.
However, this condition was temporary and by 11th century the great estates and the independent
peasantry had completely disappeared.
Geography contributed to Byzantine prosperity. Situated at the crossroads of Europe
and Asia, it became a great trading centre from the Adriatic to Southern Russia. This great
trading centre exported two main types of goods the products manufactured within the empire
itself and the products which came from the East and were re-exported from the empires
trading centres.

Constantinople was not only the greatest trading centre of the early Middle Ages, but was
also a famous manufacturer which supplied Christendom, with many products. The city
specialized in luxury goods and was famous for its textiles. The silk industry was a profitable
state monopoly and the silken fabrics embroidered with gold and silver thread were in great
demand all over Europe. The empire maintained a good solid gold currency which remained
stable for nearly eight centuries and only in the 11th century it was debased.
10.3.3 Society
Byzantine society was essentially urban and luxurious. Constantinople constituted an
industrial community and served as a forerunner of the medieval, a forerunner of the medieval,
commercial cities. Besides Constantinople, there were several famous urban centres like Tarsus,

194
Nicaea, Thessaioniea and others. In Byzantian society the merchant, the manufacturer, and
big land holder constituted the aristocracy. The aristocracy lived in luxury and leisure, cultivated
expensive tastes and patronized fine arts. The middle class merchants and manufacturers
were rich but more conservative. The condition of the peasants had been reduced to serfdom.
The life of the lower classes was poor but compared to conditions elsewhere in Europe their
condition was much better. Industrial and Commercial prosperity provided abundant opportunities
for employment. Even the serfs, when compared to the condition of the serfs elsewhere, was
much better, as in the Byzantine Empire, the landlords powers of exploitation were regulated
by law, similarly, the condition of slaves in Byzantine Empire was much better than elsewhere.

The mortality in the Empire also exhibited extremes of an extravagance and self indulgence
which existed side by side. These contradictory extremes were evident in the individuals as
well as in the Society. At the imperial court also life was characterized by “indolence luxuries
effeminacy and intrigue”. As a result the very term “Byzantine” suggested refined sensuality as
well as refined cruelty. Above all the Byzantines abandoned the typical Hellenistic virtues of
moderation and restraint.
10.3.4 Religion and Philosophy
Byzantines were very much interested in religion. They took active interest in religious
issues and controversies. The Christianity which developed in the Byzantine Empire was not
the Roman Catholicism of Western Roman Empire but was the Greek Orthodox Christianity.
The Church in Byzantine was the Greek Orthodox Christianity. The Byzantine Church not only

dominated religious and cultural life of the people but was also interwoven with the political
structure. It was a state church closely allied with the policies and administration of the empire.
Thus, it saw a department of the state and the emperor exercised wide control over spiritual
affairs. The head of the Church was called as the patriarch and was appointed by the emperor
from a list of candidates submitted by a council of bishops. This authority over church and state
was combined in the office of the emperor. This political philosophy was later adopted by the
Russian rulers.
The most important religious issues which affected the Byzantines were those which
arose out of the Monophysite and the Iconoclastic movements, even though they were exclusively
religious movements. The Merophysites believed that Christ had only one nature viz., the

Divine nature. This movement began in 5th century and reached its heights during the reign of
Justinian (527-565). It was popular especially in Syria and in Egypt. Justinian could not curb it

195
because his wife actress Theodora was an active member of the Scott. In the 7th century the
Monophysites broke away from the Eastern Church. The Scott continues even now as an
important branch of Christendom in Egypt, Syria and Armenia.
The Iconoclastic movement began in 725 when Emperor Leo III issued his famous edict
forbidding image worship as superstitious and irreverent. It was decreased that religious statues
be removed and that all church walls be white washed to cover pictures of the Saint, immediately
notes broke out in Constantinople in protest against image breaking. When the patriarch objected
to the imperial decree, he was replaced by another person who was more agreeable to the
emperors will. Those who condemned the use of icons or images in worship were called as
iconoclasts or image-bracers. The Iconoclastic movement was the result of several factors, (1)

the monophysite movement opposed materialism in religion; (2) it was a protest against
paganism and worldliness in the church and (3) it represented a revolt of some Emperors
against the increasing power of ecclesiastical system.
10.3.5 Importance of the Iconoclastic Controversy
The struggle continued until 9th century. It did not achieve much because the flat or
painted icons were ultimately resorted. It only succeeded in eliminating sculptured
representations. Still the struggle was important. (1) It represented an important stage in the
conflict between Roman Church occupied an important place in Byzantine history. (2) Those
who believed in image worship believed in symbols and ceremonies as indispensable aids to
worship. Their opponents were mostly mystics who condemned any form of institutionalism or

worship of material objects and advocated revival of spiritualism. (3) Many of the ideals of the
Iconoclasts were similar to those of the protestant Reforms of the 16th century. Thus the
movement was the forerunner of the letter Lutheran and the Calvinist movements (4) lastly, the
controversy resulted in the final separation of the Greek and Roman (branches of the) churches
in 1054. For centuries the Papacy in the West and the Orthodox Church in the East has steady
grown apart and had established distinctly separate existences each viewing the other with
suspicion and intolerance. In 1054 with the excommunication of the Patriarch of Constantinople
by the pope the break was final.
The greatest achievement of the Byzantine Orthodox Church was the conversion of the
Slavs to Christianity in about 863 A.D. the whole of east Europe was converted to Christianity.

Thus from the Orthodox Church arose the Russian Church and extension of Byzantine culture
into Russia. Even after the fall of the Byzantine Empire, the Orthodox Church continued to
flourish in Eastern Europe and still retains a great deal of importance and vitality.

196
10.3.6 Law
One of the great contributions of the Byzantines was the revision and the codifications of
the Roman civil law. In 528 Justinian appointed a commission of scholars to meet and classify
the vast, disorganized and contradictor mass of law which has accumulated during centuries
of Roman Government. The result of their work was the corpus juris or the Justinian Code.
The most important section of the code was the Digest, a summary of the writing of republican
and imperial jurists and the institutes, a commentary on the principles underlying the laws.
These two sections contained the philosophy of laws of Government which existed in the time
of Justinian. Appended to the code were the Novels of the laws issued by Justinian in Greek,
the then popular language in the Empire. The classical Roman law and revised to suit the

Oriental and his despotism. By codifying the law, the Byzantines preserved Rome’s priceless
legal heritage and passed it on to posterity.
10.3.7 Literature
In the field of literature Byzantine contribution was not much. They were not interested in
philosophy. They made important contributions to scholasticism, which emerged as the most
popular philosophy of the later middle Ages. They emphasized the importance of reason and
tried to reconcile Aristotle’s teachings of Christianity and the Christian Fathers. Byzantine
literature consisted mostly of compilations and religious writings like Encyclopaedias,
commentaries, hymns, biographies of saints, and lyric poetry and history. The most famous
historian was Procopius, author of the Secret History and contemporary of Emperor Justinian.
10.3.8 Science
Byzantine contribution to science was not much but impressive. The most famous scientists

were John the Grammarian, Aetius, Alexzendor of Tralles and Symeaonseth. John the
grammarian is famous for his work in physics. He was the first to challenge the traditional
theories of motion and gravity. He anticipated the concept of inertia, rejected the belief that the
speed of falling bodies denied the impossibility of creating vacuum. Aetius and Alexander of
Tralles are Encyclopaedists of medicine. Aetius wrote the first description of diphtheria and of
eye diseases. Symeon Seth was a physician, who wrote a medical dictionary in which he
defined curative properties of all available drugs at the time. Powerful Hellenistic influence,
which still survival made possible these achievements.

197
10.3.9 The Arts
The Byzantines loved luxury and splendour. These are expressed in their art Asceticism
prohibited the glorification of man and as a result, sculpture was not permitted to develop.
Architecture flourished and it was mystical and other worldly. The Byzantine civilization was a
mixture of Roman and Oriental elements. Art was no exception to this rule Byzantine art combined
Roman grandeur and engineering talent with the oriental colours and richness of details.
The greatest artistic achievement of the Byzantines was the Church of Santa Sophia
built by emperor Justinian. The church symbolized the inward and spiritual character of
Christianity. As such, the architects did not pay much attention to the external appearance of
the building. Byzantine art was basically Roman in character but contained Hellenistic and

Christian influences. These three influences fused and a new style which uniquely Byzantine in
character grew up.
The church was square-shaped building designed in the form of a cross over the central
square was erected a magnificent round dome which rested on four massive arches. The
dome was a diameter of 107 feet and rises to a height of nearly 180 feet. Around the run the
dome are so many windows which give the appearance that the dome is hanging in mid-air.
The church served as a model to several other structures later on. A favourite design,
with symbolic appeal, was a church in the shape of a cross, surmounted by a dome. Another
development was a fine-doomed church which was cross shaped with central dome at the

198
crossing and a smaller dome on each of the four arms. The most famous existing example of
this design is St. Mark’s Church.
The Byzantines were also good in decorative arts. In decorating Churches, they made
extensive use of mosaics. These were designs produced by fitting together small pieces of
coloured glass or to form figure of plants animals or theological scenes representing Christ,
the Virgin and the saints. The gorgeous colours of the mosaics increased the beauty of the
Church interiors, heightened the emotional appeal of the rituals.
With their interest for vivid colours and elaborate detail, the Byzantines became famous
in a number of decorative arts like carving in ivory-illumination of manuscripts and decoration
of book covers, chests, thrones and altars.
Byzantines also used wall painting for decorating churches. As in mosaics the subject

matter of Byzantine painting was treated symbolically than realistically Byzantine painting
influenced Italian painters like Ojotto and Russian painting.
In sculpture, Sarcophagus decorated with sacred monogram peacocks and fruit vines.
They produced in great abundance, jewelled ornaments, fine silks and chalices. On the whole
Byzantine art primarily due to religious restrictions lacked naturalness, imagination and
spontaneity.
10.4 The Saracenic Civilization
The civilization lasted from roughly 630 A.D. to 1300 A.D. It was important to the Western
world in several ways. It was the orbit of Islam-a new religion. It was responsible for introducing
some revolutionary social and intellectual change in Christian Europe.
10.4.1. Arabia before Prophet Mohammed
Arabia before Mohammed consisted mostly of two groups of people the urban Arabs and

the Bedouins. The urban Arabs who were traders and craftsmen, were literate and wealthy and
lived in cities like Mecca and Yathreb. The Bedouins were nomads, ignorant and superstitions,
followed primitive religion and lived on dated and the flesh and mile of their animals. They were
frequently involved in internecine warfare. There was no organized government. Their religion
was polytheistic and from time immemorial they, worshipped at the shrine, the Kaaba, which
was supposed to contain a sacred black stone miraculously sent down from heaven. The

199
Arabs were converted to Islam by the Prophet Mohammed. Islam means “Total surrender to
the will to Allah”.
Prophet Mohammed, was born in 570 A.D to Abdullah and Aminah of the Kuriash tribe in
the ancient historic city state of Mecca. His father passed away before he was born. He lost his
mother at the age of four and was brought up by his grant father Abdul Muttalib and later by his
uncle Abu Talib. At the age of 25 he entered the employment of Khadijah, a rich widow and
accompanied her caravans perhaps as far as Syria. Later he married her and inherited her
properties.
Till the age of 40, Mohammed spend most of his time in meditation and contemplation in
a little cave called Hira. In his fortieth year he attained to the Prophethood by the divine revelation
and was commissioned as a messenger to preach the message of the Supreme Divine called

Allah. Very early in his life he had come into contact with the Jews and Christians and was
impressed by their religions. He was also dissatisfied with the social and religious, conditions
in his country and realized the need for reform. He began to criticize the plutocrats of Mecca for
their greed and the people for their warfare and practice of infanticide. Gradually, he began to
consider himself as the chosen instrument of God to save the Arabian people from destruction.
Nine years of preaching in Mecca got for him few supporters. The wealthy and the common
people alike were indifferent and so he decided to spread his message among the Bedouins of

200
Yatherb. In the context to the factional strife in Yathreb, he was confident that a neutral man
like him would be able to end the strife and gain control over the city. Finding the circumstances
not favourable, he finally decided to leave Mecca with his followers and settled in Yathreb in
622 A.D. This migration from Mecca to Medina (the new name he gave to the city of Yathreb,
meaning the city of prophet) is known as the ‘Hijri’ which marks the beginning of the Muslim
era.
He was able to overcome the hostility of the Jews of the place and gradually endeared
himself to the people there who accepted him as their leader. Then he proceeded to subdue
the city of Mecca. There was resistance but he put an end to it. Thenceforward, Mecca became
the sacred city of the Muslims. Before his demise in 632 A.D. Mohammed made Islam a universal

religion and brought about universal brotherhood as well as universal oneness in Allah.
10.4.2. The Doctrines of Islam
The doctrines of Islam are very simple. They revolve around the belief in one God, Allah
and in Mohammed, as his prophet. The Muslim sacred book is the Holy Quran which contains
the actual message of Allah as revealed to Mohammed.
The Quran should not be used in translation for worship and to spread to Islam created
linguistic unity. Further it is the last word on Muslim theology, law and social institutions. It is the
most important holy book of the Muslims.
According to the Quran, the central principle of Islam is monotheism. It preaches kindness
to neighbours, leniency towards debtors, honesty and forgiveness. It preaches against
polytheism and social evils. The religion enjoins observance of certain obligations like recitation

of kalimah, praying five times a day, fasting during the day in the month of Ramzan, payment
of Zakat tax 21 ½ from the total property for the poor and making holy pilgrimage (Hajj) to
Mecca. There were no rituals in the system of worship. There are three important sects of
Islam, the Sunnis, Shias and Sufis.
10.5 Political History of Arabia
It is closely interconnected with the growth of the religion. Mohammed had not only
founded Islam but also set up Arabic states with its capital at Medina. After his death, his
followers chose Mohammed’s father-in-law, Abu-Bakr as the leader under the title Caliph, i.e.,
successor to the prophet. His successors called Ummayads continued to rule till 656 when

201
struggle began for possession of the supreme power in Islam. First the Shiates succeeded in
electing the prophet’s son-in-law and deposing the Ummayad ruler. However after five years,
the Ummayads came back to power and shifted their capital to Damascus. Here they set up
luxurious court on the Byzantine model. In 750 A.D. the Shiates under the Abbasids revolted
again and captured power. They shifted their capital to the city of Baghdad and ruled from
there as oriental despots for more than three centuries. Some of them were enlightened patrons
of learning like Harun-al-Rashid and Al-Mamun. While the dynastic changes were taking place,
Saracenic expansion was also going on. At the time of Mohammed’s death, the Muslim state
was very small. But within a century the Saracens had conquered Persia, Syria, Egypt, North

Africa and Spain and their empire extended from the borders of India to the Straits of Gibraltar
and the Pyrenees Mountains.
This expansion was not due to religious zeal alone. Religious zeal was only a minor
contributing cause. The major causes were economic and political. They were: (1) Over
population of the Arabs; (2) Arab mercenaries in Syria appealed to the Prophet for help in their
revolt against their Byzantine rulers. This resulted in the Saracens capturing not only Syria but
also Palestine and Egypt and (3) The Saracen success was facilitated by the exhaustion of the
Byzantine and the Persian empires.
The Saracen decline was as rapid as its rise. The causes for the decline were: (1) The
Arabs lacked political experience; (2)The empire was too vast and too heterogeneous in
character; (3) The factional quarrels between the Sunnites and Shiites as well as the widening

difference between the mystics and rationalists weakened the state in the long run.
In 929, Ummayads established an independent state in Spain with capital at Cordova.
The descendants of Ali and Fatima established independent states in Morocco and Egypt. The
Caliphs of Baghdad followed the practice of Eastern rulers and retired more and more into the
seclusion of the Palace and became the puppets of the Persian Wazirs and later of their
Turkish mercenary troops. In 1055, the Seljuk Turks captured Baghdad and in 1057 they
surrendered all their temporal power to the Seljuk Turks. This practically marked the end of the
Saracenic Empire, even though much of its territory was ruled by Muslims – by Seljuk Turks
until the middle on the 12th century and the Ottoman Turks from the 15th century to 1918.
10.5.1 Economic Condition

The Saracenic development was one of the marvels of history. They converted deserts
into fertile lands and small villages into magnificent cities. Their products were famous all over

202
the world. They built a vast and prosperous commercial empire. This economic prosperity
was due to the long experience of the Arabs in trade, the diffusion of the Arabic language over
a vast territory, the availability of different resources in the empire and the energy and the spirit
of adventure of the conquerors.
The main foundation of the national wealth was commerce and manufacture. The
Saracens used a number of modern instruments of commerce like cheques, receipt bills of
lading, letter of credit, trade associations, joint stock companies, etc. Moslem merchants
penetrated into Southern Russia and even into the equatorial regions of Africa. Moslem caravans
laden with a variety of goods traveled all over the world, while Moslem ships moved about in
the Indian Ocean. Persian Gulf and the Caspian seal. With the exception of the Aegean Sea

and the route from Venice to Constantinople, the Saracens dominated the Mediterranean.
Besides trade they were very good in manufactures as well. One region turned its
resources into finished products for sale elsewhere. Each important city specialized in some
particular manufacture. Thus Mosul specialized in cotton cloth; Baghdad, in glassware, jewellery,
pottery and silk; Damascus in fine steel; Morocco in leather and Teledo in swords. Besides,
the Saracens also manufactured drugs, perfumes, carpets, tapestries, brocades, woolens,
satins, metal products, etc. They also learnt from the Chinese, the art of paper-making and
other paper products. In manufacturers they followed the guild system. But unlike the Byzantian
there was less government control on its working. The government exercised only general
supervision. For the most guild’s themselves regulated the conduct of their business.

10.5.2 Agriculture
Agriculture was not neglected by the Moslems. They developed farming to a very high
level. They developed farming to converted barren wastes into fertile lands. They paid much
attention to ornamental gardening, and to the cultivation of shrubs and rare, beautiful fragment
flowers. The common agricultural products were cotton, sugar, flax, rice wheat spinach,
asparagus, apricots, peaches, lemons and olives. In warmer regions, bananas, coffee and
oranges were cultivated. Most of the land was in small holdings cultivated by owners themselves.
They were some great estates which were partly worked by serfs and slaves and partly by free
peasants as tenants.
10.5.3 Philosophy
The Saracenic philosophy was a mixture of Aristotelianism and Neo-Platonism. It
considered reason as superior to faith and said that religious doctrines were to be interpreted

203
figuratively, so that the philosophical interpretation would go with reason. The universe is
external and everything that happens is predetermined by God; so both miracles and divine
providence are impossible. But God is not omnipotent; his power is limited by Justice and
goodness. An individual is not immortal. Only the soul of the Universe is immortal. This
philosophy was developed in the 9th and 10th centuries in the Baghdad Caliphate and in the 12th
century in Spain. Three great philosophers Al Khindi, Al Farabi and Avicenna – all of them were
of Turkish Persian nationality and belonged to the 9th and 10th centuries. In the 11th century the
Saracenic philosophy degenerated into religious fundamentalism and mysticism. After 11th
century philosophy disappeared from the Baghdad Caliphate. In the West, the greatest

philosopher was Averroes of Cardova (1120-1198) who experienced great influence upon the
Christian scholastics of the 13th century.
10.5.4 Medicine and other Sciences
The Saracens made impressive contributions in the field of medicine and sciences. The
Saracenic physical, mastered Hellenistic medicine improved upon it and passes it (the
knowledge) to posterity. The 10th to 12th centuries was the golden age of Muslim learning in
general and medicine in Particular.
The first and perhaps, the greatest Muslim physician was Al Razi popularly known in the
West as Rhazes. A great doctor of all times, he wrote a famous book “on small pox” and
“measles”. In this book, we have a clear description of the symptoms and the treatment of
these diseases. His greatest work was “the comprehensive book” a huge medical encyclopedia.

In it he cited for each disease all Greek, Syrian, Arabian, Persian and India authorities. The
encyclopedia was very popular all over Europe and was considered as an authoritative work in
the late 12th century. It was later on translated and used by many European physicians.
The famous philosopher Avicenna was a great physician as well. He discovered the
contagious nature of tuberculosis, described pleurisy and several kinds of nervous diseases
and pointed out that the disease spread due to contamination of water and soil. His famous
medical work was the canon, popular throughout Europe and it was issued more than twenty
times in the 15th and 16th centuries. Even today it is read and used in the Oriental countries. He
came to be popularly known as “Father of Medicine”.
Other Moslem physicians diagnosed stomach cancer, discovered antidotes for poisoning
cases made great progress in treating eye diseases. They also discovered that plague was

204
infectious and that it could be transmitted by clothes, utensils, drinking cups and personal
contact.
Moslems also excelled in practical application of their medical theories. They were famous
in organizing hospital and in controlling medical practices. There were about 34 great hospitals
set up in important cities of Persia Syria and Egypt. These hospitals were modernized and
each hospital had separate wards for particular cases, a dispensary and a library. Hospitals
were divided into sections for men and women. The qualifications of physicians and druggists
were checked. The Moslem physicians were good in anatomy. The chief physicians lectured
to the students and graduates, examined them and issued diplomas or licenses to practice.
10.5.5 Progress in other Sciences
They made good progress in other sciences also. They were good on Astronomy,

Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry. Their famous poet Omar Khayyam discovered an accurate
calendar. Their mathematician’s development algebra and trigonometry. They learnt the system
of numerals from Hindus and transmitted it to Europe. In astronomy their great scholar –
Khwarizni wrote treatises on astronomy while their poet Omar Khayyam wrote a treatise on
algebra. They also made good progress in geography. In Physics they founded the science of
optics and made impressive contributions regarding the theory of magnifying lenses and the
velocity, transmission and refraction of light. They were also good in chemistry, made several
experiments and discovered several new substances and compounds like carbonate of soda,
borax, nitrate of silver, saltpeter, nitric and sulphuric acid etc. Finally Saracen scientists were

the first to describe the chemical processes of distillation, filteration and sublimation.
10.5.6 Literature and Scholarship
While in sciences they were influenced by the Greeks, in literature they were influenced
by the Persians. The two great characteristics of their literature were clear and concise way of
expressing themselves and vivid imaginations. Much of their literature idealized the people as
fierce, bold, hospitable and truthful.
Poetry was their favourite form of expression. The best poem was the Rubaiyat by
Omar Khayyam while Saadi wrote Gulistan and Bustan, the mythical and philosophical odes.
Ali Firdausi was another great poet who wrote the “Book of Kings”.

205
In prose the most famous work was the Arabian Nights consisting of a variety of proverbs,
adventures and stories. These stories depict sophisticated life of contemporary Muslim society.
They also composed dictionaries, grammar and books on philosophy and by 13th century
developed a good language beautiful in expression and scientific in organization.
They also contributed to historiography and their best historian was Ibn-Khaldun who
has been judged “the first writer to treat history as the proper object of a special science”. He
said that history should analyze man’s social development which Ibn-Khaldun believed was
the result of the interaction of society and physical environment he believed history as an
evolutionary process in which societies and institution changed continuously.
10.5.7 Art and Architecture

In the ancient and medical world generally religion influenced arts and the Saracens
were no exception. As the prophet opposed to idolization and idol worship, they were prejudiced
against representation of human form. This made this art more secular in character. Their
buildings consisted not only of mosques and churches, but also schools, hospitals, libraries,
palaces, private building, etc. The Muslim art was eclectic and a mixture of Byzantine, Persian
and Chinese influences. They integrated these three and evolved a distinctive and original
style. The Saracens were famous in two branches, architecture and the decorative arts. From
the Byzatines, they adopted the structural features like the dome, the column and the arch
while from the Persians they borrowed the decorative motifs in all the arts.
Great Mosque of Kairouan Prayer Hall

206
Their most important of the arts was architecture which was mostly secular in character.
Its chief features were bulbous domes, minarets, horseshoe arches and twisted columns with
decorations. For decorative purpose they used tracery in stone, alternating stripes of black
and white, mosaics and the Arabic script. They also loved ornamentation and beauty on the
walls and ceilings of their buildings. The best example is the Alhambra Palace at Granada.
Their minor arts consisted of weaving of carpets and rugs, leather tooling and making of
brocaded silks and tapestries, Inlaid metal work, enameled glass ware and painted pottery.
Most of the products of these arts were decorated with complicated patterns of interacting
geometric designs, fruits, flowers, animals and Arabic script.
10.6 Summary

Both had Oriental features. Byzantines were Christians. The Saracens included Jews;

The Saracenic or Moslem Civilization was a composite product synthesis of the civilizations

 Byzantine society was essentially urban and luxurious. Even the serfs, when compared

 Byzantines were very much interested in religion. They took active interest in religious

 The result of their work was the corpus juris or the Justinian Code. Appended to the

212
11.1 Introduction
Even before the Renaissance movement (from 14th century A.D.) Europe slowly began
to come out of her backwardness. During the late Middle Ages, the people of Western Europe
started to give less importance to religion and more importance to worldly things. This change
in the outlook of people was brought about by the influence of the Eastern cultures, monastic
education, revival of trade and the growth of cities and the consequent increase in prosperity
and the progress of enlightenment. They led to an intellectual and artistic civilization in the 13th
century. The most important element in the social and political structure of the civilization was
feudalism. The great variety of different types (most of the units having their own characteristics)
makes it difficult to generalize about the system as a whole.

The people in the western part of Europe were without the protection of the state and
were harassed by barbarians. Year after year, the Norsemen appeared and terrorized the
populace. The castle seemed to be the only refuge, which the nobleman was willing to offer in
return for possession of land and other obligations from the vassal. This resulted in the
development of small political, economic, and social units in which each group lived a more of
secluded life. The feudal idea was not new. The origin of feudalism was also not sudden. A
feudal society developed in Egypt when the Old Kingdom was destroyed. During the Homeric
Age in Greece, a form of feudalism existed in the city-states; this system prevailed in Roman
Society in which the weaker section appealed to the rich people to save them from peril and

showed allegiance to their masters and Japanese society was predominantly until the middle
of the 19th century. Medieval feudalism was but another manifestation of the same general
condition. Churches, monasteries and cities became members of the feudal system. Thus
Church, state and classes of the society were bound together by feudalism. Everything was
impressed with the stamp of feudalism. With the expansion of the Frankish kingdom, feudalism
spread to Italy, Spain, Germany and other countries. Thus feudalism exerted its influence in
the entire medieval Europe.
11.2 Meaning of Feudalism
Feudalism was a kind of socio-political organization which arose in medieval Europe and
it was one of the most complicated developments. During the Middle Ages, this was more or
less a universal institution. But it existed in a variety of shades, in different countries. As most

of the types, which developed in different areas of the world had their own characteristics; it
had become difficult to generalize this system.

213
Feudalism may be defined as a structure of society in which the powers of government
were exercised by nobles over persons who were economically dependent on them. It is a
system of over lordship and vassalage in which right to govern was conceived as a property
right belonging to anyone who was the holder of a fief. The relationship between the lord and
his vassals was something like a contract involving mutual obligations. In return for the protection
and economic assistance the vassals received, they were bound to obey their lord, to serve
him faithfully and generally to compensate to him by dues for services he rendered in their
interest. Feudalism prevailed in Europe in the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries.
The principle behind feudalism was that land was held and not owned. The land belonged

to God, who let it to the King. The King, in turn, sublet it to his great vassals, who in turn divided
it and distributed among their tenants. In medieval Europe, the weak and innocent people
needed the help of a powerful man. The king was very weak. He could not save his subjects
from the plunders of the foreign invaders. So, the common people turned to strong and powerful
leaders who were mostly the descendants of the Dukes, Counts and Margraves to make their
life and property safe.
Thus in feudalism, there were three essential features:
a) Feudal tenure b) Vassalage c) Immunity

214
The protector was variously known as the ‘Lord’, ‘Liege Lord’, ‘Suzerain’ or ‘Seignior’.
The people who sought his protection were called the ‘vassals’ or ‘liege-men’. The Lord gave
back the plot of land know as Tier to his vassal. In some places, instead of the word ‘fief’, the
word ‘feud’ was used from which the term ‘Feudalism’ was derived.
The holder of the land enjoyed only the benefits of the use of land itself. The vassal had
to perform certain services to his lord. The holder of an estate possessed immunity, i.e., he
was free from all interference from his lord. He could perform judicial, executive and even
legislative functions of the governments. Thus the king was the supreme land owner in feudalism
and he was at the apex of the social pyramid. The king divided the kingdom into several fiefs

and gave them to the barons on condition that the barons must support the king in times of war
with warriors, proportionate to their fief. The baron or the tenant-in-chief subdivided his share
into several self-contained villages or manors and gave a manor each to a knight or warrior on
his agreeing to do military service. At the bottom of the social pyramid were agricultural workers
known as villains who actually cultivated the land of the knight or baron in return for the use of
a portion of the manor fields.
11.3 The Feudal Polity, Society and Economy
There are many conflicting opinions as to the origins of the elements that appear in
feudal institutions. However, it is safe to assume that most of them were either German or
Roman in origin. Land played an important part in the development of the relationship between

vassal and lord. In many cases, all that the vassal had to offer in return for protection was land.
Land tenure was the basis of the political organization, in which the vassal gave his overlord
the services that are expected of a citizen of a state. It was practically impossible for a small
landholder to protect himself and his property; consequently he was willing to give it over to a
lord and receive it back to cultivate as a tenant-at-will. This gave him some security from
invaders and made him a member of a society that offered stability. Ownership of property by
the individual was unknown to the Germans. Land to him was the common property of the
tribe. Consequently, the very important land element in the feudal system was certainly Roman
in origin. Furthermore, there is a decided resemblance between the feudal land system and

the old Roman villa. Each was a great estate, managed from a common centre and existing
more or less as an independent unit.

215
11.3.1 Feudal Polity
Feudal government was supposed to be a government of laws and not men. No ruler
could impose his personal whims and fancies on his people. In feudal set up, no ruler had the
right to make laws. Law was the product of custom or the will of God. The authority of the King
was limited to the issuance of administrative decrees to put the law into effect. The right to
revolt against the oppressive ruler was commonly implied under feudalism, such instances
were not frequent. Feudal regime was a system of over lordship and vassalage, based upon
the principle of granting and holding of fiefs.
Feudal Regime Representation
A fief was a benefice that had become hereditary. It was always in the form of land. It
could be an office or position, or the right to collect tolls at a bridge, or the right to coin money,

etc. The one who granted the fiefs was the lord and the one who received the fief was a vassal.
Generally the king was the highest lord. Below him were the great nobles, variously called as
dukes, counts, earls, or margraves. They were called Tenants-in-chief. These nobles divided
their fiefs and granted them to lesser nobles called viscounts or barons. They were called sub-
Tenants. This practice is called sub in-feudation. At the bottom of the system were the knights,
whose fiefs could not be divided. Thus every lord except the king was the vassal of some other
lord and every vassal except the knight was the lord over other vassals. The obligations of the
vassal were more in number of days each year, attend the lord’s court, ransom his lord if he
were captured and pay a heavy tax if he inherited or sold a fief.

216
11.3.2 Feudal Society
The feudal society was highly aristocratic. Most of the nobles owed their position to
heredity. At times, nobility was also conferred to a commander for his services to the king. The
relationship between the lord and the vassal was personal. The vassal kneal before the lord
and promised to be his ‘man’. This ceremony was called the act of homage and the vassals
placed both hands in those of lord and said, “Sir, I enter you homage and faith and promise to
keep faith with you against all others and to guard you rights with all my strength”. The lord
was entitled to feudal dues on three occasions when the lord’s eldest son was made a knight,
when his eldest daughter was given in marriage and whenever the lord was captured by an
enemy and had to be ransomed. Besides these legal dues, the lords demanded many other
payments which were dreaded by the vassals.

The life of the feudal nobles was one of hardship and living condition was very poor.
Their house built with stone and timber was by no means comfortable. The food they ate was
quantitatively rich but qualitatively very ordinary – meat, fish, cheese, vegetables like turnips,
cabbages. Spices and sugar were rarely used. They led a life of adventure and sport. They
loved war and fought for the sheer love of fighting. They were voracious eaters and drank
large quantities of wine and beer. Though in the early part of the Middle Ages women were
treated with indifference and contempt, later the attitude of the aristocracy towards them changed
due to the growth of what is called chivalry, a typically feudal virtue which enjoined on every
knight to be generous truthful, kind to the poor and defenseless, particularly, to women and to
fight in defence of noble causes.
11.3.3 Feudal Economy

The land was held by the tenants-in-chief from the king on condition that they would do
military service, etc. The knights held the lands from the tenants-in-chief on the same condition.
The estates of the knights were called manors. Manor was a self contained village cultivated
by dependent cultivators who could not transfer their services elsewhere. Manorialism had a
political as well as an economic aspect. The size of the manor varied from place to place.
There was no uniformity in this. The smallest manor included at least 300 acres. Each manorial
state consisted of one or more villages.
The arable land in the manor was divided into three main blocks, i.e., the spring planting
ground, the autumn planting ground and the fallow. These were rotated from year to year so
that no block was used for the same purpose in the next year. This was the three-field-system.

217
The manorial agriculture was also conducted under the open field system. The serf got his
share of land in all the three different kinds of land. In cultivating these strips, the peasants
worked in co-operation since their holdings were scattered and they had to combine their
efforts in farming all the strips in a particular block.
The land in the manor was divided into demesse land (the part of the manor cultivated
for the benefit of the lord) and the land held in villeinage (land held by tenants). Both types of
land consisted of strips scattered over the whole village. The land held in villeinage was the
property conferred on the villain in return for their cultivation of the demesse land. Each villain
was usually given 30 acres of land and it was known as virgate or yard land.
Villeins were not free. They were not to bear arms except in cases of great emergency.

They had the right to use the land held in villeinage. They could not be legally deprived of that
land so long as they performed their duties to the lore. The villeins were to work on demesse
land for two or three days a week. They also did some special service, like sowing and reaping.
They also made various contributions to their lord in money and kind. They had to pay money
to their lord for the use of his mill for grinding corn. The villeins had also to give one-tenth of
their produce to the Parish Priest.
The borders or cotters were just below the villeins. Their holdings were smaller than
those of the villeins and so their obligations were also less. The holding of a border was
usually of five acres. They usually worked for one day in the week on the demesse land. It was
usually on Monday, and so they were called ‘Monday-men’.

The villeins and borders rendered their obligation property. The lord appointed officials
to help him in the management of his Estate. The chief among them was the seneschal or
steward who was the lord’s representative over several manors. He was to control the bailiffs,
held the manorial court, go in circuit over the manors, etc. The bailiff managed a single manor
and he was the residential representative of the lord in the manor. Another manorial officer
was the Reeve who kept an account of the tenant’s work.
The lot of the medieval peasant was a miserable one. For good part of the year he had
to work on the field from sunrise to sunset without adequate reward. He lived in a miserable
hovel built of mud with a thatched roof. He had very little clothing and ate coarse food consisting
of brown bread, some vegetables, meat and fish. He was illiterate and was looked down upon
by the rest of society with contempt and scorn. He had no doubt a few advantages to compensate

218
for these miseries. He was secure in his employment or he could not be deprived of his land.
In his old age he was taken care of by his lord. He enjoyed a number of holidays. Above all he
was under no obligations to do military service.
11.4 Merits and Demerits of Feudalism
Feudalism had many merits and it was not peculiar to Western Europe in the middle
ages. It existed in ancient Egypt, in the last days of the Roman Empire and in medieval India.
Everywhere it arose only after the breakdown of the central government in Europe. Feudalism
gave protection to the European society after the breakup of the Empire of Charles, the Great.
It provided a kind of local political authority which could maintain peace and order. However it
was not a permanent arrangement. It gave protection to the poor and established a strong

local government. The Lords were able to save the common men from the tyranny of the King.
A healthy society was created in Europe by feudalism.
Slavery could not thrive in Europe due to feudalism. Since the vassals were under a
Lord, they could not be sold as chattels. Feudalism gave impulse to certain forms of polite
literature. “It is to the feudal times”, says Guizot: “that we trace back the earliest literary works
of England, France and Germany”. It also promoted a nice code of conduct called chivalry.
Chivalry was the “flower of feudalism”. The nobles were pledged to the protection of the
Church and the defence of the weak. Finally, feudalism put an end to the worriness of the
people. Their duty was finished when they paid their ‘Homage’ to the Lord. Then the Lord had
to give him fief and save him. Last but not the least, the relation between Lord and a Vassal

was cordial. They fulfilled the need of each other. The European society breathed a healthy
atmosphere due to feudalism.
Feudalism had many defects. At first, it divided the society into two classes, viz., the
feudal class and the peasantry. The Lords acquired more wealth and power. In due course of
time they hated the vassals and did not do any good for them. This created dark clouds in the
mental horizon of common man. It recognized neither democracy not equality. It stood in the
way of national unity and patriotism. It was based on the idea of exploitation of the lower
classes. The lot of the serfs really was miserable. It also made the central government weak
and totally dependent on the powerful landlords. Even the king was at the mercy of the nobles.
He was not in a position to help the miserable serfs against the oppression of the nobles.
Moreover, the nobles fought against each other and filled the country with terror and agony.

219
When feudalism became intolerable, it was overthrown by powerful monarchs. Finally, the
feudalism made the condition of peasants deplorable. It became difficult on their part to earn
their livelihood from a small quantity of land.
11.5 Decay of Feudalism
Feudalism reached its height from the 10th to the 13th centuries and then gradually declined
and disappeared totally by the 18th century. The serfs who had no freedom disliked the system.
Likewise the kings also hated it since it gave them only the shadow of power. The businessmen
did not like the feudal warfare among the lords as it disturbed their trade. So they worked to
put an end to feudal system with the growth of trade and industry, the people got new avenues
to find employment. So people were willing to forsake their obligations under feudalism.
The Crusades and the Hundred Year’s War weakened the power of the nobles. Many

nobles perished in the Holy Land and their estates came under the control of the Kings. In
order to meet the expenses for the Crusades, many nobles, sold their estates either to the king
or to the rich merchants. Thus the power and influence of the nobles, passed out of their
hands. The influence of the Church on the masses increased considerably during the Middle
Ages. The serfs were promised freedom by the Church if they joined the Crusades. The
thousands of serfs left feudal estates, joined the Crusades and obtained freedom. Moreover,
the businessmen in the town wanted more workers for their business and they encouraged the
serfs to run away from the lord’s estates. Thus the feudal system became weak. The
businessmen, who left a powerful central government was better for the maintenance of peace
and order, helped the kings of Europe against the lord’s.

The discovery of gun-powder hastened the downfall of feudalism. It made the footsoldier armed with guns equal to the mail-clad cavalry. Moreover the same gun powder made
the castle, the stronghold of the lord, useless for defence. Above all, the emergence of strong
monarchies in Europe paved the way for decline of feudalism, for these strong kings put down
the powers of the feudal nobles and asserted their authority.
All these factors cumulatively led to the decline and decay of feudalism. The European
people became free from the tyranny of the feudal system. Orderly government of the kings
were established all over Europe by the sixteenth century.

220
11.6 Summary
 Feudalism prevailed in Europe in the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries.
 The principle behind feudalism was that land was held and not owned. The land belonged
to God, who let it to the King.
 Land played an important part in the development of the relationship between vassal and
lord.
 Feudal government was supposed to be a government of laws and not men.
 The feudal society was highly aristocratic. The relationship between the lord and the
vassal was personal.
 The land was held by the tenants-in-chief from the king on condition that they would do
military service, etc.
 The land in the manor was divided into demesse land (the part of the manor cultivated
for the benefit of the lord) and the land held in villeinage (land held by tenants).

12.1 Introduction
There were evidences of a changed order in the history of Western civilization by the
beginning of the 16th century. Conditions that have been classified as medieval were
disappearing and much that could be recognized as modern gradually appeared. Both the
new and the old existed side by side. The former gained supremacy over the latter so slowly
that only through the perspective of years were changes discernible. The decline of feudalism,
of the influence of the nobility, of the importance of the guild system, and of the influence of the
Church enabled man to think and act more freely. Of the many things that aided in the
transformation of human society two were of particular importance – the Crusades and the
Voyages of Exploration and Discovery.
From the end of the 11th century to the close of the 13th century, great numbers of crusaders

left their homes in Western Europe, travelling eastward to rescue the Holy Land from the
Turks. The significance of the word crusade is derived from the example of Christ in “taking
the cross”, a practice started by members of the First Crusade. The occasion for the crusades
was the advance of the Seljuk Turks, recent converts to Mohammedanism, in the Near East.
The eastern emperor was defeated in the Battle of Manzikert, and Constantinople was
threatened. The Byzantines appealed to Pope Urban II for assistance. At the Council of
Clermont (1095), Pope Urban called for a great crusade of Christians to rescue the Holy Lands.
In 1096, he appealed to the Franks: “Enter upon the road to the Holy Sepulcher; wrest the land
from the wicked race and subject it to yourselves”.
12.2 The Crusading Spirit
The original impetus back of the crusades was undoubtedly religious. Following Pope

Urban’s appeal, there was an avalanche of religious enthusiasm. “It is the will of God” shouted
the people, in response to Urban’s eloquent call. Many of the leaders and a large percentage
of the followers were prompted to take action because of purely idealistic motives. Nevertheless,
there were many others who accepted the invitation for selfish reasons. While great numbers
believed that they were serving Christ in the most sacred cause, some went for the sake of
adventure and plunder, and others in order to escape punishment and bondage. Nobles had
their eyes on valuable lands in Syria, merchants saw the opportunity for trade, thieves sought
an escape from justice, and debtors believed that they could evade their obligations through
participation in the holy enterprise. Besides these, common riffraff and outright adventurers
joined the procession.

224
The Church offered every inducement: forgiveness of sin, protection of property, and
spiritual blessings. The embodiment of the medieval ideal of Christian service was apparent in
the crusades. The prevailing interest in salvation and the prospect of forgiveness of sin, both
of which participation in a crusade allegedly ensured, were strong motivating influences.
12.3 Causes of the Crusades
The Crusades were a series of wars during the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries of the Christian
era between Muslim Asia and Christian Europe for finding a solution to the problem of the Holy
Land of Jerusalem (Palestine) sacred to the Christians and Muslims alike. Eventually they
turned out to be wars between Europe and Asia, between the West and the East. They were
named so as the Christian soldiers wore on them the badge of the cross, while fighting to the

wars for what they considered to be for the recovery of their Holy Land from the hands of the
Muslims.
The Crusades were by no means a religious movement. But in the events of crusades
definitely there were religious factors. It was because of expansionist tendencies. The following
are the causes of the crusades.
12.3.1 Mass Pilgrimage
In the life of man in the medieval age, religion occupied a predominant place. The
medieval Christian had a deep conviction of sin. Fearing of the consequences of sin he wanted
to avert them by penance. The most popular form of penance for many years had been the

225
making of pilgrimage to holy places. It was the cherished ambition of every Christian to go on
pilgrimage to a Holy Land, particularly Palestine. After this return from pilgrimages every
pilgrim brought back stories of their pilgrimage which inspired others also to go on pilgrimage.
These mass pilgrimages were also a cause for the desire of conquering the Holy Land.
12.3.2 Religious Wars
A war against their enemy, for the rescue of the Holy Places from desertion would enable
Latin Christians to forget their differences. They rallied behind the Pope. Already the papacy
had inspired or given its blessings to wars on behalf of religion. Gregory VIII turned first his
attention to the glorious dream of uniting all classes of Christians in support of the Church.
12.3.3 Other Religious Causes
The fighting among the feudal nobles was a menace to the security of the Church. The

rights of the clergy, peasants and other non-combatants were often trampled upon. The
merchants were robbed. The surplus idealism into a holy war against the heathers. The
surplus idealism left over from the New Clung Movement was also a cause. It stirred up the
enthusiasm.
12.3.4 Economic Causes
The Palestine land as the scripture said was believed to have been flowed with milk and
honey. This was emphasized by Pope Urban II at the Council of Clermont. The manorial
system of agriculture impaired the fertility of the soil. Many nobles had fallen into debt. The
law of primogeniture in France and England also created the problem. The new fiefs that had
to obtain and positions in the Church were scarce. The offspring’s of the nobles formed a
rebellious and disorderly class.
12.3.5 Immediate Cause
The advance of the Seljuk Turks in the Near East was the immediate cause. After the

death of the great Sultan, Malik Shah, in 1092 the Seljuk Empire began to disintegrate. This
was a good opportunity for the Byzantine Emperor, Alexious Comnenus attempted to reconquer
his lost possessions. He appealed to the Pope for his aid to recruit mercenary soldiers. Pope
Urban II the reigning pontiff took full advantage of this opportunity and he summoned a council
of French nobles and clergy at Clermont and exhorted them in a fiery speech on 26th November,

226
1098 to make war upon the Seljuk Turks. The rallying erry “Save the Holy Land” echoed
throughout the land and seized high and low and spread like a wild Contagion. By the spring
of 1107, a hundred and fifty thousand men, mostly Franks and Normans partly, rabble had
answered to the call and met at Constantinople. The first of the eight Crusades had commenced.
The crusades were numbered as five or eight according to different historians, because the
war was long and continuous and it can be counted in any manner.
12.4 Course of the Crusades
Prompted by a variety of impulses – good and evil, spiritual and materialistic, economic
and social – all classes participated. Kings, princes, bishops, noblemen, the wealthy, beggars,
old men, children, women, and dashing knights joined in the holy war. The First Crusade was

the only one to fulfill its major objective. Three groups of enthusiasts – one led by the Count of
Toulouse, a second by Godfrey and Baldwin, and a third composed of French and Normans –
captured Jerusalem in 1099. The feudal Latin kingdom of Jerusalem, which they established,
lasted until 1187, when Saladin, one of the most capable Muslim leaders, reconquered the holy
city. This prompted the Third Crusade. Although three kings participated – Frederick Barbarossa
of Germany, Richard the Lionhearted of England and Philip Augustine of France – lack of
cooperation led to failure. The Fourth Crusade (1202) is a demonstration of how the great
religious ideal of the earlier attempts had degenerated. Owing largely to the influence of
Venetian merchants, the crusaders attacked Constantinople and captured the city (1204). The
sacred altar of St. Sophia was smashed and looted.
The Crusaders

Although numerous further efforts were made by the crusaders during the succeeding
century, only the Children’s Crusade (1212) needs particular mention. It was one of the most
unfortunate episodes in this entire period. Pious individuals who were disgusted with the

227
efforts of warriors and statesmen in the various attempts to regain the Holy Lands decided to
send children, with the hope that they might accomplish what adults had failed to do. No
doubt, they relied for divine inspiration on the Biblical passage, “A little child shall lead them”. A
French shepherd boy named Stephen rallied 30,000 children to follow him, with the promise
that God would lead them and open a path through the sea, as he had done formerly for the
Israelites. Another company of 20,000 was led by a youngster called Nicholas. Both attempts
resulted in complete failure. Thousands died of exposure or in shipwreck, and others were
captured and sold into slavery. The Christians could not conquer Jerusalem till the First World
War when Allenby, the British General captured it.
12.5 Importance of the Crusades

The Roman Catholic Church gained some prestige from the earlier crusades, but it is
doubtful whether any permanent good results were derived. Certainly, the effort to keep the
infidel Turk out of the Holy Land ended in a dismal failure; Islam continued to spread. It is
certain that the religious results of the crusades were insignificant compared with the intellectual,
the economic and the social outcome. The crusades helped significantly in bringing to an end
the long period of isolation and stagnation in the West. To have brought thousands of people
out of an isolated, feudal existence, and to have opened for them a new horizon was, in itself,
a notable accomplishment The people in the western part of Europe had lived in segregation
for centuries. Generation after generation stayed on in one locality, without any appreciable

contact with the outside world. Such a life was not conducive to progress of any kind. The
small community was a spiritual and physical world in itself, oblivious of anything outside it own
limited domain. This manorial solitude was broken up when those who went on the crusades
acquired new ideas and met strange people. Those who returned had a broader intellectual
horizon and were no longer satisfied to live a dreary life in an isolated community.
Commerce followed the trail of the crusaders. Some of the more materialistic-minded
among them bargained with the heathen for merchandise. Silks, sugar, spices, new plants,
new fruits, cotton, muslin, drugs, precious stones and glass were brought back and sold in the
ready markets of France, Germany, and England. Scholars were attracted by the culture of

the East. The scientific works of Aristotle, Arabic numerals, algebra, the mariner’s compass,
and paper were introduced in the West as a result of discoveries made by the crusaders. New
points of view, gained from contacts with other people, tended to weaken the hold of the Church
on the minds of men. The prevailing medieval belief that the Church and the Christian religion

228
embodied all that was worthwhile in life and provided the necessary preparation for eternity
was challenged by men fresh from their experiences and contacts with the realities of another
civilization. The lessening of the autocratic power of the Church over the intellectual life of the
people was a necessary prerequisite to the revival of learning in the West. Finally, it can be
said that the crusades contributed extensively to the introduction of new ideas and to the
tearing down of old orders, which made the Renaissance possible.
12.6 Summary
 From the end of the 11th century to the close of the 13th century, great numbers of crusaders
left their homes in Western Europe, travelling eastward to rescue the Holy Land from the
Turks.
 The original impetus back of the crusades was undoubtedly religious. Following Pope
Urban’s appeal, there was an avalanche of religious enthusiasm.

 The Church offered every inducement: forgiveness of sin, protection of property, and
spiritual blessings.
 The Crusades were a series of wars during the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries of the Christian
era between Muslim Asia and Christian Europe for finding a solution to the problem of
the Holy Land of Jerusalem (Palestine) sacred to the Christians and Muslims alike.
 The Roman Catholic Church gained some prestige from the earlier crusades, but it is
doubtful whether any permanent good results were derived.
