13.1 Introduction
By the beginning of the 14th century most of the institutions and ideals of the Feudal Age
had begun to decline. Chivalry, feudalism, the Holy Roman Empire, the universal authority of
the papacy, the guild system of trade and industry had begun to decline. The age of the Gothic
Cathedrals was over, the Scholastic philosophy was no longer considered important or relevant

and the supremacy of the religious and ethical interpretations became less important. Instead,
new institutions and ideas gained ground and slowly gained supremacy over the old ideas and
institutions. This period of transition from feudal to modern age was accelerated by the Crusades
and the voyages of discovery. The new civilization which covered the period from 1300 to
1650 is called as Renaissance.
During this period individualism gained more importance than collectivism, which was
the chief characteristic of the earlier ages and civilizations. The rights and interests of individuals

233
gained greater importance. Individualism in the political field results in the destruction of the
medieval ideal of universal empire and the creation of nation-states. In the field of thought and
art, it led to the Renaissance. In the field of religion, it split Christendom through the Reformation
and in the field of exploration, it resulted in the discovery and colonization of the Americas and
the opening of the East to Western trade.
13.2 Meaning of Renaissance
Renaissance is a collective term used to include all the intellectual changes that were in
evidence at the close of the Middle Ages and at the beginning of modern times. The intellectual
revival was stimulated by the Crusades and the explorations. It was manifested in an interest
in the past and a desire for understanding the present. Perhaps its greatest attribute was the

development of that inquisitiveness which is necessary to intellectual progress. Interest in
what earlier civilizations had contributed was great, and the classics were revived. It should be
remembered that they had never been completely neglected, even in the darkest days of the
Middle Ages. Latin was used in the services of the Roman Catholic Church and Greek was
used in the services of the Greek Church. The works of Aristotle, Vergil, Seneca and Boethius
were studied in medieval universities as early as the 13th century. Medieval Christians studied
classical literature and philosophy and utilized Graeco-Roman architecture in the construction
of their Churches. The medieval attitude towards the classics was utilitarian. Such, however,
was not the spirit of the Renaissance. Classical culture appealed, not merely because it supplied

useful information, but also because of a genuine interest and enjoyment that the admirer
found in it.
The Renaissance included much that was not found in art and literature. In economic
life, the simple agricultural ways of the manor were altered by commerce and industry. In
social relationship, the manor, the nobleman’s castle, and the bishop’s palace gave way to the
crowded and busy towns. There was a new political consciousness manifested in the decline
of the papacy and the empire. Nationalism came into prominence. Astronomy, physiology and
medicine were investigated with sound scientific procedure, instead of by the old method of
theological scholasticism. The decline of the Church and the inroads of science on theological
scholasticism paved the way for the Reformation. Man was in the process of making a

fundamental change in his attitude towards himself and the world in which he lived. This point
of view is commonly called Humanism. The Humanists were interested primarily in classical
literature, but the effect of this interest was more than a revival of the study of the Greek and

234
Latin languages. It focused attention on things of this world – an exaltation of human nature.
The natural, the human, and the sensual were given precedence over the ascetical, the
supernatural, and the theological.
13.3 Factors contributed to the advent of Renaissance
The following factors contributed to the advent of Renaissance:
13.3.1 Fall of Constantinople
During the medieval period Constantinople was the centre of Christianity and fine arts. In
1453 Ottoman Turks achieved victory over Constantinople and forced the Christian scholars to
flee to European countries where they not only spread their education and literature among the
people of Europe but also impressed the European scholars by their knowledge and learning.
A.J. Grant has remarked, “The movement received a strong impetus in 1453 when owing to

the capture of Constantinople by the “Turks, Greek scholars were compelled to flee to Italy”.
Hayes also comments about contact between the Greek and the Christian scholars: By
coming into contracts with the other scholars of the country. They studied their books and

235
translated them into their own languages so that the general masses who were ignorant of
Lain and Greek could understand them. Among the contemporary scholars the names of
Petrarch, Dante, Chaucer, Martin Luther and Erasmus need special mention. They made a
great contribution to the rise of intellectual renaissance. Owing to the inspiration of these great
scholars the darkness and dogmatism disappeared and a spirit of enquiry developed among
the people.
13.3.2 Influence of Religious Wars
Medieval Age was popularly known for religious wars. Various warriors used to fight in
the name of religion. As a result of religious wars, the Europeans came into contact with different
races. It brought a change in the geographical knowledge and social living. Three religious
wars were fought between the Muslims and the Christians and various countries had to take

part in the religious wars. Thus they came into contact with other countries. It increased their
knowledge and widened their mental outlook. It is said that the use of paper, cotton and
ammunition was the outcome these religious wars. H. A.L. Fisher point out that the people of
Europe were forced to think about religions because of the religious conflict between the Church
and the State. A.J. Grant also writes, “A new heaven and new earth were opening for those
who had eyes to see”.
13.3.3 Invention of Printing Press
In the beginning of the modern era, printing press and paper were invented. It made the
books cheap in Europe. After the invention of printing press, the Bible and some other books of
ancient Greek and Roman literatures were translated into English, French and German
languages, so the people could be able to go through the Bible and the works of Plato and

Aristotle. It added to the knowledge of the people. During the medieval period the education
was confined only to the priests, hence the people used to accept whatever was uttered by the
priests without any hitch.
But in the modern era with the expansion of education the ignorance disappeared and
people began to accept only those commands of the pope and the priests which they found
perfectly in accordance with their own wisdom. Hayes, a prominent historian has pointed out
about the development of human capability after the invention of printing press in these words,
“The invention of the press multiplied the books and made culture accessible to every common
mass in the society. Ides, hitherto the exclusive right of the nobility and the clergy now began
to throw light into the dark and uncivilized lives of the many”.

236
13.3.4 Discovery of New Countries
The Turks had established their control over Constantinople in A.D. 1453 and started
plundering the merchants who were trading with India. Hence, the route of Europe to India was
closed for fear of the Turks. Hence, the Europeans tried to find out a new route for India. In
1492 Columbus tried to find out this route. He made a perilous journey through the dangerous
Atlantic Ocean and reached America. Earlier, the people of Europe did not know about America,
hence now it came to be known as the New World.
On the other hand, the Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama in 1498 took a round of America
and Australia and established their trade. It added to their knowledge. A.J. Grant also writes in
this connection, “The discoveries of new lands not only inspired the explorers to increase their

trade in the colonies but they resolved to spread their culture, literature and also their religion
among the people in the colonies. This meant that they aimed at establishing a greater Europe
outside the continent”.
13.3.5 Colonialism
The Europeans made various perilous journeys in order to find out the new routes for the
expansion of their trade. They established trade relations with India, America and Africa and
founded their colonies at very cheap rate and sold their manufactured articles in the same
colonies at a high price. As a result of colonialism, the European merchants came in contact
with the people of foreign countries and their knowledge about the second world grew. It helped
in the advent of Renaissance.
13.3.6 Imperialist Tendency
The people of Europe not only needed the raw materials from their colonies but they

were also in search of permanent markets for the disposal of their manufactured goods. Only
colonial markets were not the permanent solution of this problem because the rulers of the
colonies could create hindrance in the smooth running of business at any time, so the Europeans
wanted to establish their full control over these colonies. Hence, they began to interfere in the
domestic affairs of the native rulers. They resorted to the policy of ‘Divide and Rule’ and often
helped the friendly country against its enemy economically and militarily in order to augment
their power. Taking the advantages of the mutual conflicts and feuds of the native rulers they
occupied some of the small states in different regions with the help of their military power. With

237
the passage of time, these small states were converted into big kingdoms. Besides studying
the culture of vanquished countries, the ‘Europeans also preached their culture and civilization
in these countries. It enhanced and developed their outlook. A.J.Grant writes about it,
“Europeanization of the world was a principal feature of the Renaissance period and it led
immensely to the growth of new ideas, literature and culture in the continent”.
13.3.7 Contribution of Middle Class
The European trade with India, America and Africa developed a lot due to the discovery
of new sea routes. And various new states were established in Europe which helped in the rise
of middle class that consisted of merchants, small industrialists, government officials, lawyers,
doctors and teachers. The people of this class had great interest in the study of science,

administration, history, art and other subjects. This class contributed a lot to the Renaissance.
13.3.8 Downfall of Feudalism and Rise of Powerful Monarchies
During the medieval period the position of feudal lords was quite strong. They lived in
their own fortresses and the rulers used to provide them with fiefs for their subsistence. In
return thereof, they were expected to help the king at the time of war. For this they used to
maintain troops. During the medieval age, the rulers did not have permanent armies. These
feudal lords were uneducated and they passed most of their time in sexual pleasures, hunting
and mutual feuds. Their mutual conflicts had weakened them. Secondly, the kings had
established their control over them due to the invention of ammunition. Now the feudal lords
had no courage to challenge the power of the king. In this way, with the decline of the power of

the feudal lords the rise of powerful monarchies took place in Europe.
During the medieval era the institution of Church was very strong. The people of Europe
used to follow the commands of the Pope blindly. Even the kings had no power to oppose the
commands of the Pope but with the commencement of the modern era, the powerful monarchs
began to oppose the verdicts of the Pope and started working according to their own sweet
will. Thus, the first and the foremost effect of the Renaissance was that it weakened the hold of
the Church. The rulers of England and some other countries established national churches. It
weakened the power of the Pope, the head of the Catholic religion. They gave shelter to many
scholars which helped a lot in the advent of the Renaissance.

238
13.3.9 Economic Prosperity
The people of Europe became quite rich as lots of money poured into Europe due to
foreign trade. The availability of raw material and sale of manufactured goods in the colonies
encouraged the traders to establish their industries in Europe. After being free from economic
problems people began to pay attention to the study of science, literature and art. It helped a
lot in the development of Renaissance.
To determine the forces that actually put the Renaissance into operation is difficult. It
was more evident in some places than in others and, even where it was most manifest, it
represented the thoughts and actions of only a small percentage of the people. Certain leaders
stand out in retrospect. Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, St.Francis of
Assisi, Cimabue and Dante – moving spirits of the new era – lived in the 13th century. The

scientific spirit, a religious enlightenment, a new technique in art and architecture, and a new
type of literature served as a background for the Renaissance proper. In addition, wealthy and
influential individuals became patrons of the new movement.

239
There were several reasons for Renaissance starting in Italy. Italy, because of its location,
was the logical place and it was considered as a school of New Europe. Italy had a stronger
classical tradition than any other country of Western Europe. The Italians believed that they
were the descendants of the ancient Romans. The trade and commerce of Italian merchants
had concentrated there most of the wealth of Western Europe. Ideas soon spread to other
countries, and national cultures, which were closely associated with political developments,
arose. The golden age of the Italian Renaissance ended in the first quarter of the 16th century,
with the death of Pope Leo X. The spark of culture that was the spirit of Humanism had
crossed the Alps into Germany, into France, and into England. By the second half of the 15th
century, cultural activities were slowly gaining ground in Germany.

Agricola (1443 – 1485) was appointed professor of classical literature at Heidelberg
University. According to Erasmus, “he was the first to bring us out of Italy a breath of higher
culture”. Reuchlin (1455 – 1522) was the first great German scholar of the classics. In
Germany, as subsequent history reveals, the revival of learning was unproductive in art and
literature. The Germans attempted to connect Humanism and Theology and to instil the spirit
of reform into classical learning. This had its consummation in Luther’s conflict with the papacy.
The intellectual revival began to manifest itself in France at the beginning of the 16th
century. Charles VIII led a French army into Naples, where he made contacts with the learning
of Italy. Several important scholars, including Erasmus, were attracted to Paris, where they

taught at the University. Chaucer was a leader in the cultural revival in England during the 15th
century. Oxford and Cambridge universities especially Oxford, were centres of cultural activity.
13.4 Main Characteristics of Renaissance
The following were the main characteristics of Renaissance:
13.4.1 Rise of Humanism
Humanism was found in excess in ancient Greek and Roman literature but in the medieval
age owing to the influence of Church the spirit of spiritualism, escapism and worship of God
became quite popular and people began to think more of the other world than this one. But
owing to the influence of Renaissance, people again began to take interest in Ancient Greek
and Roman literature. Now they began to take interest in expansion of humanism and their
interest in the medieval culture and civilization diminished.

240
In the modern period Petrarch is supposed to be the originator of humanism. Dante and
other authors and supporters of humanism were the followers of Petrarch. First of all Florence,
a town of Italy became the centre of Renaissance in Europe because the contemporary ruler of
Florence, Lorenzo de’ Medici was not only the great patron of scholars but also a lover of arts
and an efficient politician. He provided shelter to various authors of humanism. Besides Petrarch,
Dante and others also saw their heyday in the regime of Lorenzo de’ Medici. The humanism
spread from Italy to other countries of Europe. Michelangelo, Machiavelli, Leonardo da Vinci,
Donatello, Botticelli, Robbia, Ficino, Verrochio, Perugine and Guiciardini were some significant
writers of humanism.
Michelangelo and Alberti were past masters in architecture, painting and sculpture.

They were also their contemporary and well known for his ability who contributed a lot to the
humanistic movement. They severely condemned the medieval fanaticism. John Reuchin and
Phillip Melancothan were two prominent figures of this movement in Germany. In England the
strings of this movement were in the hands of John Colet and Thomas Moore. Thomas Moore
wrote Utopia and earned a lot of fame. In this book he condemned and criticized the medieval
traditions and led the way to Intellectual Renaissance.
Renaissance art was characterized by realism and naturalism. Artists strived to depict
people and objects in a true-to-life way. They used techniques, such as perspective, shadows
and light to add depth to their work. Emotion was another quality that artists tried to infuse into
their pieces. Some of the most famous artistic works that were produced during the Renaissance
include:

 The Mona Lisa (Da Vinci)
 The Last Supper (Da Vinci)
 Statue of David (Michelangelo)
 The Birth of Venus (Botticelli)
 The Creation of Adam (Michelangelo)
The humanists believed that it is important to transcend to the afterlife with a perfect
mind and body, which could be attained with education. The purpose of humanism was to
create a universal man whose person combined intellectual and physical excellence and who
was capable of functioning honorably in virtually any situation. This ideology was referred to
as the uomo universale, an ancient Graeco-Roman ideal. Education during the Renaissance

241
was mainly composed of ancient literature and history as it was thought that the classics provided
moral instruction and an intensive understanding of human behaviour.
A unique characteristic of some Renaissance libraries is that they were open to the
public. These libraries were places where ideas were exchanged and where scholarship and
reading were considered both pleasurable and beneficial to the mind and soul. As freethinking
was a hallmark of the age, many libraries contained a wide range of writers. Classical texts
could be found alongside humanist writings. These informal associations of intellectuals
profoundly influenced Renaissance culture. Some of the richest “bibliophiles” built libraries as
temples to books and knowledge. A number of libraries appeared as manifestations of immense

wealth joined with a love of books. In some cases, cultivated library builders were also committed
to offering others the opportunity to use their collections. Prominent aristocrats and princes of
the Church created great libraries for the use of their courts, called “court libraries”, and were
housed in lavishly designed monumental buildings decorated with ornate woodwork, and the
walls adorned with frescoes.
13.4.2 Development in Architecture
The other characteristic of Renaissance is this that the ideas of Ancient Greek and Roman
philosophy were incorporated in the contemporary architecture. Florence, Rome and Venice
became the centres of the architecture of intellectual Renaissance age. Filippo Brunelleschi
was the first artist who began this architecture in Florence. Brunelleschi formulated the

242
Renaissance style that emulated and improved on classical forms. His major feat of engineering
was building the dome of the Florence Cathedral. Another building demonstrating this style is
the church of St. Andrew in Mantua, built by Alberti.
Gothic Style of Architecture
Medici Church of Florence is a fine specimen of this art. In this tower the ancient
architecture has been presented in a new style but this architecture actually flourished in Rome.
St. Peter’s Church at Rome was built by an artist named Bramnate which highlighted the
climax of this type of architecture. This Church is very beautiful. Scholars like Raphael,
Michelangelo and others contributed a lot to the development of architecture. This art developed
in France and Spain during the reign of Francis I (1515-1547), and Philip II (1556-1598)

respectively. Both of them were great patrons of art. In England this art flourished in the 17th
century.
During the Renaissance, architects aimed to use columns, pilasters, and entablatures as
an integrated system. The Roman orders types of columns are used: Tuscan, Doric, Ionic,
Corinthian and Composite. These can either be structural, supporting an arcade or architrave,
or purely decorative, set against a wall in the form of pilasters. One of the first buildings to use
pilasters as an integrated system was in the Old Sacristy (1421–1440) by Brunelleschi. Arches,

243
semi-circular or (in the Mannerist style) segmental, are often used in arcades, supported on
piers or columns with capitals. There may be a section of entablature between the capital and
the springing of the arch. Alberti was one of the first to use the arch on a monumental.
Renaissance vaults do not have ribs; they are semi-circular or segmental and on a square
plan, unlike the Gothic vault, which is frequently rectangular. Renaissance artists were not
pagans, although they admired antiquity and kept some ideas and symbols of the medieval
past. Nicola Pisano (1220 – 1278) imitated classical forms by portraying scenes from the Bible.
His Annunciation, from the Baptistry at Pisa, demonstrates that classical models influenced
Italian art before the Renaissance took root as a literary movement.
13.4.3 Development of Sculpture

Development of sculpture took place at Florence in Italy as a part of architecture. In this
art also the ancient Greek and Roman style have been presented in a new and beautiful form.
Lorenzo Gilberti was the first man who contributed to the rise of sculpture. He carved the
bronze doors of the Church at Florence which was famous for its exquisite beauty. Other
artists also represented his artistic ideals in a very attractive style. Donatello, Luca delia, Robbia
and Vorochhio were the great sculptors. Donatello is remembered for his realistic statute of St.
George and St. Mark. Luca delia Robbia was famous for his classic purity and simplicity of
style who had established a school of sculpture in glazed terracotta.
Michelangelo was supposed to be the best of all. He was expert in architecture, painting

and sculpture also. The specimen of sculpture (statute of David) which he made in the churches
of Florence is the finest examples of sculpture. He had also made the grand statute of ‘Moses’.
He had also completed the construction of ‘Basilica of St. Peter’ at Rome. Ideals and reality
have been blended in it in a very beautiful style. In the sixteenth century sculpture also developed
in England, France, Spain and Germany and the contemporary rulers encouraged and patronized
the artists.
13.4.4 Development of Painting
The painting was inspired by religious feelings but during the Renaissance the religious
ideals were mingled with realism in a very fine way. This art was also encouraged by the
Church. Like other arts painting also flourished in Italy. The painters of Italy brought excellence
and became world famous. Among the painters of the world, Leonardo da Vinci occupied a
unique position. The hidden expression in his paintings made them attractive. Leonardo has

244
become immortal for his famous painting of ‘Monalisa’. The smile on the lips of Monalisa is so
mysterious that it is beyond the comprehension of man. ‘The Holy Supper’, ‘The Virgin of the
Rock’ and ‘The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne’ are his other immortal paintings which are
appreciated all over the world.
Michael Angelo was a painter, sculptor, architect, poet and engineer in one. His paintings
like ‘Creation of Adam’ and the ‘Last Judgement’ bear testimony of his superb skill. He was
invited and rewarded by King Henry VIII of England and Francis I of France. His paintings bore
the stamp of originality in every aspect. Another great painter of that time was Raphael. His
paintings portray an air of calmness and beauty. His practice Madonna made him world famous
painter. The Vatican Palace also bears testimony of his paintings. Titian was the official

painter of the city of Venice. His oil painting was very famous. His painting ‘Christ carrying the
Cross’ appeared real and lively.
Monalisa The Virgin and the Child
In due course of time the paintings of Italy became world famous. It entered into Germany
and Antwerp. The famous artist of Antwerp was Massy. Another noted German artist was
Albert Durer. Among other artists of that period was Hobein of Augusburg. The rulers of
France, Spain and Germany also patronized this art later on.

245
13.4.5 Development of Music
Music also made tremendous progress in the fourteenth century. People began to take
much interest in the instrumental music instead of vocal. Various changes occurred in the
system of music. Like other arts, Italy led the path in music also. Italy was freed from the
clutches of medieval songs. The use of Piano and Violin made the song sweeter. Palestrina
was a great singer and musician and a composer of new songs. The contemporary musicians
were very much impressed by the ancient Greek, Roman and Hebrew (Jew) cultures. In
Churches, old songs were discarded and new songs were incorporated in prayer. Many other
countries of Europe also adopted this practice.
13.4.6 Rise of National Languages and Vernacular Literature
In the beginning of Renaissance people were greatly interested in the Latin and Greek

languages and literature but they were quite difficult and the general masses were unable to
understand them. Hence, in the 16th century attempts were made for the rise of Italian, France,
German English and Spanish languages and books of ancient Greek and Latin literature were
translated into the national languages so that the general massed could follow them easily.
Martin Luther, a well-known scholar of Germany, translated the Holy Bible in the German
language. Crammer composed the Book of Common Prayer. Calvin wrote Institutes of Christian
Religion. Chaucer, Milton, Shakespeare, Thomas Moore, Spencer and others also did yeoman
service to humanity through the English literature, Precious books were also written in Italian,
French and Spanish languages. The invention of the printing press made the books quite

cheap and they came within the reach of the people in general. The study of these books
developed the spirit of enquiry and superstitions flew away from the hearts of the contemporary
people. Scheville writes, “while the townsmen were taught in the toils of trade and industry and
were journeying into far countries to make acquaintance with strange climes and peoples, the
world in which they lived began to assume a new due to the revival of learning, spread of new
ideas and rise of a new and a distinct philosophy”.
13.4.7 Reformation and Rise of Protestantism
As a result of Renaissance a great cultural development took place in Europe. During
medieval period the education was confined only to the priests and it was too available in Latin
which was a very difficult language. But with the advent of Renaissance various national
languages flourished in Europe and religious books, such as, Book of Common Prayer and

246
Institutes of Christian Religion were translated into these languages. These books could be
made available to the general masses due to the invention of printing press. It added to the
knowledge of the people. They not only came to know of their religion but also developed a
spirit of enquiry among themselves. By this time various evils had cropped up in the Roman
Catholic religion and people began to condemn and criticize the unfair means of collection of
wealth adopted by the Pope. It created a feeling of doubt among the people about the existence
of God and supremacy of Pope. Martin Luther challenged the supremacy of Pope and founded
a new religion - Protestantism. His reformation movement became very popular and great
number of people joined Protestantism. Thus the Christian world was divided into two folds -
Roman Catholics and Protestants.
13.4.8 Scientific Progress

In the beginning of modern era various scientific inventions were made which contributed
a lot to the advent of Renaissance because it ended religious dogmas and superstitions prevalent
among the masses. People began to think in scientific terms. No doubt, invention of ammunition
and decline of feudalism helped develop a spirit of enquiry among the people.The other
significant characteristic of Renaissance was that once again people began to study ancient
Greek literature and invented new things. People began to go through the principle of
Pythagoras again pertaining to mathematics.
The name of Francis Bacon shines like a star in the realm of science. He was a great
scientist who advised to explore nature. He advised that truth was to be discerned by experiment.
This idea prompted others to regard him as the ‘Father of Modern Science’. While experimenting

on the method of preserving food, he breathed his last.
In the realm of scientific discoveries, the name of Copernicus of Poland is chanted with
reverence. In his book, On the Revolution of the Celestial Bodies, he opined that Sun is static.
He proved that the earth was also a planet like others and it revolved round the sun as a result
of which day and night occur. Though it was a wonderful contribution to knowledge, the Orthodox
Church opposed it because earlier it was propounded by Ptolemy that all the planets revolve
around the earth as it was the centre of the world. In case, any one tried to oppose this principle,
he was punished by the Church. Copernicus could not get his book published for quite a long
time due to the fear of the Church. Later on, it was published in 1543 but its publicity was quite

slow for the fear of the Orthodox Church. The view of Copernicus was supported by the
famous German scientist John Kepler. He slightly changed the view of Kepler and opined

247
that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun in ‘elliptical’ rather than ‘circular path’.
This created a storm in the field of thinking.
Another great scientist of this age was Galileo of Italy. He had joined as a lecturer of
mathematics in the University of Pisa and there he became a professor. He invented Telescope.
Through that instrument he proved before his enthusiastic audience that the theory of Copernicus
was absolutely true. He further opined and proved that the ‘Milky Way’ consists of stars. His
‘Pendulum Theory’ helped later on for inventing clock. For his radical views, he was declared
by Pope as ‘out-caste’. Galileo was compelled to withdraw his view out of fear. However, later
on, his views were accepted as true and he became world famous. From the leaning tower of
Pisa he also proved that heavy and light objects fall to the ground at the same speed. The

invention of Mariner’s Compass also contributed a lot to facilitating voyages and geographical
discoveries.
Sir Isaac Newton, the famous scientist, discovered the Law of Gravitation of Earth.
Mineralogy, chemistry and medical science also developed during this period. Galen and others
led the modern medical science. William Harvey wrote books on medical science. All these
achievements and scientific developments contributed a lot to the field of renaissance.
13.4.9 New Sea Routes
One more characteristic feature of intellectual Renaissance was geographical discoveries
of the contemporary period for it widened the parameters of human knowledge. After the
conquest of Constantinople when people discovered new sea routes, they came in contact
with America, India and Africa and they culture and civilization of these places. They also

established trade relations with these countries which made them rich and prosperous. The
Portuguese were the first who discovered and occupied various countries and islands. The
names of Azores and Cape of Good Hope need special mention.
13.5 Decline of the Renaissance
Scholars believe the demise of the Renaissance was the result of several compounding
factors. By the end of the 15th century, numerous wars had plagued the Italian peninsula.
Spanish, French and German invaders battling for Italian territories caused disruption and
instability in the region. Also, changing trade routes led to a period of economic decline and
limited the amount of money that wealthy contributors could spend on the arts. Later, in a
movement known as the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic Church censored artists and writers

248
in response to the Protestant Reformation. Many Renaissance thinkers feared being too bold,
which stifled creativity. Furthermore, in 1545, the Council of Trent established the
Roman Inquisition, which made humanism and any views that challenged the Catholic Church
an act of heresy punishable by death.
Political instability arising out of uncontrolled individualism led to jealousy among pettystates. Italy was not a united nation but consisted of several petty-states and city republics.
There was constant political strife and jealousy among them. This affected the cultural progress
and helped the sudden waning of the Renaissance. Another cause to the decay of Renaissance
culture was the ignorance and superstition among the masses. There was no system of universal
education and so there was uneven diffusion of learning. This meant that the civilization was

built on very shaky foundations.
The decline of Renaissance outside Italy was less sudden than in Italy. In some respects,
the change was very gradual resulting in the fusion of the old with the new. Scientific
achievements were merely extended, but emphasis shifted to the biological sciences. The
Renaissance art gradually evolved into the baroque art of the 17th and 18th centuries.
Renaissance humanism died out after the 16th century. In philosophy the exaltation of the
universe took precedence over man who was relegated to an insignificant place. In northern
and Western Europe (i.e. outside Italy) Renaissance due to the heritage of bitterness and
unreason left by the Protestant Reformation. Thus, by the early 17th century, the Renaissance
movement had died out, giving way to the Age of Enlightenment.
While many scholars view the Renaissance as a unique and exciting time in European

history, others argue that the period wasn’t much different from the Middle Ages and that both
eras overlapped more than traditional accounts suggest. Also, some modern historians believe
that the Middle Ages had a cultural identity that’s been downplayed throughout history and
overshadowed by the Renaissance era. While the exact timing and overall impact of the
Renaissance is sometimes debated, there is a little dispute that the events of the period ultimately
led to advances that changed the way people understood and interpreted the world around
them.

14.1 Introduction
The Geographical Discoveries of the 15th and 16th centuries had great significance
in the rise and development of Europe. Science and new discoveries provided extensive scope
to human society and this period constitute an important chapter in the history of the modern
world. It is also known as the Age of Discovery. Owing to the attack of Ottoman Turks over
Constantinople it had become impossible to reach Asia from Europe through land route. Ancient

trade routes were not advantageous for England, France, and Holland etc. They could be
useful only for those who lived in Mediterranean coastal cities. It marred the great ancient
significance of Mediterranean Sea route. Consequently, new regions were opened up in the
sphere of trade and commerce and the European merchants got rid of the Arab traders. It also
did with the narrow outlook and superstitions of Europe and people began to go around the
earth. The new sea routes to the East as well as the discovery of new continents like the
America radically transformed the course of history. The adventurous spirit of the sailors like
Bartholomew Diaz, Christopher Columbus and Ferdinand Magellan ultimately led to these historic
discoveries.

255
The hazardous sea voyages of the European sailors and the efforts of merchants, they
got success in establishing their colonies in expansive continents like Africa, America and Asia.
Moreover, in place to trade rivalry, birth of imperialism took place in favourable circumstances
and a new chapter of exploitation of the backward classed started. Besides this, relations with
the distant countries were established which enabled the attainment of success in the field of
education and science. Prof. A.J. Grant has mentioned about these geographical discoveries,
“The geographical discoveries of the period were one of the most startling developments which
heralded the Modern Age”.
Sea Voyages of the 15th and 16th Centuries
14.2 Startling Developments of the Modern Age
The Renaissance had removed all the medieval superstitions from the mind of the people

and it had injected in them the spirit of adventure. Now they started on journey to distant
countries without any fear whatsoever. Religion, politics and the spirit of adventure made
Europeans to undertake the voyages to unknown lands, but the main motive was economic.
Europeans were running out of precious metals with they paid for the goods they imported
from India and the Far East. By the 15th century the spices and herbs of South East Asia had
become necessitates for preservation of food and in pharmaceutical products. This trade till
the 11th century was in the hands of the Muslims and later on it was gradually taken over by
Italian traders. Muslims continued to bring products from the orient and sold them to the Italian
merchants who carried them to their home ports and sold them to Europeans. Each intermediary
who handled these goods made heavy profits and the Egyptian Government added further

256
charges for the use of its ports. The Europeans had only silver and gold which was getting
exhausted. So, it was necessary that new sources of precious metals and a cheaper trade
route to the Far-East be discovered if the Europeans were to trade with the East. In addition,
during this period people discovered that the earth was round like an orange. So, the sailors
concluded that they might return to the same point from where they began their journey. It
encouraged them for voyages because now they were sure that after going round the earth,
they would reach the place from where they started their voyage.
14.2.1 Travel Accounts of Marco Polo
Since the Medieval period the Europeans were endeavoring to discover a long route in
order to establish their trade relations with the distant countries of Asia. All the routes of Asia

had become safe with the rising influence of the Mongols. A merchant of Venice named Nicoli
Polo twice went to China and once he took his son Marco Polo with him. These travelers
described China, Japan and India in such an interesting way as inspired the people to have
trade relations with these countries. The book travels of Marco Polo inspired the people to
undertake voyages to distant countries. The Europeans countries possessed a very extensive
knowledge of the geography of the Eastern countries. Marco Polo who had travelled widely in
the east, had familiarized the west with the variety of products that the East could offer to the
west and also the potentialities of trade with the East. A Merchants Handbook described all
known trade routes between Europe and the Far East. Similarly, the Secrets of the Faithful
Crusader told about Asiatic cities.

14.2.2 Spirit of Trade and Economic Advantage
Europe had been maintaining trade relations with the eastern countries for many years.
One of the important causes for these voyages was Spanish and Portuguese ambition for a
share in the trade with the east, which had all along been monopolized by the Italian cities. So,
the Spanish and Portuguese merchants wanted to discover a new route to the East independent
of Italian control. The western countries used various articles manufactured in the eastern
countries and in the trade the Europeans earned a lot of profit. Among the chief centres for
having trade with the Eastern countries in Europe, Italy influenced the trade with the eastern
countries of other countries began to be jealous of Italy. The search for sea routes was inspired
by this commercial rivalry. Scheville writes about it, “the strongest incentive to geographical

exploration was furnished by strongest incentive by commercial and economic ambition and
rivalry. The merchants of different European countries tried with one another to have a share in

257
the lucrative trade with the east and this led to their adventurous discoveries of the new routes
to the east.”
After the occupation of Constantinople in 1453 by the Ottoman Turks, it had become
impossible to travel to Asia from Europe. Hence the Europeans had to search new routes in
order to reach Asia and to amass wealth as much as possible. In fact, the mercantile profits
and economic achievement mainly inspired the Europeans for making geographical discoveries.
14.2.3 Spirit of Imperialism
End of feudalism and development of cities were chief characteristics of the modern era.
Consequently, autocratic government and spirit of nationalism developed a lot. Later on, the
autocratic rules endeavored for the expansion of empires in order to increase their power.
Europeans were also inspired to establish big empires and colonies. This spirit of imperialism

lured the people towards geographical directions.
14.2.4 Religious Wars
During the medieval period religious wars took place between the Christians and the
Muslims, in which the Muslims stood victorious and the Christians had to flee to some other
countries for shelter. These settlers related the wonderful stories of the economic prosperity of
the countries of the east to the Europeans which inspired them to establish trade relations with
these countries. Another cause was the missionary zeal of the Spaniards who wanted to spread
the Christian religion in the East. Besides the search of trade centers, the Christian missionaries
also contributed to the spirit of geographical discoveries.
14.2.5 Religious Expansion by the Christian Missionaries
The missionaries of Europe travelled to eastern countries in order to spread their region.

The Christian missionaries who went to china in order to convert Kublai Khan, the Mongol
Emperor, and other Mongols and after making an extensive journey of about three thousand
miles, he met bare Khan in the capital of Mongols. Later on, William Rubruquis also travelling
through Black Sea and Caspian Sea reached Mongolia to see bare Khan. He remained there
for some months and then came back. Although both of them failed to achieve success in their
mission, listening to their experience and going through the memoirs, the other brave people
of Europe were enthused to make journeys to the eastern countries and they discovered some
new countries by their voyages. A.J.Grand writes in this connection, “The commercial motive

258
of Europeans was seconded by their missionary zeal which urged them on to evangelize distant
pagan lands”.
14.2.6 Scientific Inventions
A spirit of adventure prompted some of the European merchants and navigators to
undertake these voyages of discovery. In the beginning of the modern era, the new scientific
inventions contributed a lot. Among all these inventions, the invention of Mariner’s Compass
was the most significant one. It gave great importance to geographical discoveries. It is an
instrument meant for knowing the directions. Its needle always points towards north and saves
the people at sea from being lost and people dared travel to distant places due to correct
knowledge of geographical directions. The keen rivalry among the European nations to be the
first to discover a new route to the east provided the inventive to the explorers.
14.3 Geographical Discoveries

Thus, being inspired owing to economic, commercial, religious and imperialist reasons
the people of Europe indulged themselves in geographical discoveries in the 15th century and
it reached its climax in the 16th century.
14.3.1 Attempts of Portugal
In the 15th century after occupation of Canary Islands, the Portuguese began to
make efforts for western side of Africa. The Portuguese Prince, Henry made great efforts in
this direction. He is also known in History as Henry the Navigator (1394-1460). As a result of
his efforts, the Madeira and Azores Islands were discovered. He provided great financial help
and inspiration to the navigators of his country and they resorted to this difficult task. They
devoted themselves to the noble and adventurous cause of finding a new sea route. The main
project of Henry the Navigator was the exploration of the west coast of Africa. His sailors

discovered the Cape Verde Islands. Although Henry died in 1460, his zeal provided stimulus to
the Portugese for further explorations.
In 1487, the Portuguese Captain Bartholomew Diaz was the first man to discover the
southern tip of Africa. It was named “the Cape of Storms” by the discoverer due to a terrible
storm he experienced there. Later, the Portuguese King, John II renamed it as “the Cape of
Good Hope” because it provided hope that access to the Indian Ocean was possible. Later on,
in A.D. 1498 Vasco da Gama succeeded in reaching India by sailing round the Cape of Good

259
Hope where he sought concession for the Portuguese merchants. Thetcher writes about this
journey, “The hero of this important voyage that established a more profitable and easier link
with the East, was Vasco da Gama.” Pedro Alvares Cabral was sent out to exploit the discovery
that had been made and the monopoly had been established for the Portuguese crown. But
Cabral was thrown off his course right across the southern Atlantic along the seaboard of
Brazil which he claimed for Portugal.
The result of the adventurous voyages of Bartholomew Diaz and Vasco da Gama proved
significant. Now Portugal established its supremacy over the trade and commerce of the East.
Gradually, the Portuguese established their control over Ceylon, Sumatra and Java. In 1517,
the Portuguese reached Canton in China and then proceeded to Japan in A.D. 1542. Father

Francis Xavier was a great missionary and he made every effort for the spread of Christianity.
He converted a great number of Indians and Japanese to the fold of Christianity. The efforts of
the Portuguese proved unstable and soon they lost their trade monopoly but, however, the
relations which were established between the Europeans and the people in the Far East proved
everlasting.
Vasco da Gama Christopher Columbus Ferdinand Magellan
14.3.2 Discovery of America
Attempts were being made to reach India through the route of Atlantic Ocean. Christopher
Columbus, a poor sailor of Geneva was making constant efforts to reach India and other
countries of the East through the route of Atlantic Ocean. Being disappointed with the attitude
of the Portuguese Emperor John II, he appealed to Ferdinand, the Emperor of Spain but he

also did not pay heed to his request as during this time he was busy in the problem of Grenada.
However, the Spanish king Ferdinand promised help to Columbus due to the intervention of
Queen Isabella after the war.

260
At last Columbus started for this journey with the help to the Spanish king in August
1492. Columbus thought that in case, he went to the West crossing the Atlantic, he would,
undoubtedly, reach India, in the East. Three small vessels and a few sailors were the only
companions with him but he had a great courage which helped in the achievement of his
mission. He reached America on 11th October 1492 after great difficulties. He thought that he
had reached the shores of India. Therefore, he called the natives of that island Indians. This
was the most significant discovery of Columbus and it came to be known as the “New World”.
Columbus made three more voyages and explored the islands in the Caribbean Sea and Central
America. These islands are even today called as the West Indies. Later in 1501, Amerigo

Vespucci, an Italian navigator, with the support of the King of Spain explored the areas of
South America. He came to the conclusion that what Columbus discovered was not India.
Therefore the new continent was named as America. However, Columbus is considered as
the discoverer of America.
14.3.3 Attempts of Spain
Both Portugal and Spain from the point view of commercial prosperity and imperialism
divided the world between them with the help of Pope. In 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued a
Bull in order to prevent any dispute between Spain and Portugal in exploring new sea-routes
and new lands. It is popularly called the Papal Bull (order of Pope). According to it an imaginary
line was drawn dividing the globe into east and west. Spain was given the right to possess the
lands of the west and Portugal on the east of the Pope’s line. As a result Africa, Asia, and

Brazil were given to Portugal and Spain was asked to establish her control over most of the
part of Northern and Southern America. Thus, Spain could not use sea route through the Cape
of Good Hope to reach the East Indies. And the fate of the world was decided without seeking
the help or support of any other person.
Therefore, Spain planned to reach the east by sailing westwards. On 10 August 1519,
Ferdinand Megallan had sailed with five Spanish ships namely, Trinidad, San Antonio,
Concepcion, Victoria and Santiago from the port of Sevilla. The fleet of Magellan crossed an
arduous 373 mile long passage on the southern end of South America. This strait is now
named the Strait of Magellan. Then he entered an Ocean which was calmer than the Atlantic.
Therefore, he named it the Pacific Ocean. While crossing the Pacific, the sailors suffered for

want of food and drinking water. At last, on 6 March 1521, they reached the Philippines, where
Magellan was killed by the natives. The survivors with the only remaining ship, the Victoria

261
arrived at Sevilla through the Cape of Good Hope on 9 September 1522. It was the first
voyage undertaken round the world.
14.3.4 Other Geographical Discoveries
While Portugal consolidated her control of the Sea route to Indian and Spain began
colonizing central and South America, the rulers of England and France sent out explorers to
discover the North West route to the Far East. In 1497, John Cabot was sent by Henry VII of
England to explore the seas. He discovered the Newfoundland. In his next expedition, Cabot
reached North America and he was the first European to land on the mainland of America. But,
he was not able to find any people there and returned to England disappointed. His discoveries
enabled England to claim the whole of Canada, New found land and Labrador and the territory
along the Atlantic Coast which constituted the 13 American Colonies. English attempts to discover

a Northwest Passage to the East and a North east passage above Russia to the East ended in
failure.
The French also tried to discover a Westerly route to the East. Between 1534 and 1541
Jacques Cartier, in search of the Northwest Passage, explored much of the St. Lawrence River
and enabled France to claim sovereignty over eastern North American. However, he found the
Red Indian settlements and named that region as Canada. Another Frenchman Samuel de
Champlain founded a colony at Quebec and journeyed over the lake which bears his name
and Westward to the Great Lakes. Rena La Salle in 17th century opened the interior of North

262
America by exploring the Mississippi River. In 1661 he sailed down the river to the Gulf of
Mexico, occupied the whole territory, called it Louisiana and enabled France to claim the entire
Mississippi Valley. Thus, England and France were not serious competitors of Spain and
Portugal in colonization or trans-oceanic trade before the end of the 16th century.
14.3.5 Spanish Colonies in America
America, a big continent was full of forests during this period. Besides Mexico and
Peru, the entire continent was inhabited by the Red Indians of America. Columbus established
his control over the island in the name of the King of Spain but the Spanish people did not
behave properly. They established their colonies in America and poured there in great numbers,
in search of gold and silver. Spain amassed a lot of wealth. It lured the other countries of

Europe to establish their colonies; France, England and Holland were prominent among them.
Therefore, all these countries began to fight among themselves for supremacy.
14.3.6 Trade with the Eastern Countries
After making a round of the African coast, the Portuguese reached India and monopolized
their trade with India and other countries of the East. Seeing them prospering, the other countries
of Europe, such as France, England, And Holland also wanted to start their trade with the
Eastern Countries. They established their trading companies and constructed ‘kuthis’ in the
eastern part of India. The chief aim of these foreigners was to establish their control over the
trade of the Eastern countries.
14.3.7 Establishment of Empire in the East
With the passage of time the countries of Europe began to show the signs of their

imperialist attitude. They felt disgusted with their trade and commercial relations with the
countries of the East. In political condition of the Asia countries was quite deplorable. In the
same way Java, Sumatra, Malaya etc. were small and weak undue interference in their internal
affairs. Gradually, they established their political supremacy in the Eastern countries along with
trade and commerce.
Thus the discovery of America and new sea route made the countries of Europe
prosperous. So far, the people of Europe did not know anything about India and Africa but the
geographical discoveries enabled them to make a tour round the world. It brought a complete
Renaissance in Europe.

263
14.4 Influence of the Geographical Discoveries
After the occupation of Constantinople by the Ottoman Turks in 1453, age of geographical
discoveries began. Progress of science, tendencies of imperialism, desire of religious preaching
and the outbreak of industrial revolution encouraged the people towards geographical inventions
and thus a new chapter began which influenced the course of history in the following spheres:
14.4.1 Intellectual Development
The development of the world also contributed to the mental development of mankind
and the feeling of joint development of mankind and the felling of joint development took root
in the people’s minds. A.J. Grant has written about it, “Contact with the new world, new peoples
and new modes of life dispelled the silly notions of medieval ignorance and hastened the pace
of intellectual revolution started by Renaissance.”

14.4.2 Economic Influence
As a result of new sea routes and geographical inventions various changes took place in
the economic life of the people. Scheville has remarked in this connection, “Change of routes,
resources and commercial articles gave birth to commercial revolutions”.
These changes brought a speedy development in the trade and commerce of the
Europeans. It also contributed to the establishment of big cities and as result of ht established
of colonies, the Europeans became wealthy and prosperous and various Joint Stock companies
and banks were established.
14.4.3 Social Changes
The new discoveries and inventions freed the people from the narrow dogmas and
superstitions. The culture of one place began to reach the other places due to fast means of
transportation. Thus the mingling of two cultures helped the rise of modern culture. Besides

the merits of the geographical discoveries they had some demerits. The slave system flourished
as a result of the social changes. However, the social life of people in general became happy
and prosperous. Hayes remarks, “Socially, most important result of the new discoveries was
the advent of the middle class”.

264
14.4.4 Political Influence
As a result of the geographical discoveries political conflicts began in Europe. The
geographical knowledge of the people of Europe grew and an international spirit developed. It
inaugurated the Europeanization of the world. Thus, the geographical discoveries brought
great and far-reaching changes in the outlook, thought and the standard of living of the people.
14.5 Impact of the Geographical Discoveries
 The age of geographical voyages and discoveries had an exhilarating the liberating effect
upon man’s minds, filled them with a sense of achievement and opened broad horizons.
Europeans came to know of the exotic civilizations and cultures outside Europe.
 The voyages expanded commerce. The Mediterranean trade was transformed into world
trade. The Atlantic seaboard became more important than the Mediterranean. The Italian

trade centres like Genoa. Pisa and Venice lost importance and the Italian monopoly of
oriental trade was broken. New trade centres and harbours arose at Lisbon, Bordeaux,
Liverpool, Bristol and Amsterdam.
 There was also a great increase in the volumes of commerce and in the variety of articles
of consumption. Besides the spices and textiles from the Orient, potatoes, tobacco and
maize from North America, molasses and um from the West Indies Cocoa, Chocolate,
Quinine and the Cochineal dye from South America and ivory slaves and ostrich feathers
from Africa were in demand. Further supply of articles like sugar, coffee, rice and cotton
increased to such an extent that they were no longer articles of luxury.
 Geographical discoveries encouraged shipbuilding and the organization of the naval power.
 The voyages shifted the centre of political gravity from land to sea. This resulted in the

rise of colonial empires based on sea-power and history after the geographical discoveries
became the history of the world. It resulted in expansion of Europe and gradual spreads
of European influences throughout the world. These discoveries paved the way for modern
imperialism.
 European concepts of trade and diplomacy changed radically as now ambitions and new
rivalries developed over colonies, trans-oceanic trade and the amassing of precious
metals.
 The most important result was the expansion of the supply of precious metals. Gold and
silver from the mines of Mexico, Bolina and Peru powered into Europe.

265
 The diffusion of American wealth stimulated the growth of capital and the spirit of enterprise
among merchants, bankers and manufactures in North Western Europe.
 It resulted in the growth of a capitalistic economy with profit as the chief motive of business,
the barter system broke down and it encouraged speculation. These economic aspects
resulted in the Commercial Revolution and the rise of Mercantilism.
 The system of slavery was followed. The European planters in America imported Negro
slaves from Africa to work in their plantations.
 The geographical discoveries solved the problem of over population in Europe and many
Europeans began to settle in the American continents.
 The culture of Europe had spread to Asia, Africa and other parts of the world very rapidly.

to discover the North West route to the Far East.
 Thus the discovery of America and new sea route made the countries of Europe
prosperous.
 So far, the people of Europe did not know anything about India and Africa but the
