15.1 Introduction
Since the beginning of the Modern era some revolutionary changes occurred in the life of
the people of Europe and Renaissance brought about a revolution in their religious life. So far,
people were controlled by religion. The Pope of Rome was the head of the Roman Catholics
and Cardinals, Archbishops, Bishops and Priests all were his subordinates. The organization
of Church was quite strong. People of Europe accepted the words of the priest like speechless
animals. No one had the power and courage to act contrary to the will of religious authorities
because they considered them to be the representatives of God and their orders, the command
of God.

But with the commencement of modern era the situation began to change. The spirit of
enquiry developed among the people due to the result of Renaissance. Various books were
translated in the vernacular literature, the study of which not only revolutionized their mental
attitudes but also freed them from mental bondage to the priests. The translation of Bible
injected a new vigour into the people and the superstitions about Church began to collapse.
This movement is the name of the opposition which continued in Europe since the fifteenth
century, the chief aim of which was to mitigate the influence of the Pope, to establish the
national Church and to provide independent religious thinking to the people. H.A.L. Fisher, a
prominent historian writes about it, “The name ‘Reformation’ is generally given to that religious

revolution of the 16th century which culminated in the separation of many nations of Europe
from the Church of Rome”.
15.2 Meaning of Reformation
The concept of unity in the middle Ages was attacked by Humanism and by the spirit of
individualism. The Renaissance rebelled against intellectual unity and centralized control.
The rise of the national state shattered the medieval concept of a universal state. The final

272
assault was the Reformation, which attacked the monopolistic power of the universal Church,
one of the greatest of all medieval institutions. This great religious upheaval not only was the
evidence of a great religious change, but also proclaimed the dawn of a new era.
Scheville throwing light on the meaning of this movement writes, “It was, in fact, a dual
movement having for its objects the renovation of the moral life of Christendom and the
repudiation of the papal claims to ecclesiastical supremacy”. A.J. Grant also writes in this
connection that as a result of this movement the rebirth of the religious life of people took place
in Europe and it got a political shape due to opposition to the rights of the pope.
Some historian opine that in the beginning of the 16th century a large number of Christians

became the opponents of the Roman Catholics Church due to rise of the spirit of enquiry. They
wanted to reform the institution of church completely. This effort for reformation led to the
outbreak of Reformation movement and some new sects emerged in the Christian religion; all
these taken together are called the Reformation Movement.
While both the Renaissance and the Reformation aided in the breakdown of the old
order, and each contributed to the establishment of the new, they operated individually and, in
some cases, were opposed to each other. Some Protestant Humanists utilized classical studies
in religious controversies, but Humanism stimulated pagan learning, which austere Protestants
condemned. It rebelled against the otherworldliness of scholastic Christianity, while leading
Protestants revived supernaturalism, even witchcraft. Many of the early Humanists were loyal

Roman Catholics critical of ecclesiastical excesses, but interested primarily in merely reforming
the established church. Some Protestants were, in fact, bitter critics of the cult of humanity
and of beauty expressed in the Renaissance.
15.3 Causes of Reformation Movement
The following causes contributed to the upsurge of Reformation Movement:
15.3.1 Corrupt Life of Pope and his Subordinates
Earlier, the life of the Pope and the priests was quite simple and they devoted themselves
to the religious contemplation. The Roman Catholic religion spread through the entire Europe
but by the end of the 15th century and the first half of the sixteenth century, the life of the priests
became quite corrupt. They did not possess any moral quality in them. The Pope and his
subordinates considered themselves the representatives of God hence they held themselves

273
responsible only to God. The main duty of the Pope was to safeguard the Christendom and
he was increasing his power day by day in order to perform his duty properly. He used to
maintain a vast army in order to punish his opponents.
The Pope incorporate some new rules in Roman Catholic religious books for his own
benefit and led a sensual life. All Popes, Alexander VI (1492-1503), Julius II (1503-1513) and
Leo X (1513-1521) failed to bring about any reform in the contemporary system. On the other
hand, the Pope Leo X created some new problems on the issue of repair of the Church of
St.Peter at Rome. He resorted to some foul and objectionable methods for the collection of
money. He created some new posts in the Church and sold them at high premiums. A Professor
of History writes that the opposition of Martin Luther proved fatal for the rights of Pope in

Germany. It was a protest against the autocratic views of the religious authorities, wastage of
money by Pope and their immoral acts.
15.3.2 Renaissance
In the beginning of the modern era, as a result of Renaissance, new knowledge, spirit of
enquiry, opposition to superstitions and interest in science, art and literature developed among
the people of Europe. Various authors and scholars wrote and condemned the Church for the
evils it represented. Besides In Praise of Folly, Houghton also wrote Letters of an Obscure
Man. He criticized Church and demanded reforms in the ecclesiastical system. Martin Luther’s
translation of Bible invoked a new spirit among the people. The new knowledge developed
among the people of Europe, which made the advent of Reformation inevitable.
15.3.3 Blind Faith in Religion Perished

Like other religions of Europe and other countries in the beginning, Roman Catholic
religion was simple and sacred. There were no evils in it. A famous English poet, Lord Tennyson
has remarked, “old order changeth, yielding place to new”. So various evils and foul practices
had come to be associated with the church in the Medieval Age. The clergy began to lead a life
of sensual pleasures; hence it had become necessary that some new traditions should be
established in place of the old ones. Pope’s selling of posts and his accumulation of wealth
through unfair and foul means forced the people to raise their voices against all these evils.
The Renaissance which was the result of expansion of education, made the blind faith vanish
into thin air and ultimately the Reformation Movement was ushered in Europe.

274
15.3.4 Rise of Nationalism
The Pope was considered to be the representative of God earth in the Christian world.
The other religious authorities such as Cardinals, Archbishops and priests also considered
themselves to be belonging to the same category. Moreover, they considered themselves
responsible only to God and non else. Hence, as a result of the Renaissance the spirit of
nationalism emerged and all the people began to wish that they should remain faithful to the
nation. Thetcher writes about it, “they decided to free themselves from the vexatious papal
interference both in the religious as well as in the political field”.
15.3.5 Economic Reasons
The Roman Catholic Church had amassed huge wealth by the end of the 15th century
because every Christian used to pay one-tenth of his income to the Church in the form of Tithe.

The Pope and the priests also imposed some taxes on the general masses for their own selfish
ends. Appointments on clerical posts were made on the basis of bargaining and the highest
bidder was given the post. They wished that the accumulated wealth in the Churches should
be spent for the good of the general masses but the clerics were altogether against and they
did not discharge their religious duties properly. Hence the Reformation Movement spread in
Europe.
15.3.6 Political Causes
Although Reformation began as a religious movement, it had political and literacy
significance. The Roman Catholic Church was very well organized and nobody had the power
to disobey the command of the Pope. Scheville writes, “The exactions of the Pope and his
interference in political affairs of the countries in Europe were greatly resented by the Europeans”.

Since the beginning of the 16th century, besides religious power, the political power of the Pope
had also increased. In 1378 the papal authority was divided into two parts- one Pope used to
live in Rome but the other lived in Avignon. Both used to condemn each other. It hurt the
prestige of the Pope and his honour decreased. The mutual feud of the Popes encouraged the
powerful monarchs to violate the orders of the Pope. Thus the Reformation in Germany flourished
easily.
15.3.7 Immediate Cause
The Pope had enhanced his expenditure too much, for which he wanted to increase the
sources of his income. He resorted to the sale of letters of indulgence. Martin Luther led these

275
oppositions. He was born in a poor family. His father was a miner but he educated his son
properly well and he was appointed professor of Theology in the University of Brandenburg.
Martin Luther began to educate people that no person could get rid of his sins by way of
purchasing the indulgence. The Pope felt very much annoyed with Martin Luther and wanted to
punish him but Luther enjoyed a lot of public support, hence the Pope had to give up his idea
of punishing him. However, the political, economic and religious reasons can also not be rejected.
15.4 Martin Luther and Reformation Movement in Germany
Since the fourteenth century people began to oppose the rights of the Pope. First of all,
John Wycliffe, an English priest put forth the shortcomings of the Church before the people.
Later on, being inspired by the preaching’s of Wycliffe, John Husse of Bohemia preached the

principles of John Wycliffe in Prague University. Although his predecessors could not succeed
in their mission of reforming the religion, he succeeded in his aim and the Protestant religion
was established in Europe. His thoughts later on came to be known as Lutheranism.
John Wycliffe
15.4.1 Why Lutheranism Emerged in Germany?
Reformation was a small event in the beginning but soon the social and political conditions
of Germany became very intricate due to the international relations of the big countries of
Europe. Charles V, the ruler of Spain was elected as the Emperor of Holy Roman Empire also
in 1519. Neither was he a great emperor nor an efficient diplomat and commander. He was a
staunch opponent of Protestantism. The political condition of Germany was quite favourable
for such movement. The position of the Emperor was not very strong in Germany. In fact, it

276
was not an empire. It was merely a confederation of various small states which had no
interference from any central power. Scheville writes that Germany was only an empire by
name. In fact, it was a confederation of various small states which did did not have any
interference from the Pope. In the beginning the Emperor Charles V paid no heed to the
crushing of the reformation movement. Hence the feeling of reformation was strengthened
and the influence of the Roman Catholic religion declined in Germany and the nearby regions.
The rise of Martin Luther injected new life into the rise of Reformation.
15.4.2 Early Career of Martin Luther
Martin Luther was born in A.D. 1483 in a small village in Saxony in a family of a farmer.
After completing his elementary and intermediate education, he got education of law and theology

in the University of Erfurt. In A.D. 1505 he became a monk of Augustan Sect but in 1508 he
was appointed Professor of Theology and Philosophy in Brandenburg University. In 1517 a
most significant event took place which forced Martin Luther to raise a standard of revolt against
Roman Catholicism. At this time the agents of Pope were selling letters of indulgence for
renovation of the Church of St. Peter in Rome.
Hayes also comments, “Luther’s Ninety-five Theses” (Arguments) against indulgences
in 1517 led to a sort universal revolt in Germany against the Pope and his Catholic religion and
in a way facilitated the foundation of the Protestant Church. Charles V declared Martin Luther
an atheist and removed the safety measures of empire from him. Luther escaped to Saxony
where Frederick gave him shelter.
Martin Luther Martin Luther directs the
posting of his 95 Theses

277
15.4.3 Expansion of Lutheranism
In the beginning Martin Luther had only opposed the sale of indulgence but immediately
the opposition took a fierce turn. Martin Luther challenged the Pope by accusations and in
1520 Pope Leo X excommunicated him. Martin Luther had to turn here and there for the safety
of his life and ultimately he died in 1546 when Europe was busy in religious wars.
According to his own thinking Martin Luther propounded the following principles in the
religious sphere:
1. Luther did not consider the external show such as fasts, repentance, pilgrimages etc. fit
for getting salvation.
2. Luther opposed the sale of indulgences because it was not the way of attaining salvation.
He used to say, “Faith was the bridge, if he had faith, he could be saved despite his
inherent and desperate wickedness”.

3. Luther considered all Christian like priests after baptism was done, hence he desired, the
priests should also be permitted to marry.
4. Luther was against too much of religious ceremonies and favoured only a few like birth,
repentance and death.
5. Martin Luther believed that God loved both, the world and the heaven. Hence there was
no need to escape from the world. Man can attain salvation by doing service to humanity
and performing his duties sincerely.
6. Luther was against the religious authority and believed in the establishment of a national
church. He intended to establish the rule of Bible in place of that of the Pope.
7. Luther wanted to expand his ideas through peaceful means without disturbing the peace
of the continent.
15.4.4 Diet of Worms
The Pope wanted to punish Martin Luther for which he sought the cooperation of some

rulers. The Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire declared Martin Luther an atheist but Luther
burnt the declaration in public. Hence Charles V summoned the Diet of Worms in order to
punish Martin Luther. In 1522 the Bible was translated into German language. Some people

278
resorted to violence. At this occasion Martin Luther came out of the fort of Brandenburg and
established peace. The Diet of Nuremburg was called in 1522 on the orders of the Pope but
it too failed to take any action against Luther for fear of a civil war.
15.4.5 Revolt of the Farmers
As a result of the Reformation Movement of Martin Luther the farmers of South Germany
revolted against the Catholic ruler as both the Church as well as the Catholic rulers used to
realize heavy tax from them and the condition of the farmers was not better than that of the
serfs. Gradually, this movement took a violent shape. Martin Luther had sympathy with the
farmers but he was also afraid of the violent form of the movement. He wrote letters to the
princes and emperors for crushing the farmers’ revolt because he was afraid that in case the

revolt of the farmers continued, his own Reformation Movement would be crushed. In 1529
this revolt was crushed mercilessly and a large number of enthusiastic farmers were killed. As
a result of it Luther lost the sympathy and support of the lower class. The popularity of Luther
was also adversely affected and he lost the support of various friendly rulers.
15.4.6 Expansion of Lutheranism
1. The first conference of Holy Empire was held in 1526 at Spier. By this time the rulers
were divided between the supporters of the Pope and the supporters of Martin Luther,
hence no final solution could be arrived at in this conference.
2. The second conference of Spier took place in 1529. In this conference severe contention
arose between the Catholics and the Protestants because the Emperors Charles V
supported the Catholics vehemently and the proposal of the Diet of Worms was confirmed

and stress was laid on the suppression of the Reformation Movement. W.Stubbs writes
about it, “Against this action of Diet of Spier, the supporters of Luther entered a formal
protest. It was from this protest that the followers of Luther came to be called Protestants”.
3. League of Schmalkaldan was formed by the Protestants in 1531 for their safety as Emperor
Charles V was severely against them and wanted to crush them. Saxony, Brandenburg,
Hesse etc. were the members of this League.
4. After 15 years of the formation of the League of Schmalkaldan, Charles V directed his
attention to the crushing of this league. At the same time in 1546 Martin Luther breathed
his last and some differences emerged among the followers of Luther. No doubt, it

279
enhanced the power of Charles in Germany but civil war began in Germany which lasted
up to 1555.
15.4.7 Treaty of Augsburg (1555)
After the escape of Charles V, his brother Ferdinand concluded an interim pact known as
the Convention of Pissu with the Protestants but soon after this convention the treaty of Augsburg
was signed so that permanent peace could be established in Europe. The following were the
provisions of this treaty:
1. The idea of imposing a type of religion in Germany was given up and freedom of religion
was awarded to each state. In case somebody did not want to act according to the religion
of the state, he was permitted to leave the state and settle in any other state where his
religion was being patronized.
2. Now only two religious were recognized in Germany-the Roman Catholic and the

Protestant. The state which did not follow either of the two religious, were not included in
this treaty. Thus, Protestantism was declared legitimate.
3. Some immovable property of the Catholic Church was confiscated by the Protestants and
they were permitted to maintain their authority over it.
4. One of the most significant terms of this treaty was ecclesiastical reservation. According
to it, if some Catholic priest joined Protestantism, he would have to forgo all the privileges
of the Catholic post so far being enjoyed by him.
The shortcomings of the Treaty of Augsburg are:
1. The rulers of the states were authorized to select their religion instead of the people of the
states.
2. The authority of the rulers was established about ecclesiastical rights in place of the
Pope.
3. The huge property of the Roman Catholics continued to be their own.
The criticism of the Treaty are:

The treaty had shortcomings. It did not authorize the people to select their religious
rights were given to the rulers in place of the Pope and the people had to obey the religion of

280
the state. Scheville also writes, “This very clause proved a fruitful source of quarrel between
Catholics and the Protestants and in the long run culminated in the Thirty Years’ War”.
Although Martin Luther breathed his last in 1546, his name became immortal in the
pages of the history of Europe because he dared raise a voice against the Pope, suffered for
his protest and led a Reformation Movement in Germany. He challenged the evils and reformed
Christianity; hence his contribution is remembered even today.
15.4.8 Causes for the Success of Martin Luther
The following factors contributed to the success of Martin Luther:
 The character and personality of Martin Luther were very attractive. He had great faith in
his religion and he possessed great courage and enthusiasm for its expansion. He was
completely against corruption and he inspired the people of Germany towards his religion

by his knowledge and honesty.
 Martin Luther was a great scholar. He knew it fully well that people did not know Latin,
hence he used German language of his country for the expansion of his ideas. He directed
the people to the study of Bible in their own language so that they could understand it
properly and act according to the teachings of the Bible without following the instructions
of the corrupt priests.
 During the time of Martin Luther the entire Germany was divided into 300 small states
and there was no political unity in the country. Most of the states intended to remain
independent. Many states became the supporters of Martin Luther and thus he gained
the sympathy of their Protestant public. Thus, the political condition of Germany contributed
a lot to the success of Martin Luther.
 Germany and Italy were very close to each other and the headquarters of Holy Roman

Empire had shifted from Italy to Germany by now. The Renaissance had triggered great
deal of intellectual awakening and had affected the people of Germany. Hayes writes,
“The Renaissance weakened the traditional respect for the authority of the Church and
the Pope. It helped Luther immediately to spread his influence in Germany”.

281
 This was an era of the development of nationalism and various big and small states of
Germany considered the Pope a foreigner and wished to uproot his authority from the
German states about religious matters because a large part of ecclesiastical taxes were
sent to Rome every year. Hence they thought it worthwhile to support Martin Luther and
oppose the Pope for the unwanted payments made to a foreigner.
 Martin Luther was an opportunist. He won the sympathy of the kings and princes by
opposing the farmers’ revolt and this got their help for the expansion of his movement.
This confidence inspired him very much and he preached his faith round the clock with
great courage and enthusiasm.
 Charles remained overbuys in the Italian wars, hence he could not get time to suppress
Lutheranism in the beginning. Moreover, there was no joint front in Germany to oppose

the faith of Martin Luther.
To sum up, we may say that the character and personality of Martin Luther, contemporary
political condition, Renaissance and the cooperation of the German princes and rulers made
Martin Luther successful in the expansion of his faith.
15.5 Reformation in England
The humanists of England had already opposed the Pope and the Catholic Church before
the accession of Henry VIII. Edward I and Edward II also endeavoured to bring the influence of
the Pope during their regimes. They were also influenced by the preaching of humanists, John
Colet and Sir Thomas Moore who preached against the Church and the state. In spite of all this
the influence of the Pope and the Catholic Church continued in England up to the accession of
Henry VIII and his conflict with the Pope.
15.5.1 Henry VIII and the Early Religion Movement

Like other countries of Europe, during the 16th century, the Catholic religion was in vogue
in England and the rule of Tudor dynasty was established in England in the end of the 15th
century. Even then Henry VIII did not oppose the Pope in the beginning. It pleased the Pope no
end and he awarded him the title of ‘Defender of the Faith’. Henry VIII also severely punished
the supporters of Martin Luther.

282
English Reformation
15.5.2 Henry VIII and the Problem of Divorce
The Protestantism which emerged in England was not motivated by religious causes but
it was inspired by the political and personal causes. The wife of Henry VIII was the princess of
Spain and the widow of his brother Arthur. This marriage was performed due to political reasons.
Henry VII, the father of Henry VIII, wanted to establish friendly and cordial relations with Spain.
Hence he married his son Arthur with Catherine and after the death of Arthur she was married
to Henry VIII. She was five years senior to Henry VIII in age. Soon their relations grew tense.
It made Catherine very sad.
He requested the Pope for divorce through Wolsey in 1527 but he did not succeed in his
mission because Catherine was very close to Charles V and the Pope was afraid of him. As a

result, he dismissed Cardinal Wolsey and confiscated his property. Now Henry VIII wanted to
keep both the political and religious power in his hands. Moreover, the permission of this marriage
was granted by the Pope Julius II and hence the Pope Clement VII had no right to declare this
marriage null and void.
People of England already had bitter feelings against the Roman Catholic Church and
the corruption of the Pope and they were greatly influenced by the work of Erasmus. The
Lutheranism had also influenced the Cambridge and Oxford schools of thoughts and the
intellectuals. Now Henry VIII was not at all prepared to tolerate the religious authority of the
Pope. So in 1532 the British Parliament passed an Act, according to which sending of money

283
to Pope was declared illegal. In 1532 sending of religious appeals to the Pope was banned.
Henry appointed Crammers, the Archbishop of Canterbury and he declared the marriage
ceremony of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. H.A.L. Fisher writes, “The good and intimate
understanding between the Pope and Henry VIII was sadly disturbed by the use of a great
Divorce Question”.
The fifth Parliament of England declared the marriage of Henry VIII and Anne Bolyn legal
and accepted the divorce. The British Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in A.D.1534. In
1539 Henry VIII got passed the act of Six Articles in the Parliament. According to this Act
severe punishments were awarded to the opponents and the property of the Catholic monasteries
who opposed Henry VIII or had faith in the Pope or were the centres of corruption was
confiscated.
15.5.3 Reformation during the Reign of Edward VI

Henry VIII ruled in England from 1509 to 1547 and was succeeded by his son, Edward VI
in 1547. Crammer got published an English Book of Common Prayer, in 1549 and declared
‘Forty-two Articles of Religion’ in 1522. In these articles the principles of Martin Luther and
Calvinism mingled. It is known as the Second Book of Prayer. After this all prayers and worship
began to be held in English instead of in the Latin language. As a result of the conspiracies of
the Earl of Warwick Somerset was killed in 1551. At that time Edward VI was fifteen years of
age. The Earl of Warwick was made the Duke of Northumberland. He made some reforms in
the Protestant religion. Edward VI died in 1553.
15.5.4 Religious Policy of Mary Tudor
Mary’s succession to the throne was applauded and welcomed by most of the people. No

doubt, Henry VIII broke his relations with the Pope of Rome but according to Warner, Martin
and Muir, he continued to be a Roman Catholic throughout his life, hence people were not
afraid of Mary for her being staunch Catholic but soon she tried to uproot Protestantism from
England. She had a desire that whatever wrongs had been done to Catholicism from A.D. 1529
to 1533 should be mad good. Return to Papacy was her chief mission and in order to achieve
this goal she resorted to two ways to execute her plan.
Thus after restoration of Catholicism in England, Mary started to punish those who opposed
the establishment of supremacy of the Pope in England or who were staunch Protestants. She
reappointed all the suspended Catholic priests and tormented the Protestants so much that

284
she came to be known as ‘Bloody Mary’. She awarded capital punishment to more than 300
Protestant reformers including Latimar, Ridley and Crammer. In 1555 Latimar and Ridley were
burnt alive in Oxford and Crammer was also put to fire in 1556. She was succeeded by Elizabeth,
the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn who ruled from A.D. 1558 -1603.
15.5.5 Religious Policy of Elizabeth Tudor
Religious policy had ever been an acute problem for the Tudor kings. Henry VIII’s religious
policy resulted in a breach with the Roman Church and Mary was called by the name of ‘Bloody
Mary’ due to her fanaticism. She made some changes in the Prayer Book of Crammer. Its 42
terms were reduced to 39. Actually, Protestantism could not be crushed in spite of all the
bloody acts of Mary Tudor and it began to flourish in the reign of Elizabeth as the queen herself

was the follower of Protestant faith. In 1558 she got passed the Act of Uniformity in the Parliament
so that an equal religious system could be provided to all the people. In 1570 the Pope of
Rome excommunicated Elizabeth but she faced him very boldly and punished all the Catholics
who opposed her. Scheville writes that at last Elizabeth succeeded in establishing and
consolidating the Anglican Church. It made for midway between Catholicism and Protestantism.
15.6 Reformation in France
Like other countries the Reformation created a great upheaval in the religious sphere of
France also. Calvinism and Lutheranism were the result of the preaching’s of the followers of
John Calvin and Martin Luther. Actually, the Protestantism which was started in Switzerland
by Zwingli was reawakened and given an international form by John Calvin. Thus Calvin

wanted to bring about a change in the Church altogether and root out the corruption.
John Calvin was born in 1509 at Noyens in France. His father wanted to make him a
priest for which he was provided training in Theology in Paris University for some time. After
this he was sent to Orleans University for the study of law because his father later thought the
study of law to be more beneficial for his son than any other subject. But all of a sudden, in
1533 he joined the new faith. H.A.L. Fisher mentions that the personal life of Calvin was pure
and controlled. He restricted his desire and aimed to attain his high ideals through penance.
Gradually, the number of his followers increased. Calvin wrote Institutes of Christian Religion
for the good of people. It was based on logic and it greatly influenced the people. Calvin

offering this book to Francis I wanted to bring Francis I to the fold of Protestantism but he could
not succeed.

285
In 1536 Calvin went to Geneva. Soon he became very popular in Geneva due to his
ability and people began to obey his commands. He imparted the lesson of morality to his
followers, and those who acted otherwise were severely punished. It created discontentment
among his followers and he had to leave Geneva in 1538. In 1541 Calvin again went to Geneva
on the invitation of his followers and he made Geneva the chief centre of Protestant religion by
his hard labour and devotion. A university was established in Geneva 1539, the credit for which
goes to Calvin, where students came from far and near to get higher education. W.Stubbs
praise him thus, “Thus leading conception of Calvin’s Theology was his faith in the absolute
supremacy of God’s will”. He died in 1546.
15.6.1 Principles of Calvin
1. Calvin believed that God was omnipresent and omnipotent. He believed that salvation

can only be attained by the grace of God.
2. Calvin was a fatalist. He used to believe, ‘what is fated cannot be blotted’. Hence some
people suffered throughout life while the others enjoyed life. There could be no equality in
the world because some were born in high and prosperous families whereas others in
poor families.
John Calvin Ulrich Zwingli
3. He considered that the state and religion were two different things. He did not like the
interference of state in the Protestant religion. Similarly, he wished that the church should
not interfere in the matters of state.
4. Calvin gave democratic structure to church. He preached that religious issues should be

286
settled by the religious authorities in consultation with the people. He also gave due regards
to Presbyters, hence a sect known as Presbyterianism came into being.
5. Calvin had a firm faith in the Bible. He preached that the people should lead their life
according to the teachings of the Bible. He did not pay much heed to rituals and stressed
that the priest had nothing to do between God and the devotees.
6. He believed in morality and laid stress on leading a moral and sacred life. He did not like
the people who believed in magic and totems and was completely against corruption and
licentious life.
7. Calvin was a great disciplinarian. He forced the people of Geneva to lead a strict disciplined
life. He formed a committee known as Consistory which kept a watch on the conduct of
people and punished all those who acted otherwise.

8. Calvin was intolerant towards all who did not go hand in hand with him. Calvin gave death
punishment to a doctor of Spain who did not agree with him but about the existence of
God. A.J.Grant writes about his death, “Servetus came to Geneva and hoped for a
disputation with Calvin. But Calvin had already declared him worthy of death for his
heresies. He was deported to Geneva by the Perrinist party but on his arrival was arrested,
tried by the civic authorities and on their sentence and with the approval of other Swiss
Churches, burnt in October 1553”.
15.6.2 Expansion of Calvinism in other Countries
Besides France, Calvinism spread in Brandenburg, Vaden, and coastal province of Rhine.
It also expanded in Switzerland, Holland, Scotland, Hungary and Poland. England was also a
centre of Calvinism. The Protestant Huguenots of France were greatly influenced by Calvinism

and the Presbyterian Church of Scotland was a similar sect of Calvinism.
15.6.3 Consequence and Influence of Calvinism
Calvinism influenced Europe to a great extent and its consequence proved far-reaching.
1. Calvin had staunch faith in God and the Bible. He wanted to remove all rituals and religious
dogmas for which he had great enthusiasm.
2. Calvin could oppose the Catholics due to solidarity of the character. When Lutheranism
became quite weak and feeble, Calvinism injected new vigour into the people.

287
3. Calvin stressed democratic organization of the church. Presbyterianism was the foundation
stone of democratic system. In the organization of Calvinism beside the priests, some
other persons were also included who used to solve the religious problems jointly.
4. Calvinists directed their followers to follow the path of truth and oppose all that was against
religion. It created feelings of love and sacrifice among them and they could cross all the
hurdles successfully.
5. Calvinism created new courage and enthusiasm among the Protestants of Holland. A
feeling of sacrifice for the safety of their religion was ushered in, in them and they revolted
against the torturous ruler Philip II of Holland and a republic was established there.
6. John Noax, a priest of Scotland was greatly influenced by Calvinism. He established
Presbyterianism in Scotland which was the other form of Calvinism.

7. Calvinism also influenced the Protestants of England and Puritans opposed the autocratic
rule of the Stuart dynasty and put an effective check on its despotism and autocracy.
A.J.Grant writes, “It was the Calvinists of France who nearly brought Protestantism in
victory there”.
8. Owing to the influence of Calvinism the Huguenots of France also continued a prolonged
struggle against their autocratic rulers.
9. Besides this, Calvinism laid stress on the significance of labour and accelerated production.
10. According to the terms of the Treaty of Augsburg (1555) both Roman Catholic and
Protestant religions were recognized in Germany and Calvinism was not included in it.
11. Calvinism separated the church and the state and gave rise to secularism. People felt
that the king had no right to impose his own religion on his people and the king should

never interfere in the matter of the church and the religion.
15.7 Reformation in other countries of Europe
Martin Luther’s opposition to Roman Catholic Church was the most significant event in
the history of Europe. He pointed out towards the defects of Roman Catholic Church. The
religious movement of Martin Luther not only affected Germany and England but also influenced
the other European countries. Moreover, it also became quite clear even before the death of

288
Martin Luther that the results on which he arrived might be accepted by those who condemned
the corruption rampant in the Roman Catholic Church and had faith in the Bible.
15.7.1 Reformation Movement in Scandinavia
Denmark, Norway and Sweden were included in Scandinavia. The political development
of this region was the chief cause of Reformation here. All these three countries were ruled by
one ruler; hence they were included into one unit for quite a long time. Like other countries, the
power of the church was greater than that of the kings. In 1513 Christian II became the ruler of
Scandinavia. Being under the influence of his mother he decided to uproot the influence and
power of the feudal lords. It hurt the Pope and the Catholicism very deeply. The property of the
Church was confiscated and spent for public works of the empire. The revolt against the rulers

of Sweden and Norway gave birth to Reformation. The revolutionaries of Sweden thought it
worthwhile to confiscate the property of the Church for the progress of revolution under the
leadership of Gustavas Vasa. Thus in the Scandinavian countries the reformation could be
successful, as a result of which the power of the Church and the feudal lords could be destroyed
and the rulers gathered power.
15.7.2 Reformation Movement in Switzerland
The Swiss confederation had obtained freedom even during the reign of Miaximillian.
Democratic system of Government was in vogue in these states. Humanism could develop in
these states due to liberal government. Like other countries the reformation influenced
Switzerland too. Ulrich Zwingli was the person who made the Reformation successful in the
country. He was born on January 1, 1484. Like Martin Luther he opposed the sale of indulgences

and put forth the evils of the Church before the people. After becoming the priest of Zurich,
Zwingli started his reformation movement.
The opposition of Zwingli was based on political reasons and hence the influence of
politics on the reformation was bound to occur. He also endeavoured to reorganize the federal
constitution. His religious views were more revolutionary than of Martin Luther. W. Stubbs
opines, “His views about religion were more revolutionary than those of Martin Luther because
he was in favour of complete independence about religious matters”.
Actually, his views were motivated by the contemporary political system. Zwingli wanted
to grant freedom to every unit in the mattes of religion. Hence here too, a civil war broke out
between the supporters of Catholicism and Zwinglianism. A fierce battle was fought at Cappel

289
in 1531 in which Ulrich Zwingli was killed along with a large number of supporters. Scheville
also opines that it was decided in the treaty after the battle that it was permitted to adopt any
religion of its own choice. Consequently, Switzerland also became Catholic like Germany up to
some extent.
15.7.3 Comparison between Lutheranism and Zwinglianism
Luther was the leader of reformation of Germany and Zwingli led the reformation of
Switzerland. Both tried to uproot the dogmas, corruption and evils which were rampant in
Catholic Church so that the people could follow the path of truth and attain spiritual peace. He
believed in communication whereas Zwingli considered it merely as a token principle. The
difference between the two went on increasing with the passage of time. They condemned and
criticized each other and unity could not be established between the two. It was made all the

more powerful by his supporters after the death of Zwingli.
15.8 Counter Reformation
Martin Luther opposed the evils and dogmas rampant in the Catholic Church very firmly.
His statement was based on truth and reality and hence his reformation movement earned the
sympathy of the people and spread in entire Europe rapidly. Martin Luther, Ulrich Zwingli and
John Calvin exposed all the evils and corruption of the Roman Catholic Church before the
people. Hayes has written about it that the movement of sixteenth century which took place to
check the progress and development of Protestantism came to be known as Counter
Reformation. Scheville writes,”The movement known as Counter Reformation was really
reformation applied to the Catholic Church”.
Southgate writes about Counter Reformation that “the aim of Catholic Reformation was

to re-establish the sanctity of the Roman Catholic Church and its high ideals. Owing to the
election of the new Popes the defects of Catholic Church were removed by the latter half of the
16th century and Catholicism had been reformed. Various sects and classes of Catholic Church
proved significant to make the Counter Reformation a success”.
The following factors contributed to the outbreak of Counter Reformation:
15.8.1 Expansion of Protestantism
Martin Luther opposed the evils and corruption rampant in Roman Catholic religion in
Germany. Later on, this movement became quite extensive. It created confusion in the minds

290
of the Catholics and they decided to make some reforms in their religion in order to keep it in
existence.
15.8.2 Mutual Difference of the Catholics
Fortunately, when the Catholics tried to make reforms in their religion the circumstances
were quite favourable. Martin Luther was the originator of Protestant religion. With the passage
of time, his differences grew with the preachers of other countries. It divided Protestantism into
three categories. Lutheranism also gave birth to Zwinglianism and Calvinism. Their mutual
differences inspired the Catholics to amend their own religion and re-establish its lost prestige.
15.8.3 Internal Reforms in Catholic Religion
Shortcomings of Catholic religion were the main factors contributing to the growth and
progress of Protestantism. The adjective ‘Protestantism’ was used for the religion which opposed
Catholicism in Europe. The clergy were inspired by their lives. Keeping in view the idea of

291
reforms, a committee was organized at Trent which worked for 18 years in order to remove the
evils rampant in the Roman Catholic religion.
15.8.4 Establishment of New Institutions
As soon as the followers of Catholicism realized that reforms were necessary for the
existence of Roman Catholic religion, they devoted themselves to this great task. In order to
make this work easy and practical they founded Jesuits’ Society, Trent Council, Inquisition and
various other institutions for the good of Catholicism.
15.8.5 Preachers of Catholic Religion
Fortunately, the Catholic could find some such preachers in their religion who really wanted
to reform Catholicism. All these persons belonged to high category and were very influential.
Among these persons the name of Ignatius Loyola was the most famous. Moreover, he became

lame on account of his wounds that he sustained in the battlefield and became unfit for the
military services; hence he studied theology and philosophy for some years in Paris University
and established Society of Jesuits, Trent Council and Religious Inquisition which helped a lot in
reforming the Roman Catholic religion.
15.8.6 Working of Jesuit’s Society and Ignatius Loyola
Jesuits’ Society of Ignatius Loyola was one of the active institutions which worked for
the good of Roman Catholic religion. Soon he was summoned by his followers. Among them
Francis Xavier and Iago were his most devoted disciples. Hence the Pope got the support and
cooperation of this institution at a very appropriate time, when his power was on the verge of
declining. The followers of this society had taken a vow to follow, the orders of the Pope Paul

III in 1540 and after getting his approval, Loyola organized a powerful movement for the
reformation of Roman Catholic religion. The working of this department was divided into 12
sections in which Japan and China were also included.
The chief characteristic of this society was strict discipline and complete surrender to the
Pope. Ignatius Loyola had composed a book of ‘Spiritual Exercise’ for the daily routine of the
followers of Jesuits’ Society. Hayes has written about it that “it was like a military organization
for religious work, the members of which were the devoted soldiers of the Pope”.

292

The members of Jesuits’ Society tried to inject new life into Catholicism by their acts of

2. The religious authorities were directed to lead a life of simplicity, truthfulness and purity.
